Katalog Berita (Halaman 8/58)

#10022. Docker has always used microVMs (well, since 2016)

There's a lot of buzz about "microVMs", where a workload runs with a stripped down Linux kernel, on a minimalist VMM such as firecracker on top of a hypervisor like KVM or Xen. MicroVMs are often contrasted to, and considered more secure than, traditional Linux Docker containers. What if I told you that Docker Desktop has always used microVMs? (since 2016)

Unikernels can be considered an early form of microVM. Rather than booting a full Linux kernel on a full VMM, a unikernel links an app with only the drivers, filesystems and subsystems it actually needs; other code is omitted. For example a MirageOS unikernel app would have no processes, probably no filesystem, only one vCPU. Certainly no ssh or shell (unless you really want those). The VMM that hosts the Mirage unikernel was also minimal (see Solo5 and mirage-solo5 ). No legacy required. We were so confident in the security of the system that we ran a bitcoin pinata offering 10BTC to any hacker able to claim it. The BTC went unclaimed.

Boot can be really fast too: the "Just-In-Time Summoning of Unikernels" project (paper, code) optimized x86 VM creation time down to about 20ms (120ms on an underpowered 2015 ARM dev board)

The main (obvious) downside of unikernels is having to link your app with a bunch of kernel code. A lot of people would like to run existing Linux programs!

While we were developing Unikernels, Docker was busy inventing the modern form of Linux containers and revolutionising how software is built, shared and run. Docker acquired Unikernel Systems in 2016 and we combined the best of Unikernels (microVMs) and Linux containers into Docker for Mac (later Docker Desktop).

A vertically integrated OS: applications take responsibility for much of their own system code.

The SOSP paper describes the Xen hypervisor, the foundation of the public cloud.

Bromium's co-founder and CTO uses the term micro-VM for a hardware-isolated task, such as opening a document or browsing a web page, with access restricted to the resources it needs.

The ASPLOS paper: compile an application and its OS libraries into a specialised VM image.

10 BTC offered for breaking a MirageOS TLS unikernel. The bounty remained unclaimed in June’s review.

The Jitsu paper: boot an x86 unikernel on demand in response to a network request.

Lightweight VMs for container workloads: kvmtool on KVM, direct Linux boot without BIOS or UEFI, and virtio devices. Intel reports startup under 150ms with roughly 18–20MB of memory overhead.

A skunkworks project to bring Docker to more developers, and Docker's first use of unikernel technology. Solomon Hykes recalled its origins in 2018.

The MirageOS and Xen expertise behind Unikernel Systems joins Docker.

Uses a microVM system: Mirage libraries in the VMM, a minimal Linux kernel and minimal Linux userspace (later open-sourced as LinuxKit).

Containers run inside a minimal Linux VM, with HyperKit and MirageOS libraries on the host.

Combines Intel Clear Containers and Hyper's runV to run container workloads in lightweight VMs. In Kata's Kubernetes model, each pod runs in its own VM, with its containers sharing the guest Linux kernel.

AWS announces its minimal KVM-based VMM for serverless workloads.

A separate locked-down microVM and Docker daemon for each coding agent session with support for governance.

Our priority back then wasn't to add microVMs to Docker for their own sake. Instead our goal was to make Docker feel like a native app on Mac and Windows, rather than a bundle of components. Using our Mirage Unikernel libraries we started building a "library VMM": a VMM which could be embedded inside the Docker application, and which would be single purpose, minimal, secure and fast. The first version was called hyperkit (a fork of xhyve, itself derived from bhyve ). We linked the C code directly with the MirageOS block layer and used the Mirage userspace TCP/IP stack in a gvisor-like network stack vpnkit. The VMM code continues to evolve and is now called Docker VMM.1

The VM kernel and root filesystem were minimal too, based on the LinuxKit project. The current version is an even more slimmed down and efficient variant but conceptually the same, similar to containerd/nerdbox.

Docker for Mac began in 2015 as Project Piñata, a skunkworks project to make Docker useful to more developers. In this 2018 tweet, Solomon Hykes recalls Docker's first use of unikernel technology and the collaboration between Paris, Cambridge and San Francisco:

“It was our first use of Unikernel tech, and our first Paris/Cambridge/SF collaboration.”

For Docker for Mac (later renamed Docker Desktop) this allowed:

Here's the OG 2015 Docker for Mac beta installation experience:

The Docker microVM tech is the foundation of both Docker Desktop and also Docker Sandboxes (why microVMs), where each sandbox runs in a separate microVM, completely isolated from each other and the host. Docker Sandboxes enables you to do things like run your favourite coding agent and harness securely, with strict isolation and governance.

To see what Docker microVM's can do, install Docker Sandboxes (sbx) and try `sbx run claude`.

To read more about the history of the tech, check out the article A Decade of Docker Containers (Communications of the ACM).

1 Although we were aiming to make everything a library and link into a static unikernel-like process, for technical reasons it makes sense to still have a single host process per VM. ↩

#10021. Chrome zero-day whack-a-mole continues as 2026 tally hits 8

Another Chrome memory bug gets squashed, but not before attackers got their hands on it

Google has patched its eighth actively exploited Chrome zero-day of 2026, matching its total for the whole of last year with nearly two months still left on the calendar.

The latest flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-125350, is a high-severity use-after-free vulnerability in Chrome's XML component. Google confirmed in a security advisory published Monday that attackers are already exploiting the bug, although it hasn't said who's behind the attacks or who might be getting targeted.

"Google is aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," the company said, offering little else about the attacks.

The vulnerability was reported anonymously on November 6 and involves a memory management error that occurs when software continues using a pointer to memory that has already been freed. Such bugs can potentially allow attackers to corrupt memory and execute malicious code, although Google hasn't disclosed how this particular flaw is being exploited.

Google is keeping further technical details under wraps until enough users have installed the fix, a familiar approach intended to stop other attackers from getting their hands on a working exploit.

The patch arrives in Chrome 157.0.8103.50/.51 for Windows and macOS, and 157.0.8103.50 for Linux. The update also addresses eight other security vulnerabilities, including high-severity flaws affecting WebGL, FileSystem, GPU, Compositing, and the V8 JavaScript engine.

The release fixes another use-after-free bug in Chrome's XML component, CVE-2026-125346, which was reported by Arni Hardarson of Neonix Security in October, though Google hasn't indicated that this second vulnerability is being exploited.

The latest discovery adds to what's becoming a rather long list of Chrome zero-days this year. By June, Google had already patched five actively exploited Chrome zero-days, including flaws in its V8 JavaScript engine, Skia graphics library, and WebGPU implementation. The list has only grown since then, with two more V8 bugs fixed in September and the latest XML vulnerability bringing the total to eight.

That puts 2026 level with 2025, when Google also fixed eight Chrome zero-days exploited in the wild. Whether the browser maker can make it through the remaining weeks of the year without adding another to the pile is anyone's guess.

Google says the latest update will roll out over the coming days and weeks, but users can check manually by heading to Chrome's Settings menu and selecting About Chrome. With attackers already making use of the vulnerability, it's probably worth doing that sooner rather than waiting for Chrome to get around to it. ®

#10019. Two apps one process

So what if you can handle thousands of concurrent users per core? Even the front page of HN gets you what? 100 concurrent users on a good day?

Exactly! Most successful apps have like what 10 or 20 concurrent users at any given time? This is basically academic for most projects. What does performance give you other than knowing that your app won't need to scale past a single server? Pointless!

Well what if you could run multiple apps in one process?

Isn't that the same as a bunch of apps behind a reverse proxy?

No. It's not. Separate processes have to compete for OS resources, have their own thread pools, schedulers, heap, GC, caches and so on. Each process needs to be sized relative to the other apps running on the system.

But, in a single process you can size the process for the machine and then run an arbitrary number of apps in that process. If the apps share a process, they can share all sorts of things: a single JVM, GC, caches, buffers, http server, HTTPS certificate management, batching, game loop etc. You'd eliminate thread contention between apps. This lets you scale further with less resources!

Performance lets you run as many apps as you want in that one process.

Disclaimer: all my writing and code is handcrafted by me. By the end of this you may wish it wasn't.

If you have multiple JVMs you duplicate a bunch of fixed costs:

If you have multiple HTTP servers you duplicate:

If you have multiple framework engines you duplicate:

All of this adds up to more memory, more threads and more contention. If you own all your app and don't need the isolation a processes give you, then it can be a big performance win to have one JVM, one http server, and one framework engine.

X * n where X is you fixed cost for the above and n is your number of apps. If all of the above takes 500MB, then four apps is an extra 1.5GB.

Indeed. If you think about it an app at it's simplest is a domain, a database and some routes.

But, my reverse proxy handles HTTPS certs and stuff! Where is your god now?

Yes certs are a pain. But Clave: Automatic HTTPS certificate management and renewal via ACME, implemented in pure Clojure with minimal dependencies exists. I use it with aleph. But, it also works with jetty and it's simple to extend to other servers.

To bundle our apps we import them as dependencies into a separate project who's only purpose is to configure and start the server.

So adding a new app is as simple as importing it and adding it to the list of apps:

We can then build this project as an uberjar and scp it to the server.

Well this is nice and all, but whenever you deploy an app, you restart the process. DOWNTIME! UNACCEPTABLE!

Here's a gif of me deploying the jar to production:

If a deploy is indistinguishable from network blip did the app really go down?

That's it. We've reduced the overhead and cost of deploying a new app to zero.

Code can be found here. All three apps are running on the same JVM, on the same 10$ VPS , here, here and here.

Thanks to Everyone on the Datastar discord who read drafts of this and gave me feedback.

#10017. Fresh European Fridge Attacks Put Cold-Chain Security in Focus

Beyond food storage, the same combination of Internet connectivity, remote access, and inadequate security practices can put temperature-controlled infrastructure across other critical sectors at risk.

A second wave of attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe this week has heightened concerns about the broader "cold chain's" vulnerability to similar attacks, given that supermarkets aren't the only businesses that rely on cold storage.

As in mid-October, an unknown threat actor appears to have gained access to refrigeration controllers at multiple European supermarkets and switched the systems to defrost mode, raising temperatures to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) and causing food spoilage.

Reporting by the BBC, Reuters, CNBC, and other outlets suggests the latest attacks were smaller in scope compared with the first wave in October that affected more than 700 retail and grocery stores, primarily in France. A smaller number of stores in Belgium, Germany, the Netherlands, Portugal, Poland and Spain were also caught up in the October attacks.

Related:Why Europe's Freezer Hacks Spread So Far, So Fast

BBC reported the new attacks as impacting "dozens of supermarkets" in seven European countries including Belgium, Luxembourg, Estonia, Ireland, Sweden and Finland. Spokespersons from several supermarket chains that include France's Carrefour, Belgium's Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt Group, and Sweden's Coop chains confirmed varying but relatively limited impacts from the new attacks.

In a Nov. 2 statement, Carrefour said a cyberattack targeting its refrigeration systems had impacted 15 out of 700 stores in Belgium. In an undated statement, US-based Copeland, which manufactures technologies for regulating commercial refrigeration systems, alluded to a cybersecurity incident affecting refrigeration systems in France, which it said related to a discontinued generation of supervisory controllers.

No individual or group has claimed responsibility for either the first or the second wave of attacks, and the motivation behind it remains a mystery. European authorities are currently investigating the attacks.

Researchers, including those at France's CERT, have linked the hacks so far to Internet-connected refrigeration controllers made by Denmark-based Danfoss, Italy-based Dixell, and Copeland. Organizations using these controllers often connect them to the Internet to enable remote maintenance and support, but in doing so also potentially expose them to unauthorized access and remote attack by threat actors.

Risks include unpatched vulnerabilities in these technologies that attackers can exploit, like three in Danfoss' AK-SM 800A controllers that researchers at Claroty disclosed this August and another two they reported the same month in Copeland controllers. Weak configurations and poor security hygiene are other major problems.

Related:Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour

"Misconfigurations and systemic hygiene failures represent the vast majority of the threat surface," says John Gallagher, vice president at operational technology (OT) and Internet of Things (IoT) security vendor Viakoo. "While unpatched vulnerabilities exist in older firmware, they are rendered dangerous only because basic architectural hygiene was skipped, especially [when] making them Internet-facing."

Common mistakes that include widespread use of default passwords, vendor-shared service codes, or static credentials across hundreds of locations make brute-forcing trivial, Gallagher adds.

The weaknesses are not confined to supermarket refrigeration systems. The same combination of Internet connectivity, remote access, and inadequate security practices can put temperature-controlled infrastructure across other critical sectors at risk, according to security experts.

Sean Tufts, field chief technology officer (CTO) at Claroty, points out that "pharmaceutical storage and distribution, food distribution centers, and industrial facilities all rely on connected operational technology to maintain precise environmental conditions."

Related:AI Takes Control of Robotic Arm in 16 Minutes Flat

The level of exposure will vary depending on how these systems are deployed, connected, and secured. But many organizations that rely on remotely accessible refrigeration or temperature-control equipment face similar challenges around asset visibility, third-party access, and securing legacy systems, Tufts says. "The same types of weaknesses can exist across different industries, even if the equipment and operational requirements differ."

The potential consequences of a compromise, Tufts says, can vary by sector.

"A disruption to pharmaceutical storage could compromise temperature-sensitive medicines, while an incident affecting food distribution could lead to spoilage and supply chain disruptions," he notes. "Industrial environments may face additional operational consequences depending on the materials and processes involved."

The supermarket attacks are a reminder that refrigeration and temperature-control systems are part of essential operations and not just back-of-house equipment, Tufts adds. Organizations should identify these assets and know how they connect to the Internet and third parties.

"Where remote access is necessary, use a VPN, strong authentication, or a centralized secure-access tool with session tracking." Changing default passwords, keeping firmware current, and segmenting are also recommended security practices, he says.

Gallagher says that while it's unclear how the attacks on the commercial refrigeration systems played out, the most straightforward theory is the threat actor likely compiled a target list by scanning the public Internet for specific controller fingerprints, such as those tied to Danfoss, Dixell, and Copeland. They then likely deployed an automated script across that target list to exploit known web vulnerabilities or push default credentials, triggering the defrost mode simultaneously.

Gallagher says the same attacks that worked on commercial refrigeration systems can potentially work across almost any form of OT and IoT systems. That's because these systems often are managed outside of IT, lack automated controls to keep firmware and passwords updated, and have porous network borders. "The growth over the last three years in operational ransomware and in cyberattacks causing physical damage shows that these attacks are on the rise and not specific to any one kind of system."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#10016. MosaicLeaks: Can your research agent keep a secret?

A research agent at a healthcare firm is working through a routine question, and along the way it fires off a handful of ordinary-looking web searches. One references a cloud-migration milestone, one a January 2024 security disclosure, one narrows down which vendor got hit. No single query necessarily gives away the whole secret. But anyone watching the agent's outbound traffic can reassemble the fragments: MediConn had migrated 70% of its infrastructure to the cloud by January 2025, a fact that lived only in private documents. This is the mosaic effect, and it's the failure mode at the centre of MosaicLeaks.

MosaicLeaks treats those web queries as the leakage channel: the adversary never sees the private documents or the agent's reasoning, only the cumulative query log, and tries to infer private enterprise information from it.

We measure leakage in three ways, depending on what the adversary can infer from the observed queries:

These three represent increasing levels of concern. Intent leakage reveals what the agent is investigating. Answer leakage means the query log holds enough to answer a private question someone already has in hand. Full-information leakage is the strongest case: the observer can discover and state private facts without being told what to look for.

How the mosaic effect drives MosaicLeaks's three leakage measures: Intent (predict the research questions), Answer (answer given questions about the private documents), and Full-Information (state verifiably true private claims). Here the agent searches twice about Lee's Market's 2020 traffic growth, leaking its intent, then issues a third query to answer a follow-up. Each query looks benign alone, but seen together they let an observer deduce that the answer was 15%, and so claim that Lee's online traffic grew 15% in 2020.

Each chain interleaves local and web sub-questions. The answer to one sub-question becomes a bridge entity in the next, so the agent must retrieve local information before it can form the next useful web query. Local documents come from DRBench-style enterprise tasks, and web documents come from BrowseComp-Plus. The final split contains 559 training chains, 98 validation chains, and 344 held-out-company test chains.

The final web hop doesn't inherently contain any private information and can be answered from public web documents. However, because the path to it depends on private local facts, a query that carries forward "MediConn", "70%", and "January" gives the adversary enough context to recover internal information.

We use a simplified agent harness adapted from DRBench. The model answers each sub-question with a short answer and justification, allowing us to evaluate each hop individually with normalized string matching.

At each iteration, the model can use four tools. Plan produces local and web search queries, which are executed and returned as document cards. Choose selects which retrieved documents to read. Read attempts to answer the current hop from each selected document in parallel. Resolve decides whether to answer, read more documents, or plan another search.

One agent rollout. Each row is a hop, labeled local (L) or web (W) with its accepted answer. The colored blocks show the wall-clock time spent planning, retrieving, choosing, reading, and resolving that hop.

The obvious fix is to just ask. Add a line to the Plan prompt telling the agent not to issue web queries that leak local information, and see what happens to performance, leakage, and query behavior.

The prompt helps slightly for some models, but its effect is inconsistent and significant leakage remains. It also often has a negative effect on task performance. For Qwen3-4B, the prompt lowers answer/full-information leakage from 34.0% to 25.5%, but strict chain success drops from 48.7% to 44.5%. The primary behavioral change appears to be fewer web queries, not consistently safer query construction.

The first is a situational task reward. A single research trajectory can run to dozens of model calls, so giving them all the same final trajectory score is very weak credit: a successful run can reinforce a leaky search, and a failed run can punish a locally sound decision. Instead, we judge each call against other calls made at the same stage and hop, with the same information available. A Plan call is rewarded for searching the correct source and retrieving the right document; if that document is already in hand, it is rewarded for not searching again. A Choose call is rewarded for selecting the document that holds the answer. We train these stages because their desired behavior can be checked directly.

Task-only RL improves research performance but increases leakage. PA-DR keeps almost all of the performance gain while sharply reducing it.

And it did not get safer by simply searching less. PA-DR actually issues more web queries than the base model, but those queries drop the revealing details: specific metrics like "15%" or "2024", and clues about the kind of answer it is looking for. The agent still finds the right public documents. It just stops carrying private fragments along in the query text.

Training efficiency. The final column is how many generated samples each method needs to reach ~55% strict chain success. Lower is better.

Situational rewards reach outcome-reward-level task success using roughly 5-6x fewer generated samples. PA-DR keeps the sample-efficiency benefit while sharply reducing leakage.

MosaicLeaks is a controlled benchmark, not a measurement of leakage in deployed systems. The enterprise documents are synthetic, the web corpus is fixed, the chains span three company contexts, and every result comes from a single agent harness running multi-hop question answering rather than open-ended research. That control is what makes leakage measurable hop by hop, but broader tasks, real deployments, and other agent designs still need their own study.

Fascinating work on the mosaic effect. It makes me wonder how PA-DR holds up when agents are deployed for active threat intelligence or software auditing. For instance, if an enterprise research agent is tasked with analyzing potential security vectors or reverse-engineering third-party mobile apps from repositories like https://toemodapk.com, its web-query logs could easily leak proprietary internal app versions or specific device compliance criteria to an outside observer. Teaching agents to scrub those granular technical identifiers during deep web retrieval is going to be massive for operational security.

#10015. Stanford's century-long AI study admits it's already out of date

Five-year review charts upheaval in work, science, and public life – with little consensus on who's in control

Twelve years into Stanford's 100-year study of artificial intelligence, the project's third report raises more questions than it answers.

The 2026 AI100 Study Panel report acknowledges its limitations in its twelfth takeaway: "This report will be out of date by the time you read it."

But it's nonetheless a worthwhile exercise for those who haven't been paying close attention to the development of machine learning over the past few years and for policymakers who may benefit from a review of AI's metastatic growth.

"The last five years constitute a watershed moment in the history of AI," said Professor Sheila McIlraith, chair of the AI100 Standing Committee, in a statement. "This report examines what led to the extraordinary capabilities of today's AI systems, and how they are reshaping society. As we look ahead, we anticipate continued increase in AI capabilities alongside transformative advances in science and medicine.

"Rapid change will challenge governments and industry to support and safeguard our people, our institutions, and our critical infrastructure. Both the benefits and the risks of AI technologies require the same clear-eyed scrutiny."

Established in 2014, the One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence (AI100) is overseen by a Standing Committee of AI experts and administered by Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI). It's charged with producing reports every five years, the first of which debuted in 2016.

The 2026 report's other key points highlight the transformation brought about by increasingly capable machine learning software.

It identifies scaling as the engine of AI's advance, but also points to the growing cost and difficulty of obtaining training data as constraints on further progress.

The report likens AI's disruptive potential to that of the World Wide Web – without dwelling on the irony that the web itself is among the things being disrupted. It points to creative industries, computer programming, and mathematics as fields once deemed beyond the reach of automation that are now being upended.

Science, the report says, is being transformed by AI as it accelerates research timelines and opens up novel challenges. At the same time, the report cautions that "we will need to understand how AI-mediated information environments reshape collective cognition and moral behavior." The recent retraction of some 1,400 scholarly papers for failure to meet academic standards highlights the urgency of that message.

Then there's the AI investment boom and "fears of a financial bubble," which won't be assuaged by recent NASDAQ volatility and revelations about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged intelligence operative for China.

Concerns about the concentration of frontier AI development, the pressure AI puts on cybersecurity, and the active use of AI for military applications are also noted in the report.

So too are worries about what AI-generated media does to trust.

Item nine on the report's takeaway list is perhaps the most noteworthy: "AI is reshaping the lives of billions of people, yet the public has had little say in how it is developed and deployed."

The recent US midterms suggest voters are finding ways to make themselves heard about AI datacenters, even if that falls short of shaping broader AI policy.

Item ten posits that longstanding academic concerns about AI bias, ethics, and safety are beginning to converge with what until recently seemed like worries inspired by speculative fiction, such as AI agents hacking into companies without human oversight.

And item 11 frames the entire report by calling out the lack of a coherent regulatory response to AI: "AI governance is fragmented and increasingly framed in terms of national security, with little international consensus among states on its direction."

Those takeaways introduce the AI100 Study Panel's examination of 12 standing questions about what AI makes possible and how humans are handling it. Easy answers are in short supply.

But as the report's disclosure section makes clear, even the people taking the century-long view are using the technology to assess itself.

"Reflecting the progress in AI over the period this report covers, AI tools were used extensively in its production," the report explains.

"The report was written by humans, and its authors used AI primarily to transcribe and summarize meetings, support dictation, and check drafts for typos, consistency, duplication, tone, and structure. In some cases, AI suggested rewording of human-written text. AI was also used to compare this report with previous AI100 reports, identifying where expectations and reality have diverged or converged over five years. After completion, AI tools checked for inadvertent plagiarism and signs of AI-generated content." ®

#10013. The race to secure record-like information for domains

It’s sort of surprising, but we’re still figuring out how to secure simple, record-like information for domain names in an application-accessible way.

Think about it. How would you bind the following to a domain name?

Since we’re talking about domain names, lets start with DNS. The classic solution adds configuration as TXT records:

Notice that we use an underscored subdomain label to make it clear we aren’t talking about a hostname. The protocol name is then repeated to make it abundantly clear this record is related to the protocol.

As is, we can’t claim this solution is secure. DNS-based network interference is trivial and widespread. The best practice for securing DNS records is DNSSEC, which uses cryptographic signing.

I’m not going to debate the security properties of DNSSEC in this post. There are strong opinions on both sides and the most helpful answer likely depends on the context in which you work. For the sake of this blog post I’ll wave my hands and call this “secure enough” to side-step the issue. In any case, the rest of the post doesn’t depend on a favorable or unfavorable assessment of the security properties of DNSSEC.

Even the strongest supporters of DNSSEC need to face the reality that DNSSEC isn’t widely adopted.

There’s no single answer that quantifies DNSSEC adoption. At Fox Loop Software I collect adoption metrics for various Internet protocols; we just released the first dashboard. Our approach highlights that adoption rates vary widely depending on which cohort you measure. For example, here are the adoption rates of DNSSEC signed MX records among second-level domain names that accept email:

From the perspective of an application developer, it is not reasonable to expect that a customer domain name will support DNSSEC. Until this changes, application developers must use alternate solutions if they need security.

If my application is web-based then there’s a pretty obvious solution as I already have an HTTPS secured endpoint. I can use the HTTPS .well-known approach (RFC 8615).

These records are secured by HTTPS. The developer experience is excellent: adding a record could be as easy as dropping a file in a web server directory. Fetching records is a simple HTTP GET request.

But not everything is a web-based application. Can we extend this solution to other protocols?

Email is a very old protocol, predating not only TLS but the entire Internet as well. Over time all sorts of additions have been bolted on to modernize and maintain the protocol. Many of these additions added new DNS TXT records, such as SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. These records can be secured by DNSSEC but do not require it, so tampering of these records is unmitigated or otherwise tolerated.

Let’s look past these examples to a problem that clearly requires a secure record.

Email has an awkward problem, which is how hostnames are managed. When a message transfer agent (MTA) relays an email it needs to discover the destination MTA. This is solved using an MX record, which specifies the target MTA’s domain name. I’ve measured that around 80% of domains host their email on a different domain name, often using providers like Google or Microsoft.

When sending an email, the MTA will discover a chain from the user’s email address to the receiving MTA’s TLS certificate, like this:

The sending MTA now needs to decide if it trusts the connection. Unfortunately, smtp.provider.com, as seen in the TLS certificate, does not match example.com, as provided in the email address. The only link between the two domain names is an MX record, which typically unsigned and therefor insecure. Without trustworthy information, certificate validation cannot succeed and the sending MTA must skip validation.

Lack of certificate validation means that receiving MTAs can use a self-signed, expired, or even a certificate with the wrong name; the sending MTA does not care. This approach is known as “opportunistic encryption” and it provides strong protection against passive eavesdropping. But without a way to validate the receiving MTA’s TLS certificate, active attacks remained unmitigated.

Email cannot enforce authenticated MTA-to-MTA transit encryption until this hostname mis-match problem is solved in a secure way.

Many email security conversations focus on end-to-end encryption. It is a great solution to many of the security problems facing email, but it doesn’t fully address the problem being discussed here.

Message relaying requires the MTA to know the recipient’s email address. This is known as “envelope information” and it cannot be end-to-end encrypted. Methods like PGP encryption can not and do not protect this information, as they only encrypt the message body.

The only way to protect this information from network-level attackers is to ensure the message is delivered to the correct MTA, which requires authenticated transit encryption.

When I first encountered this issue I was surprised as there is no analogous problem on the web. The issue relates to the semantic difference between a CNAME and an MX record. A CNAME record pointing at a web hosting provider’s server is a matter of identity and that server can get a TLS certificate to prove it. An MX record does not permit the target email server to get a corresponding TLS certificate.

A web browser is able to compare the name in the TLS certificate with the name shown in the address bar and can expect these to strictly match. An MTA doesn’t compare the name in the TLS certificate with the domain name in the “to” address as a mismatch is typically expected.

Further, email is sent asynchronously so there are no humans involved in MTA-to-MTA communications. While web browsers can show a certificate warning message to allow users to make their own security decisions, an MTA is all on its own. Email providers often tout support for transit encryption but the lack of certificate validation makes email traveling between MTAs about as secure as a user browsing the web while always clicking through invalid certificate warnings.

Interestingly, email has adopted two solutions to this problem: a DNSSEC-based approach and an HTTPS .well-known approach. This give us a unique opportunity to compare these approaches head-to-head as they attempt to solve the same problem.

The DNSSEC approach is SMTP DNS-based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE) (RFC 7672), which was standardized in 2015. DANE requires DNSSEC signing in both the customer and email provider’s DNS zones for the protection to have full effect.

DANE adds the TLSA DNS record. Here’s an example:

This record indicates that the MTA-to-MTA connection can use authenticated encryption. Specifically, this record indicates that the receiving MTA should provide a TLS certificate with a public key digest of “6111A…”. Validating this pinned certificate does not depend on the certificate authority (CA) system.

SMTP DANE signals that it should be possible to cryptographically validate the chain from the domain name in the email address to the domain name on the receiving MTA’s TLS certificate.

One key benefit of DNSSEC, which we’ll revisit, is that blocking of a signed record can be distinguished from a non-existent policy. When the TLSA record does not exist, the authoritative DNS server should provide a signed proof of non-existence (NSEC). This acts as a fail safe: if DNSSEC is enabled and the sender cannot determine the DANE policy, then the sender can conclude that it is not safe to send the message as network interference may be present.

Email providers realized that slow adoption of DNSSEC was delaying authenticated transit encryption between MTAs. They looked at what other tools were available and found inspiration from the HTTPS .well-known approach. Standardized in 2018, SMTP MTA Strict Transport Security (MTA-STS) (RFC 8461) provides an HTTPS-based solution.

Notice that the mta-sts subdomain is used instead of the bare domain. This best practice stems from the need to isolate security policies from whatever website lives at the bare domain; often a marketing website which may not have a security posture suitable for cross-protocol policies like MTA-STS. To distinguish any pre-existing use of the mta-sts subdomain the “_mta-sts” TXT record must also be set.

Finally, policy caching was added as a partial mitigation of intermittent network interference.

Like DANE, MTA-STS signals that the sender should strictly authenticate TLS. The MX record is duplicated in the MTA-STS policy, relying on HTTPS to secure the link. MTA-STS requires the receiving MTA to have a TLS certificate issued by a well-trusted CA.

An MTA-STS policy document is fairly unchanging, making it well-suited for inexpensive, widely available, and highly scalable static web hosting. Many domain owners implement MTA-STS by adding the subdomain to an existing web server, as a virtual host, although it turns out this isn’t always a good idea.

The TLS certificate renewal process is an obvious point of failure for MTA-STS. When a user-facing website goes down users complain, support tickets are filed, and the certificates are quickly renewed. The MTA-STS policy server fails open when it’s certificate expires. Senders will fall back to using opportunistic encryption and users won’t notice any disruption. As such an expired TLS certificate on an MTA-STS policy server can go unnoticed. To address this lack of visibility, TLS Reporting (RFC 8460) was created, which allows email servers to share deliverability reports with each other.

Another problem, which I think is an even larger issue, are web servers that block email servers from accessing their MTA-STS policy. You’ve probably noticed a sharp rise in bots, scrapers, and other unwanted automated traffic impacting the web. In the rush to protect web servers from these ills many sites inadvertently blocked access to their MTA-STS policy. An email server fetching an MTA-STS policy can look a lot like unwanted traffic: it’s automated and its coming from data center IP ranges. Misapplying security policies intended to protect user-facing websites from unwanted bot traffic degrades API-like interfaces.

One unique benefit of SMTP DANE is that the policy cannot be blocked without the sender noticing. An MTA-STS policy server can be blocked just like any other web server and this blocking cannot easily be distinguish from a non-existent policy.

While MTA-STS caching can protect against intermittent network-level blocking of the policy server, the first email sent to a domain is always vulnerable due to an empty cache. The effectiveness of MTA-STS in preventing an on-path attacker from intercepting email is questionable if the same on-path attacker can block the sender from discovering the MTA-STS policy.

By these measures, DANE seems like the stronger option.

DANE’s reliance on DNSSEC signing is its major weakness. Measurements show that 0.9-1.2% of domain names that receive email have DANE support, which doesn’t provide much practical protection yet. Worse, large providers like gmail.com lack DNSSEC support, so the per-user impact may be larger. Unless DNSSEC adoption can grow among large email providers, DANE can only be a partial solution. In contrast, HTTPS is very widely adopted making MTA-STS familiar to practitioners, even with these challenges.

The web has blazed a path that MTA-STS can likely follow. HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) (RFC 6769) is essentially MTA-STS for the web (or visa-versa). HSTS is similarly vulnerable when the cache is empty. Web browsers mitigate this issue using a preload list, which ships in the browser. Out-of-the-box, the web browser knows that popular websites, like wikipedia.com, strictly use HTTPS. While there are challenges with HSTS, like the size of the list, this may have marginal impact for a server-side technology like email.

I think MTA-STS can copy this solution. There are unknowns, like who would build an MTA-STS preload list, why we trust them to do so, and the exact semantics needed for a domain to be added. In any case, I think we should wait on increased MTA-STS adoption before we take those next steps.

The adoption rates of MTA-STS and SMTP DANE tell an important story about how application protocols can secure domain information in practice. The fact that email has both a DNSSEC and an HTTPS approach gives us a way to spectate.

Current measurements show that MTA-STS has overtaken DANE among the top-ranked domain names.

Given the importance of protecting messages, including envelope information which cannot be end-to-end encrypted, these results are disappointing.

Prior work shows that TLS downgrade attacks on email are widespread. With the slow adoption of email security protocols since that study, the situation is unlikely to have improved. We can and should do better.

MTA-STS isn’t the only protocol that works this way.

OpenPGP Web Key Directory (WKD) (draft-koch-openpgp-webkey-service-22) uses an HTTPS .well-known approach to secure PGP key distribution, facilitating end-to-end encryption of message bodies.

The WKD “advanced method”, seen above, follows the best practice of using a protocol-specific subdomain.

The analogous DNSSEC-based approach is OPENPGPKEY (RFC 7929).

Other protocols like Mail AutoConfig (draft-ietf-mailmaint-autoconfig-07) simplify the process of setting up an email client and similar applications.

Again we see this protocol follow the security best practice of using a protocol-specific subdomain.

There are over 100 registered .well-known URIs, showing the popularity of this approach. Many of these tolerate lower security properties and use the bare domain name instead of a protocol-specific subdomain.

While I’ve thus far framed the discussion as a competition, DNSSEC and HTTPS .well-known are actually complementary. We don’t need one approach to defeat the other: we’ll see ecosystem improvements as both solutions are adopted, side-by-side. HTTPS .well-known can offload large policy documents and allow rapid experimentation, avoiding the size limits of UDP packets and the slow process of adding new DNS record types. DNSSEC can sign the CAA record, providing improved security during TLS certificate issuance.

DANE could even replace the CAs entirely, a topic of renewed interest after the recent eMudhra mishap. After all, we wouldn’t need the CAs if we had a secure DNS.

I see complementary nature of DNSSEC and HTTPS .well-known emphasized in another draft, Domain Authority (DA): A DNS-Designated Service Endpoint for Domain Information (draft-swaminathan-da-00), which seeks to standardize the use of HTTPS to add capabilities to domain names beyond what DNS can natively support. While I think the current draft is too ambitious in scope, it provides a great summary of the benefits an HTTPS-based policy retrieval layer can provide beyond DNS.

Unfortunately, we still have an insecure DNS. But progress in the domain name ecosystem is not blocked by DNS. MTA-STS shows that an HTTPS approach is immediately usable.

#10012. We got local models to triage the OpenClaw repo for FREE!*

*Free as in beer, excluding the cost of electricity, and assuming you already own the hardware

June 2026 will go down as the moment that people realized closed models can be taken away. With the removal of Anthropic's latest flagship model Claude Fable 5 fresh in memory, one can see why it is more important than ever to own your AI stack and be able to run models locally, especially if you are building your business on top of AI.

In that light, we wanted to share how we use local models like Gemma and Qwen in an agent harness, to run classification tasks[1]. This approach is different from using a model like BERT for classification. A local model in an agent harness like Pi can be used in tandem with structured outputs, to assign labels. We chose this approach because we already had local models and the harness on hand, and have conviction that similar setups will increase in popularity as local models improve in capability.[2]

Our starting point was open source contributions in the OpenClaw repo. OpenClaw gets hundreds of issues and PRs every day, which need to be triaged, prioritized and routed to maintainers. I, Onur, am working to make local models work well with OpenClaw. Being a maintainer of this specific vertical, I need to react quickly to any P0 issues.

With SOTA closed models like GPT-5, Opus, or Sonnet, this is a pretty straightforward task. But I happen to sit on 128 GB of unified memory, namely an NVIDIA GB10. So I took on the task:

Can I build a real-time notification system that filters and notifies me for only the issues that I am responsible for... with local open-weight models?

If I set up my OpenClaw main agent running on a $200/mo ChatGPT Pro plan to trigger a job on every new issue or PR, that would use up my quota. I might instead set it to run every 2 hours, or 6 hours. This would batch issues over longer periods, so we would be trading real-time notifications for delayed processing.

If I were to run this on a local model on the hardware I already have up and running, I would not only have near-instantaneous notifications, I would also be able to do it for free (or rather, for the cost of electricity).

We came up with a finite set of labels representing the categories of issues we need to triage, and then use a local model to classify each issue into one of those categories, like local_models, self_hosted_inference, acp, agent_runtime, codex, ui_tui and so on.[3]

But how do we classify pull requests? A simple single request to a Chat Completions endpoint with a tool JSON schema, with the topics as an enum?

Kind of. But this is 2026, not 2023, and we have AGENTS. We can do better!

For the local model choices, we tested gemma-4-26b-a4b and qwen3.6-35b-a3b. With performance optimizations, both can generate hundreds of tokens per second locally.

We use an agent harness to drive the classification run. For this, we bundle pi as a harness that can call local model endpoints.

The agent by default receives the PR title, body and a truncated excerpt of the PR diff in the first prompt. Then, it can choose to use the bash tool to perform read-only operations on the OpenClaw repo (in case it needs to look at the codebase), or the final_json tool to submit the final classification result.

You wouldn't want to give full bash access to a local model running in this high-throughput setting, because a prompt-injected issue or PR could otherwise steer the model into doing something unrelated to classification.

For that reason, we use reposhell instead of bash: a restricted bash-like shell that only allows read-only operations (ls, find, cat, grep, etc.) on the OpenClaw repo. The model thinks it is using bash, but any operation that is not allowed is rejected:

Here is a concrete example where this mattered. In one saved session example, qwen3.6-35b-a3b was classifying openclaw/openclaw#84621, titled Fix Kimi tool-call rewriting stop reason handling. The thinking block shows the model initially considering coding_agent_integrations because the changed path extensions/kimi-coding made it look plausible. The model used reposhell to inspect the local repo with simple read-only commands like ls extensions, ls extensions/kimi-coding, and cat extensions/kimi-coding/package.json. That package metadata showed the extension was actually @openclaw/kimi-provider, an OpenClaw Kimi provider plugin. So the model corrected the final labels to inference_api and tool_calling, and explicitly excluded coding_agent_integrations.

We have mentioned earlier that we bundle a specific pi configuration that can only perform read-only operations and return classification output. We call it localpager-agent, named after localpager, the main project here. Each PR and issue generates a prompt, which is then passed to the CLI like below, alongside other args:

So then what orchestrates everything in between the incoming PR/issue and the final notification on Discord?

The orchestration around this is very simple; only the classification step involves an LLM:

Below is a figure showing the overall architecture of localpager:

The architecture is semi-agentic. Labeling is done agentically, while sending a notification is handled by deterministic rules. This is to make the notification pipeline faster by removing the need for inference for the most straightforward parts of the task. Local inference is free but each task has a resource contention cost: GPU bandwidth should be reserved for tasks where inference is absolutely needed. This also reduces chance of errors from notification.

Let's be frank: the first local versions of this system were noisy. The first model tested - gemma-4-e4b-it was useful for getting the end-to-end local pipeline working, but it also had a tendency to put too many unrelated labels on a PR or issue. False positive labels make the Discord feed noisy and don't focus my attention on the right issues. That pushed us toward testing larger local models, including gemma-4-26b-a4b and qwen3.6-35b-a3b, on the 330-row evaluation set below.

For early prompt work, we also used DeepSeek-V4-Flash through the antirez DS4 implementation[4] to create the earlier dataset labels. That setup used the DS4 server over CUDA. We eventually gave up on DS4 as the labeler because it was not labeling consistently across runs. We also did not consider it as the main localpager-agent model because it was too big to get enough throughput on our hardware: the DS4 server gave us around 14 tokens per second, with maximum concurrency of 1.

To test model performance, we selected and generated labels for 330 GitHub issues and PRs. Each item was labelled five times (3x GPT-5.5 and 2x Opus 4.8) with the models needing to be in agreement to be accepted. This process involved hand adjudicating, improving label definitions and highlighting internal product design choices for the models. This gave us a set of stable, reproducible labels to compare our smaller models against.

We did not need to do prompt optimization for gemma-4-26b-a4b or qwen3.6-35b-a3b before getting useful results on this evaluation set. Using the same routing prompt, Gemma had higher recall and lower wall-clock time per row, while Qwen had higher precision, higher exact match, and fewer false positives. We also ran DeepSeek-V4-Flash on the same set as a reference. It had the fewest false positives, but the model size and throughput make it impractical for executing these tasks in real time on the NVIDIA GB10. Since each row can have multiple labels, false positives and false negatives are total label counts across all rows. The Qwen results below are after retrying structured-output failures where the model ran out of output tokens before calling final_json. For Gemma and Qwen, repeated-run metrics report mean ± sample standard deviation across three runs. DeepSeek-V4-Flash was run once as a reference.

The throughput and wall-clock numbers here are not definitive maximum performance numbers for these models on this hardware. They are the settings we used at the time with the optimizations we had available. For example, in a separate probe, gemma-4-26b-a4b also supported concurrency 32 and reached over 700 aggregate output tokens per second.

For the Gemma benchmark, we served gemma-4-26b-a4b with vLLM using the optimizations we found available for this setup. A big part of that is the NVFP4 quantization: on GB10-class Blackwell hardware, it is not just a smaller model file, but a hardware-friendly format that can use the NVIDIA/vLLM execution path more directly than a portable GGUF quantization like Q4_K_M. In practice, that means less memory traffic and more room for batching. We also enabled prefix caching, FP8 KV cache, the CUTLASS MoE backend, and language-model-only mode. The full 330-row run finished in about 7.5 minutes at concurrency 16.

We have mentioned earlier that instead of running a job with a local model for every new issue or PR, we can run a batch job with a SOTA cloud model, like GPT-5.5 running in OpenClaw, every n hours (e.g. every 2 hours) to achieve the same end.[5]

In that case, we would need a ChatGPT Pro plan. Since the model is SOTA, we can still expect it to perform reasonably well, despite batching 2 hours of issues/PRs together.

Because we want to see how well the local classifier performs against GPT-5.5, we run both simultaneously, and let GPT-5.5 be the judge of false positives and negatives, every 2 hours.

To be safe, we run the OpenClaw job in a sandbox, with only access to the public repo we report results to. In our case, we let the OpenClaw job update a machine-readable file, then a simple script reads the Codex-assigned labels and computes the false positive/negative status. Example output:

The instructions on how to classify, edit the machine-readable file, get the false positives and false negatives using a script are present in an agent skill which is referenced in an OpenClaw cron job that runs every 2 hours. The OpenClaw agent then ingests any new issues or PRs, adds them to the JSON file with appropriate labels, runs the scripts and reports back in the same Discord channel. This way, we can observe the local model's performance every few hours, and get notified of the misses.

We think that the issue/PR triage task is a specific case of a broader set of tasks which we call "high throughput triage". This post explored the idea of using a local model to filter out information in real time in only one domain, that is, open source contributions. The ability of medium-sized local models like gemma-4-26b-a4b and qwen3.6-35b-a3b to zero-shot classify with good accuracy without any need for fine-tuning makes them a good first choice for quick prototyping, before one moves on to more cost-efficient traditional classifier models.

However, the same approach can be applied to other domains as well:

The list can be extended, but we think that the idea should be clear.

Besides triaging, we have also explored how classification can be performed with agent harnesses running fast local models in a secure manner. A good naming for the approach would be agentic classification: the model is not fed the entire body of information upfront, but can search for more context before returning structured data. While we cannot exactly call this a novel approach, we hope for this blog post to be a good reference for the specific Pi+a restricted shell+final_json recipe.

#10011. PP-OCRv6 on Hugging Face: 50-Language OCR from 1.5M to 34.5M Parameters

Evaluate PP-OCRv6 online, then integrate lightweight, production-ready OCR with PaddlePaddle, Transformers, or ONNX Runtime backend.

PP-OCRv6 is the latest generation of PaddleOCR’s universal OCR model family. It is designed for real-world text detection and recognition across documents, screenshots, multilingual images, digital displays, industrial labels, and scene text.

The model family scales from 1.5M to 34.5M parameters, with three tiers: tiny, small, and medium. The medium and small tiers support 50 languages, including Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, English, Japanese, and 46 Latin-script languages. Try PP-OCRv6 online quickly: PP-OCRv6 Online Demo.

On PaddleOCR’s official in-house multi-scenario OCR benchmarks, PP-OCRv6_medium reaches 86.2% detection Hmean and 83.2% recognition accuracy. Compared with PP-OCRv5_server, it improves text detection by +4.6 percentage points and text recognition by +5.1 percentage points.

PP-OCRv6 focuses on a practical OCR need: producing accurate, structured text outputs with small models and flexible deployment options. For a deeper discussion of why specialized OCR models remain useful in the VLM era, see our previous blog: PP-OCRv5 on Hugging Face: A Specialized Approach to OCR.

PP-OCRv6 introduces architecture, training, and data improvements across detection and recognition. The main design goal is to improve OCR accuracy while keeping model sizes suitable for different deployment settings.

PP-OCRv6 provides three model tiers, covering different model sizes and OCR accuracy levels.

PP-OCRv6 uses PPLCNetV4 as a unified backbone for text detection and text recognition.

For developers, the main benefit is consistency across the model family. The tiny, small, and medium tiers are not unrelated models; they are part of the same OCR family and share a common architectural direction.

Text detection is the first stage of the OCR pipeline. Detection quality affects the crops sent to the recognizer, and poor crops often lead to poorer recognition.

PP-OCRv6 upgrades the detection module with RepLKFPN, a lightweight large-kernel feature pyramid network designed for multi-scale text detection while keeping inference efficient.

This is relevant for real-world OCR inputs, where text may be small, dense, rotated, low-resolution, or embedded in complex backgrounds.

For text recognition, PP-OCRv6 uses EncoderWithLightSVTR. It combines local context modeling with global attention to improve recognition quality on challenging text crops.

The recognition improvements are especially relevant for multilingual text, screen text, industrial characters, special symbols, dense text, and noisy image regions.

The medium and small tiers support 50 languages in one model family, covering Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, English, Japanese, and 46 Latin-script languages.

This helps reduce the need for separate OCR models across common multilingual OCR scenarios.

Run OCR with Paddle Infernece(Default backend):

The OCR result can be saved as visualization images and structured JSON output. The structured output can then be used by downstream systems such as document parsing, search, extraction, RAG, analytics, or agent workflows.

PP-OCRv6 can be used with multiple inference backends through PaddleOCR. PaddleOCR 3.7 provides a unified inference-engine interface, where engine selects the underlying runtime and related configuration can be passed through the pipeline or module API.

For Hugging Face users, PaddleOCR supports running selected OCR and document parsing models with a Transformers backend. This can be enabled with:

For more details on how the Transformers backend works in PaddleOCR, see:

PaddleOCR: Running OCR and Document Parsing Tasks with a Transformers Backend

Run PP-OCRv6 example with Transformer Backend:

ONNX variants are also available in the PP-OCRv6 Collection for environments that use ONNX Runtime through engine="onnxruntime":

Together, these backend options make PP-OCRv6 available across different runtime environments while keeping the same OCR model family on the Hugging Face Hub.

PP-OCRv6 extends PaddleOCR with a lightweight, multilingual OCR model family for real-world text detection and recognition.

The release includes three model tiers from 1.5M to 34.5M parameters, up to 50-language OCR support, improved detection and recognition accuracy over PP-OCRv5_server, and multiple model formats on the Hugging Face Hub, including safetensors, Paddle inference models, and ONNX models.

Together with the hosted Hugging Face Space and the available PaddleOCR inference backends, PP-OCRv6 provides several entry points for evaluation and integration:

Transformers Backend Blog: PaddleOCR with Transformers Backend

PaddleOCR Documentation: PP-OCRv6 Documentation

PaddleOCR Official Website: https://www.paddleocr.com

You can evaluate PP-OCRv6 with the online demo, explore the available model assets in the Collection, and use the inference backend that matches your own OCR workflow.

#10009. Experimenting with the proposed Cross-Origin Storage API in Transformers.js

(This is a guest post by Developer Relations Engineer Thomas Steiner from the Chrome team at Google.)

Transformers.js provides Web developers with a simple way to use the power of transformers in their Web apps through task-specific pipelines. To run inference in the browser, developers create an instance of pipeline() and specify a task they want to use the pipeline for. As a concrete example, the following snippet shows how to set up an automatic speech recognition (ASR) pipeline.

You will notice in the source code that I specified Xenova/whisper-tiny.en as the model, which is a very decent choice for common English automatic speech recognition tasks. In fact, it's even the default model according to the Transformers.js default model resolution, as per the linked excerpt.

When you run this example in the browser, Transformers.js automatically takes care of downloading and caching the relevant model resources and Wasm files. The following screenshot shows the Chrome DevTools Cache storage section after visiting the app. When you reload the page, the resources are served from the Cache API, and the model returns results almost instantly.

However, Xenova/whisper-tiny.en being a popular model (and, as mentioned before, even being the ASR default model in Transformers.js), you can well imagine that more than just one app that you visit would use it. To simulate this situation, here's the same example app from before, but served from a different origin. When you visit this different origin app, rather than being usable almost instantly, the browser instead has to download and cache all the model resources again, even if they're byte-by-byte the same as before. Even in this toy example, this adds up to 177 MB of duplicate download and storage, as you can examine in the Storage section of the Chrome DevTools Application panel. You can imagine that this quickly adds up.

But it gets worse. Let's add a second pipeline to the toy example: sentiment analysis. Sentiment analysis by default uses the Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english model. By not specifying the model, Transformers.js' default model resolution automatically picks it for you.

Two entirely different AI models, but they depend on the same 4,733 kB ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm WebAssembly (Wasm) runtime file from the underlying ONNX Runtime library that Transformers.js is built on top of. Open the extended demo on a different origin, and you will notice in the Network tab how also the Wasm runtime gets downloaded and cached again.

So even if you run apps that don't share the same AI models, your browser still makes redundant requests for shared Wasm resources you already have, and on top of that also caches them again, which consumes space on your hard disk.

By default, AI model resources come from the Hugging Face Hub, and ultimately the Hugging Face CDN. The browser makes a request for a resource like https://huggingface.co/Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english/resolve/main/config.json which then gets redirected to the final CDN URL like https://huggingface.co/api/resolve-cache/models/Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english/0b6928efcb76139cae2c6881d49cda67fe119f42/config.json?%2FXenova%2Fdistilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english%2Fresolve%2Fmain%2Fconfig.json=&etag=%223c36342ef1f74de2797d667c68c6b7b988d0b87c%22 in this case.

The Wasm runtime resources are served from the jsDelivr CDN by default. For example, ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm comes from https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/onnxruntime-web@1.26.0-dev.20260416-b7804b056c/dist/ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm at the time of this writing.

The concrete implementation may vary by browser, but in Chrome, cached resources are keyed using a Network Isolation Key in addition to the resource URL. The Network Isolation Key is composed of the top-level site and the current-frame site. Take the previous toy examples hosted on the origins https://googlechrome.github.io and https://rawcdn.rawgit.net. If they both use the Wasm runtime from https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/onnxruntime-web@1.26.0-dev.20260416-b7804b056c/dist/ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm, their cache keys will look like in the following table.

So even if the resource URLs are exactly the same, since the Network Isolation Keys don't match, there's no cache hit, which means duplicate download and duplicate storage. This is the challenge that the Cross-Origin Storage proposal aims to tackle.

💡 Note: The Cross-Origin Storage API is an early-stage proposal that isn't final. While the proposed API is not yet natively implemented in any browser, you don't have to wait to experiment with it. Install the Cross-Origin Storage extension to inject the navigator.crossOriginStorage polyfill on all pages and test the complete flow.

The proposed Cross-Origin Storage (COS) API introduces a dedicated navigator.crossOriginStorage interface through which web apps can store and retrieve large files across origin boundaries, identified not by a URL, but by a cryptographic hash.

That last point about cryptographic hashes is key. Because COS identifies files by their hash rather than by their URL or origin, the same ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm Wasm runtime you downloaded while visiting https://googlechrome.github.io is recognized as identical to the one https://rawcdn.rawgit.net is about to request, no matter where either of the two origins fetched it from. See the following code snippet that illustrates the basic flow.

If the resource is in COS, you get back a FileSystemFileHandle from which you can read the blob directly via getFile() (the resulting File inherits from Blob). If the resource is not in COS, you fall back to the network, and write the resource into COS for the next app that needs it, which could be your app, or another unrelated app, potentially on a completely different origin.

The API is deliberately shaped after the File System Standard's FileSystemDirectoryHandle.getFileHandle() you likely are familiar with from the Origin Private File System (OPFS) API. The hash parameter plays the same role as the name parameter in OPFS: uniquely identifying a resource. The options.create flag works the same way: absent or false for read-only access, true when you intend to write.

Not every resource should be globally shared. COS gives developers precise control over visibility through the origins option when storing a file.

One important rule: visibility can be upgraded but never downgraded. If a file is already globally available, a later attempt to store it with a restricted origins list is silently ignored. This prevents a malicious actor from re-storing a public resource and narrowing its availability. The reverse is possible: a file initially stored with a restricted origins list can later be made more permissive. Any site, not just the original storer, can call getFileHandle() for the same hash (hashes are not a secret) with create: true and a broader origins value, and given the browser verifies the hash matches, the resource becomes available to the wider audience from that point on. Note that the upgrading site must still write the full file through the returned handle. This requirement exists to prevent sites from exploiting the upgrade path as a side-channel to detect whether a particular file was already stored in COS.

A subtle but important property of COS is that the browser verifies the hash when you write a file. If the data you write doesn't match the declared hash, the write fails with an error. This makes integrity checking automatic: an app reading a file from COS can be confident it's getting exactly the bytes it expected. The same guarantee it would have had if it had computed the hash itself after a network download.

This turns out to be doubly useful in the Transformers.js scenario. Today, after downloading model weights, most apps have no practical way to verify that the CDN served the right bytes. With COS, every file in the store is implicitly verified on write, no matter where it came from, the official Hugging Face CDN or a random site's self-hosted mirror.

Of course a cross-origin shared cache raises the same question as the partitioned HTTP cache in reverse: if any site can probe for the presence of a file by hash, couldn't an attacker learn something about the user's browsing history by checking whether, say, a game engine Wasm module is cached?

COS addresses this through two complementary mechanisms:

Crucially, this means an error is not a definitive answer. It might mean "not stored", or it might mean "stored, but the browser isn't telling you". Apps should always handle it the same way: fall back to the network.

Going back to the toy examples from before: the ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm runtime weighs in at 4,733 kB and is shared by every Transformers.js-powered app regardless of which AI model it uses. With COS, the first app to load it downloads it once and stores it under its SHA-256 hash with origins: '*'. Every subsequent app, whether on https://googlechrome.github.io, on https://rawcdn.rawgit.net, or any other origin, finds it in COS immediately. The 177 MB of duplicate Whisper model weights? Same story: Xenova/whisper-tiny.en gets downloaded once, recognized by hash the second time around, and served from COS in milliseconds. And of course, the same also happens for Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english.

Transformers.js itself is already piloting the COS API at the library level. Pull request #1549 introduced an experimental COS cache backend behind an opt-in flag. Enabling it takes a single line before you set up your pipeline:

Note the experimental_ prefix on the flag. It's intentional and signals that the underlying browser API has not yet been standardized and may change without a major version bump. With that flag set, Transformers.js resolves the SHA-256 hash for each Xet-tracked model file (the large ONNX weight files) by fetching the raw Xet pointer (example raw pointer file) and extracting its oid sha256: field. It then uses that hash as the key for navigator.crossOriginStorage. If the model is already in COS (because another site stored it there first), it's served instantly without a network round-trip. If not, it falls back to a regular download and stores the result in COS for the next caller. With the toy example, the advantage in practice is that Xenova/whisper-tiny.en and Xenova/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english (and of course ort-wasm-simd-threaded.asyncify.wasm) only ever need to cross the ether once, regardless of how many different origins ask for them.

The toy example works just fine with Xenova/whisper-tiny.en, but of course you possibly wouldn't say no if the user already has any of the other Whisper variants in their COS cache. For example, the user might already have Xenova/whisper-large-v3, which, as the name suggests, is a lot larger than the tiny variant. Transformers.js's Model Registry makes being flexible about your models possible. If you know your app's needs can be addressed by, for example, any of Xenova/whisper-tiny.en, whisper-medium.en, or Xenova/whisper-large-v3, you can check the registry for the associated files for each model, probe for their existence in the COS cache (which may partially or completely contain the model resources you need), and then take a decision what model to choose eventually. The ModelRegistry.is_pipeline_cached() API directly integrates with COS (and of course the Cache API), so this operation is really ergonomic.

The COS API is not yet natively implemented in any browser, but you don't have to wait to experiment with it. Install the Cross-Origin Storage extension to inject the navigator.crossOriginStorage polyfill on all pages and test the complete flow. Check out the source code of the extension and follow the usage instructions to get started.

With the extension installed, try the full end-to-end experience right now: open the first toy example with COS enabled, let it load Xenova/whisper-tiny.en, then open the toy example with COS enabled from the second origin. Instead of the 177 MB re-download you saw before, the model is served from COS in milliseconds. When you open the extension's popup window, you can see COS in action. If you View by Resource, you can see the resource with the SHA-256 hash 950978b1dbcbf250335358c1236053ba19a7f7849b33dc777f4421b72b7626fa shared across https://googlechrome.github.io and https://rawcdn.rawgit.net. It may not be obvious, but as you can verify by comparing the SHA-256 hash on Hugging Face, you're looking at https://huggingface.co/Xenova/whisper-tiny.en/blob/main/onnx/decoder_model_merged.onnx. For now, the extension is mostly aimed at power users like you. Once implemented in the browser, there will be a friendlier integration in the browser's Settings page. The screenshot below shows the extension's popup window with the View by Resource tab active, where you can see the shared resource with its hash and the two origins that have it in their COS cache.

If you're building your own Transformers.js app, the call to action is simple: add env.experimental_useCrossOriginStorage = true before your first pipeline() call, install the extension, and watch the duplicate downloads disappear from your Network tab. Every site that opts in makes the experience faster and cheaper for every other site's users. Opting in is completely risk-free: if the COS API isn't supported because the user doesn't have the COS extension installed, the code just falls back to the default path (the Cache API).

Transformers.js is not alone in experimenting with COS. WebLLM (opt-in, see documentation) and wllama (automatic, see PR) are likewise excited about this proposed API.

On the Chrome team, we're considering implementing the COS API natively in the browser. As an early stage proposal, we welcome feedback on the API, and the shape of the proposal itself. The Cross-Origin Storage repository is the place to file issues, express support, or open PRs.
