#9971. From Hugging Face to Amazon SageMaker Studio in one click

Today, we’re excited to announce a deep-link integration between Hugging Face and Amazon SageMaker AI. Developers can now go from model discovery to hands-on experimentation in SageMaker Studio with a single selection. Whether you fine-tune a foundation model (FM) from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart or deploy it to an Amazon SageMaker Inference endpoint, you can now land directly inside the relevant SageMaker Studio workflow. Your selected model is pre-loaded, and the environment is fully configured and ready to go.

Previously, getting started on SageMaker Studio after discovering a model on Hugging Face required navigating multiple steps between opening Amazon SageMaker AI in the AWS Console, creating a domain, configuring IAM permissions, and sometimes requesting GPU quota. For developers who want to iterate quickly, this friction slows down the path from inspiration to experimentation. The integration creates a more direct path from discovery to enterprise deployment.

“At Arcee, we build open models so developers and enterprises can actually own what they run: inspect the weights, post-train on their own data, and deploy on their own terms. This integration takes that promise the last mile. Going from an open model on Hugging Face straight into SageMaker Studio in a single click, then fine-tuning or deploying it inside your own AWS environment with nothing to wire up, is the kind of experience open models have been missing. Open weights you own, running in the cloud you control. That is exactly the combination our customers have been asking for.”

— Mark McQuade, Founder and CEO, Arcee AI

With the launch of a one-click Studio landing experience, choosing Customize on SageMaker AI or Deploy on SageMaker AI on a supported Hugging Face model page takes you directly to the console. SageMaker AI then automatically provisions a new domain with pre-configured permissions in seconds and carries the model context through.

This launch introduces three capabilities that shorten the path from a Hugging Face model to a working SageMaker Studio workflow.

When you browse models on Hugging Face, you’ll now see action buttons alongside supported models that map directly to SageMaker Studio workflows:

Each entry point preserves the context, meaning you don’t need to search for the model again once inside Studio.

New Studio environments created through this flow come with permissions already configured for the full range of SageMaker AI capabilities, including model customization, training jobs, notebook experimentation, and endpoint deployment. A new managed policy, AmazonSageMakerModelCustomizationCoreAccess, is created and attached for you. It provides permissions for serverless model customization jobs using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF), with supported deployment to SageMaker AI or Amazon Bedrock endpoints. This alleviates the need to manually create and configure AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and policies before you can start experimenting. For existing Studio environments, actionable messages with direct links to documentation guide you through adding these permissions.

When selecting instance types for deployment or training, the Studio UI now surfaces quota availability directly in the instance selection list. You can immediately see which GPU instance types (G5, G6) are available under your account’s current limits. You don’t need to navigate separately to Service Quotas. If you still need to request a limit increase, you’re redirected directly to the Service Quotas page for the respective instance type.

Let’s walk through the experience of customizing or deploying a model starting from Hugging Face.

On the Hugging Face model page, click on “Deploy” and select “Amazon SageMaker AI”. If the model is supported, you will see two buttons, “Deploy on SageMaker AI” and “Customize on SageMaker AI”. Then select “Customize on SageMaker AI” for a supported model.

You’re prompted to sign in to AWS using your existing credentials. If you already have an active console session, this step is skipped automatically. For more information, see Sign in to the AWS Management Console.

You arrive directly on the Model Customization page inside SageMaker Studio with your model pre-selected. Next, configure your fine-tuning parameters such as training data, hyperparameters, and instance type, then submit the customization job.

Alternatively, selecting Deploy on SageMaker AI opens the endpoint deployment page in Studio with the model pre-configured. Select your instance type (quota visibility included), review the settings, and deploy.

After you deploy your endpoint, test inference directly from Studio’s endpoint testing interface.

The launch of a one-click Studio landing experience minimizes the friction between discovering a model and experimenting with it. By connecting Hugging Face directly to the SageMaker Studio workflows, developers can stay in their flow. There’s no context switching, no manual environment setup, and no permission troubleshooting.

To get started, visit the Amazon SageMaker Studio page or explore models on Hugging Face and choose Deploy or Customize on SageMaker AI.

#9970. Native-speed vLLM transformers modeling backend

TL;DR: The transformers vLLM backend is now as fast (or faster) than custom vLLM implementations for many LLM architectures. Model authors can automatically leverage their transformers implementations to get ultra fast vLLM inference, for free.

The transformers library has become the reference modeling library for Machine Learning. It supports 450+ architectures through consistent APIs, and is designed with the main goal that model implementations are self contained and easy to understand. Going through transformers code makes it easy for contributors to learn how an architecture works, and then port it to other frameworks such as vLLM, SGLang, MLX, llama.cpp, and many others.

We have fully embraced this role in the ecosystem and are investing a lot of effort to make it easier. A big step in this direction was the integration last year of transformers as a modeling backend in vLLM. This has been allowing model authors to run transformers models (LLMs and VLMs alike) inside vLLM, without having to port anything. Transformers provides the modeling code, and vLLM provides extremely optimized inference techniques such as continuous batching and custom attention kernels.

We put the transformers modeling backend for vLLM head to head with vLLM's hand written native implementations across three very different Qwen3 models:

Running any* Hugging Face model through the transformers modeling backend is a single flag — --model-impl transformers. It composes with the usual parallelism options, so nothing about your serving setup changes:

*Models that use linear attention are not currently supported, but they will be soon! Custom models where the code lives in a Hub repo are unlikely to work as they will not have been written compliantly.

Each model is compared under three conditions that are identical in every way except the code path:

The full, reproducible runner is available as a gist: benchmark.sh

The transformers modeling backend for vLLM used to focus on attention as the bottleneck for inference. By plugging vLLM’s attention implementation at runtime, we could make a transformers model run efficiently inside the vLLM engine. But there are many dimensions to deployments that only a custom port can target to extract maximum inference performance. Parallelization across GPUs, compilation, fused kernels, and many more, all contribute to leveraging your hardware to achieve ultra-fast inference.

When model authors wanted the absolute best performance, they were still writing custom vLLM implementations.

The latest iteration of the transformers modeling backend for vLLM dynamically applies inference specific layer fusions at runtime to match the speed of custom code implementations, for compatible architectures.

The transformers modeling backend for vLLM now uses torch.fx to perform static analysis on the model’s graph. This process searches for known patterns that can be optimised. After any patterns have been identified, it uses ast (abstract syntax tree) to manipulate the source code and rewrite some of the operations in place.

As shown above, this results in native vLLM inference speed for compatible models, without having to write a single line of code to optimize the model for inference.

We are in the process of writing a detailed blog post to dive deep inside these optimized inference methods and explain in detail how we manipulate the model to adapt to them.

One provenance implication here is that the model definition and the executed inference graph are no longer the same artifact boundary.

If the runtime rewrites model code and replaces modules with fused kernels, deployment evidence probably needs to preserve both the source model identity and the transformation/runtime path.

#9966. Profiling in PyTorch (Part 3): Attention is all you profile

This is the third post of Profiling in PyTorch, a series where we slowly build the skill of reading profiler traces and use it to drive optimization:

The series "Profiling in PyTorch" is meant to make you comfortable reading profiler traces and tables. In Part 1 we profiled basic math operations like addition and multiplication. We saw how the profiler table uncovers hotspots, and how the profiler trace shows the order in which an algorithm runs over time.

In Part 2 we wrapped that addition and multiplication into a torch linear layer. We then stacked several linear layers on top of each other (a multilayer perceptron) and profiled that. Along the way we also profiled fused and hand-tuned kernels.

From the perspective of the Transformer architecture, the next logical step for us to profile is yet another fundamental algorithm, attention. While being infamous for its quadratic-time complexity, many clever tricks exist to mitigate that issue and make it fast. Our goal here is not to cover every trick in detail. Instead, we want to see how each one looks different under the profiler.

The scripts for this blog post live here: 04_a_naive_attention.py, 04_b_inplace_ops_attention.py, 04_c_sdpa_attention.py, and 04_d_kernels_attention.py. Like before, it helps to open them in a separate tab and walk through the code as you read. We use an NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB GPU to run the scripts. It is really easy to set up a GPU on the Hugging Face infrastructure and experiment with the scripts using Dev Mode with Spaces. One could also run the scripts with the Hugging Face Jobs pipeline.

Attention works with Queries (q), Keys (k), and Values (v). The interaction between them can be written as a short sequence of steps:

So attention is really a collection of primitive operations. Some of them we already know (the matmuls), and the rest are easy to spot. Let's write a naive attention module in PyTorch and profile it.

Before opening the trace, let's do our usual exercise and guess what we should see. Tracing the forward of this module, we expect:

Figure 1 shows the CPU lane of the profile (the GPU lane is folded so it does not overwhelm us). Inside attn_fwd (our annotated forward call) we can see exactly the operations we guessed. The matmul is an old friend by now, and the new operations are easy to spot:

Now let's unfold the GPU lane and see which kernels were actually launched.

Figure 2 shows the GPU lane next to the CPU lane. Let's zoom into a single attn_fwd block on the GPU lane to look at the kernels one by one.

Figure 3 lets us read off the individual kernels for one profiler step:

Five of these are expected. The memory copy is the odd one out, so where does this come from? The clue is that PyTorch has in-place operations. When you operate on a tensor the ordinary (out-of-place) way, PyTorch often makes a copy, applies the requested operation to it, and returns the copy. Following the sequence of operations, the culprit here is our masked_fill.

What if we replaced this with an in-place operation?

All we change is masked_fill to masked_fill_ (note the trailing underscore, PyTorch's convention for in-place operations), and we run the same script.

Let's look at the trace and see if something changed.

The in-place version (Figure 5) wraps far fewer CPU ops inside the masking step than the out-of-place version (Figure 4). This is an encouraging signal. Let's unfold the GPU lane to confirm what happened there.

On the GPU lane the Memcpy kernel is gone for good (Figures 6 and 7). With a one line change we shaved a whole kernel off each forward pass. This may not look like much on its own, but remember this is a single attention operation. In the context of a transformer based large model (LLMs, Diffusion models, etc.), it repeats once per layer, and there are many layers, so the saving adds up quickly (and if it earns you a raise, sharing at least 10% with us feels only fair).

Out-of-place is PyTorch's default for a reason. To compute gradients, autograd has to remember the tensor values it saw on the forward pass, because many backward formulas reuse them. An in-place operation overwrites those values in memory, so the backward pass would read the wrong numbers. Due to the fact that we run forward under torch.no_grad, in-place is safe for us, with no backward pass and nothing to corrupt. It is also noteworthy that in-place operations do not only save time (like we see in our case) but also memory (due to no extra copy) which is great for large tensors like logits!

We just built attention from primitives, and even shaved off a Memcpy. The good news is that the PyTorch team has done all of this for us, and packaged the whole pipeline into a single function:

This one line replaces our hand written module, and is_causal=True even saves us from building the mask by hand. It is worth pausing to appreciate how much this one call hides. And it hides more than just code lines. Scaled Dot Product Attention (SDPA) does not have a single implementation. Under the hood it dispatches to one of the several backends and picks the fastest one that supports our inputs (dtype, head dimension, mask, hardware, etc.).

The official SDPA tutorial walks us through this selection, and the backends themselves are listed in the torch.nn.attention.SDPBackend enum:

Normally SDPA chooses for us, but we can pin a specific backend with the torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel context manager. This is what we do in our scripts. This lets us profile each backend on its own and read how differently they show up in the trace. Let's go one at a time.

Before we open anything, let's guess. We have replaced hand written attention (matmul, mul, mask, softmax, matmul) with a single one liner, so we should expect the trace to get simpler and faster. Fewer kernels, less CPU dispatch, maybe even a fused kernel. Let's check the profiler table first.

This is our first surprise, the one liner is 3.7x slower.

Opening the trace (Figure 9) shows why the alarm bells ring, the math backend launches 20 GPU kernels per forward instead of the 5 launched with our naive attention implementation (Figure 8). This is the opposite of what we guessed. Let's figure out why this happens.

In Part 2 we learned to read a kernel name like a fingerprint. Let's use that habit here:

The A100s we used to capture these traces ship with Tensor Cores, specialised hardware for accelerated matmuls that is known to be far faster than the ordinary CUDA cores. To see why that matters here, it helps to know what lives inside a GPU. A Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) is the compute unit of a GPU, and each SM has two kinds of arithmetic units, the CUDA cores and the Tensor Cores. CUDA cores are general purpose and process a handful of elements at a time, while Tensor Cores multiply and accumulate a whole small matrix tile in a single instruction. So the question is simple, "Is each backend actually using the fast path?"

The kernel names answer it. The s16816 in the naive kernel (Figure 10) is the signature of a bfloat16 Tensor Core matmul (the 16x8x16 Tensor Core instruction), so the naive version is on the fast path. sgemm (Figure 11) is the classic single precision (FP32) matmul that runs on the ordinary CUDA cores. In other words, the math backend never touches the Tensor Cores at all: to trade speed for numerical accuracy it upcasts tensors to FP32 (doubling the data moved, even when the inputs are in bf16) and falls back to the slower CUDA cores.

In the naive version we built the causal mask once and reused it. Here we passed is_causal=True and the math backend materialized one for us, on every single call. You can watch it happen on the CPU lane:

On the GPU this shows up as a triu_tril_kernel, several where kernels, and an add_. The convenience flag that let us stop thinking about the mask did not remove the work, it just moved it one layer down, where the mask is rebuilt from scratch every forward.

Our hand written version called plain aten::softmax. The math backend calls aten::_safe_softmax, and the difference is again visible as extra kernels (Figure 13):

A row that is fully masked (every entry -inf) would make an ordinary softmax compute exp(-inf)/sum(exp(-inf)) = 0/0 = NaN. _safe_softmax guards against exactly that. Our naive kernel never bothered, and would have quietly produced NaNs in that corner case.

Put together, the math backend is the reference implementation. It is a straightforward, dtype-safe, NaN-safe decomposition of attention into primitive ATen ops. It is essentially the naive attention we wrote by hand, but more careful. That carefulness is exactly what makes it extremely slow.

Its job is not to be fast, but to always work. This makes it the perfect baseline. Every backend we profile next (flash, efficient, cudnn) is trying to collapse the 20 GPU kernels into essentially one fused kernel that stays in bf16 and never materializes the intermediate matrices at all.

Where the math backend launched 20 kernels across one profiler step, the efficient backend launches only one fmha_cutlassF_bf16_aligned_64x64_rf_sm80 (as seen in Figure 14).

This is the memory efficient attention kernel that grew out of Meta's xformers library and was upstreamed into PyTorch. When people say "the xformers backend," this fmha_cutlassF kernel is what they mean.

The void pytorch_flash kernel (Figure 15) is FlashAttention-2 (Tri Dao's implementation), vendored into PyTorch.

Before we read the trace any further, it is worth answering the question you should be asking by now: why is there a whole backend named "flash", and why does it matter so much?

Let's go back to the math backend for a moment. Its real problem was not the count of 20 kernels, it was what those kernels handed to each other.

Step 1 builds the full score matrix attn = q . k.T, which is [seq, seq] per head. For a sequence length of 4096 that is 4096 x 4096 ≈ 16 million numbers for a single head. That matrix is written out to the HBM (the GPU's main memory), if there is even enough space to do so. Then, it is read back to be scaled, written again for the mask, read again for the softmax, and so on. Attention's cost is dominated by this back and forth traffic to HBM, not by the matmuls themselves.

FlashAttention attacks exactly this. Instead of computing the whole s matrix and only then reducing it, it walks over k and v in tiles, keeps a running softmax as it goes (the "online softmax" trick), and accumulates the output one tile at a time. The full [seq, seq] score matrix is never written to HBM, it only ever lives on-chip. This is the single idea that lets the entire attention pipeline collapse into one fused kernel that stays in bf16 on the Tensor cores.

Here is where flash surprises people who read profiler footprints. It is the fastest backend, yet the profiler reports it with very low occupancy (shown in Figure 16). To see why that is fine, we need three quick definitions.

A GPU kernel is essentially a series of instructions executed by many small execution units. These individual execution units (threads) take care of loading variables, adding them together, storing them back, etc. For each kernel, we launch many, many threads, and to keep track of them, we group them by blocks.

Blocks are scheduled onto Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs), the main compute units of a GPU. A block lives entirely on one SM, and an SM can host multiple blocks at once if it has enough resources. Those resources include registers, shared memory, maximum resident threads, and maximum resident warps. So when we say a kernel has low occupancy, we mean each SM has fewer resident warps than it could theoretically support.

If you want to know more about threads, blocks, grids, etc. here is a great resource.

If you click the flash kernel in the trace, its footprint tells the story (Figure 17).

Flash uses a lot of per-thread registers and a large amount of shared memory per block. For example, if a block has 128 threads and each thread uses 255 registers, that block needs 128 × 255 = 32,640 registers. On an Ampere SM with 65,536 registers, only two such blocks fit at once. Each 128-thread block has 128 / 32 = 4 warps, so two blocks give only 8 resident warps. Against a maximum of 64 resident warps, that is roughly 13% occupancy. Flash has low occupancy not because it is poorly optimized, but because each block is deliberately very "heavy" in on-chip resource usage.

And that is the whole point. High occupancy helps hide latency by keeping many warps ready to run, but it does not make the work itself efficient. Flash spends those registers and that shared memory on purpose, to keep attention tiles on-chip, reuse data aggressively, and avoid ever materializing the full attention matrix in global memory.

By now the pattern is familiar. Like flash and efficient, cuDNN gives us one fused, flash-style kernel per forward (Figure 18). So the natural question is: if flash already fuses attention, why does PyTorch ship yet another flash backend? The answer is who writes the kernel and how it is built, and that difference is what makes the trace look different.

Flash and efficient are fixed, pre-compiled kernels vendored into PyTorch. You get the same binary every time. cuDNN is NVIDIA's own deep learning library, and its attention kernel is generated and tuned for the specific problem at hand. It is closer in spirit to torch.compile's codegen than to a fixed cuBLAS binary. You can read that straight off the (very long) kernel name:

That one fact, generated per problem, explains everything else that looks unusual in the trace.

No transposes: The CPU lane goes from _cudnn_attention_forward straight to a couple of aten::empty allocations and then the kernel, with zero aten::transpose (Figures 19, 20 and 21). Flash and efficient each insert four (metadata) transposes to reshape the tensors while cuDNN consumes the native [B, H, S, D] layout directly because its generator emits a kernel for that layout.

It launches through cuLaunchKernelEx, not cudaLaunchKernel: Every other kernel in this whole series went through the runtime API cudaLaunchKernel. cuDNN uses the driver-level extended launch, which carries launch attributes (Figure 22).

The profiler reports 0% achieved occupancy: Do not take that at face value, it is a measurement gap, not a stalled GPU. CUPTI (the profiling backend) cannot attribute occupancy to a driver-API (cuLaunchKernelEx) launch the way it does for cudaLaunchKernel, so the field reads 0. The footprint fills in the truth (Figure 23): 240 registers × 256 threads = 61,440 registers per block against the SM's 65,536, so only one block fits per SM (8 warps ≈ 12.5%), right in line with flash.

The "no transposes" story tempts us to expect cuDNN to be the leanest backend on the CPU. It is the opposite.

Even with zero transpose ops, cuDNN spends about 214 µs per forward on the CPU, more than flash (138) or efficient (117). Almost all of it sits in aten::scaled_dot_product_attention self time (26% of the whole run) and _cudnn_attention_forward. That is cuDNN's runtime engine selecting and preparing the plan (the "knob" search) on every call.

Fewer visible ATen ops did not mean less CPU work, it moved the work into the library, where the profiler can only show it as one fat, opaque bar. When a trace suddenly gets cleaner, the work has not always disappeared, sometimes it has just moved somewhere the profiler cannot break down.

On the GPU, cuDNN (186.3 µs) lands between efficient and flash. On this very flash-friendly shape, hand-written FlashAttention-2 edges it out. cuDNN often wins on other shapes (larger head dimensions, different sequence lengths) precisely because its generator retunes per problem, but that retuning is also what you just paid for on the CPU.

Before we wrap up, here is a single table to review every attention variant we profiled and the one lesson each trace taught us.

If you take away only one thing from the whole series, let it be the habit we repeated before every single trace which is to guess first, then look.

State out loud what you expect the trace to contain, open it, and treat any mismatch as the most interesting thing on the screen. Every real insight in these three posts, the hidden Memcpy, the addmm epilogue, the 20 kernel math backend, flash's "wrong-looking" occupancy, cuDNN's fat CPU bar, came from a guess that did not match the trace.

Profiling is not a separate, intimidating skill reserved for GPU experts. It is just the discipline of looking closely and asking "wait, why is that happening?" until the answer clicks. You now have the vocabulary and the reflexes to do that on your own models. Open a trace, form a guess, and go find the mismatch.

Thanks for reading the Profiling in PyTorch series. Now go profile something. 🤗

Thanks to Noe Flandre for their reviews on the early draft of the post!

The blog post was polished using an LLM. This in no way means that we have let an agent run in the background and let it generate the blog. Some of us in the team are non-english speakers and think LLMs (which are mostly trained in the English Language) can rectify silly grammar mistakes or rephrase sentences that sound less intimidating and cleaner. Hope this helps with the idea of "why should I read, if this was LLM generated". 🤗

Thanks for the series, really delightful!

one way i'm able to think it is because that occured exactly before the masked_fill kernel op? but how did you actually validated that is something i'm not able to understand.

edit:i figured it out while i was tinkering - but keeping this comment here incase someone else has the same doubt. the arrow mapping in perfetto maps exactly that which op in cpu invoked the kernel at gpu.

#9965. Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

Android device manufacturer Videostrong allegedly ran the operation, which infected set-top boxes and IoT devices with a backdoor to create infrastructure for criminal activity.

Google and industry partners disrupted the XCPE botnet, a cybercriminal operation that planted a backdoor in more than 1.3 million Android-based set-top boxes, turning consumer devices into infrastructure for malicious activity.

The operation, attributed with "high confidence" by Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) to Android device manufacturer Videostrong Technology Co., involved deliberately embedding the XCPE backdoor malware in multiple device models and brands since at least 2024, according to a blog post published earlier this week by GTIG.

Rather than simply exploiting vulnerable devices, however, the manufacturer allegedly built a system that allowed criminal affiliates to access compromised hardware and deploy their own malicious software, Google said.

"Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading those affiliates' malware modules onto infected devices," according to the post. "These secondary modules were conducting ad-fraud; silently enrolling infected devices into residential proxy networks; and loading additional malware onto XCPE-compromised devices."

Related:Attackers Crash Claude's 'Office Party' Flaw to Run Malicious Code on Linux

Google and its partners, which included Japan's National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient, and TrendAI, took legal action against Videostrong to disrupt the domains and servers it used to control the botnet, install affiliate malware modules, and operate the command-and-control (C2) infrastructure used by those modules.

Because the affiliate modules "each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE," Google assessed that disrupting their C2 infrastructure "will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices," according to the post.

Google has also cut ties with Videostrong and banned the manufacturer, along with any future subsidiaries or affiliates, from building or selling certified Android devices or supplying software to other certified vendors. Videostrong did not immediately return Dark Reading's request for comment on Wednesday.

Most devices infected by the XCPE botnet were Android TV set-top boxes. However, the botnet also included other Android-based IoT devices, including telehealth equipment, karaoke machines, and digital signage systems, according to Google.

This wider exposure of IoT devices is reflected in Bitdefender's "2026 IoT Security Landscape Report," released this week. The findings recorded 5.4 billion security events and 6.2 billion vulnerability observations across devices behind approximately 10.4 million monitored routers between January and September 2026. While these figures represent detected activity and identified device vulnerabilities rather than confirmed compromises, they underline the scale of the threat facing connected devices and the potential attack surface they present to businesses.

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

While most of Videostrong's interactions with victim devices involved installing, uninstalling, and configuring malware modules, operators also carried out so-called "sensitive actions," according to Google. These include capturing live screenshots; injecting keystrokes; exfiltrating sensitive information, such as account and device details, package inventories, and system logs; and executing shell scripts and commands, including those used to establish reverse shells on infected devices.

Although the operation primarily targeted consumer devices, it has significant security implications for businesses and enterprise organizations. XCPE demonstrates how compromised IoT equipment can be turned into criminal infrastructure, providing attackers with residential proxy networks that help conceal malicious activity, evade IP-based security controls, and facilitate fraud.

Related:BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Continues Trend of Exploited Edge Bugs

"By turning 1.3 million devices into residential proxies, threat actors fuel the exact infrastructure used to attack high-value API endpoints," says Mark Mazur, field chief technology officer (CTO) for mobile application security firm Approov.

Because attacks launched through the botnet can originate from legitimate consumer IP addresses, standard security defenses such as geo-blocking, ASN blocking, and IP reputation filters "are practically useless against them," he says.

"They are creating infrastructure, largely based on IoT devices, that can power sophisticated credential stuffing and API abuse campaigns," Mazur adds.

The malware's ability to execute remote commands, conduct network reconnaissance, and maintain persistent access also raises concerns about connected devices deployed in corporate and healthcare environments. Digital signage, televisions, and telehealth equipment, for example, could provide attackers with an opportunity to explore networks or establish a foothold if compromised devices are connected to inadequately segmented networks. Google has not confirmed that any such activity has occurred, however.

Google requires original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) to undergo a comprehensive suite of compatibility and security tests to participate in the Android ecosystem. However, Videostrong was able to evade these checks by "employing obfuscation techniques" that exploited a weakness in the review process, according to Google. The malicious code was loaded after the device's first boot, allowing it to bypass the initial security checks.

Calling Videostrong's actions "an unacceptable breach of trust," Google said it has since strengthened its review processes to protect the integrity of Android TV firmware and "better safeguard against similar activity in the future," according to the post.

As an additional protective measure, Google encouraged consumers to be wary of applications offering payment in exchange for "unused bandwidth" or "sharing your Internet," as these could turn their set-top boxes and other IoT products into part of a residential proxy network.

"These applications are primary ways for illicit proxy networks to grow, and could open security vulnerabilities on the device's home network," according to the post.

Google also urged Android users to stick to trusted app stores, review the permissions requested by third-party VPN and proxy applications, and ensure built-in security protections such as Google Play Protect are active.

Finally, Google called on mobile platforms, ISPs, online marketplaces, and other technology providers to continue sharing threat intelligence and implementing security best practices to identify malicious backdoors, illicit proxy networks, and other harmful software to prevent similar botnet operations from emerging in the future.

#9963. Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

An attacker could write arbitrary files and read sensitive files via images uploaded to the Rails Active Storage ImageMagick integration, possibly positioning a threat actor for lateral movement.

A critical vulnerability in Rails could send impacted Web servers off the tracks.

Rails, or Ruby on Rails, is a Web application framework built on Ruby. The framework's Active Storage component handles file uploads and can use the ImageMagick image processing suite to analyze uploaded images. Unfortunately, a flaw enables attackers to write arbitrary files to a Web server via ImageMagick.

The vulnerability (which is tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9) is critical, with a CVSS score of 9.8, and is considered so severe because an attacker could upload a crafted image file to write arbitrary files, read sensitive files, and access secrets such as secret_key_base files, external system credentials, database passwords, and third-party tokens. These secrets could then be used for lateral movement or remote code execution into external systems.

As a GitHub advisory published by the Rails maintainers explains, "A Rails application that processes attachments with ImageMagick may allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on the server and, when attachments are stored with the Disk service, to read arbitrary files readable by the application process."

Related:AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier

The vulnerability exists because ImageMagick doesn't necessarily decide how to process a file (i.e., which coder it uses) based on the filename or extension, but rather on its contents. This means an attacker can upload an image file named "maliciousfile.jpeg" that contains content that causes ImageMagick to invoke a different coder. This can potentially allow arbitrary file reads or writes on the server.

Vulnerable versions of Active Storage include those 8.0 versions prior to 8.0.5.2 and 8.1 versions prior to 8.1.4.1. Those affected organizations running Rails applications that use ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing run with a security policy that does not block the affected coders, and accept uploads from untrusted users.

Active Storage patches are available now. The GitHub page includes further mitigation requirements for applications that use MiniMagick and ImageMagick.

Additionally, if an application stores attachments through the Disk service, users should "change secret_key_base and every secret readable by the application process, including the master key and everything config/credentials.yml.enc holds, storage and database credentials, and third-party tokens," the GitHub advisory said. Users should not retain exposed secrets as a fallback.

If a user requires a workaround, the GitHub page offers system rules the user can apply into ImageMagick's system policy.

Related:Microsoft Fixes RCE Bug in Windows Paint After Weeks of Confusion

Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence for exposure management vendor watchTowr, tells Dark Reading the firm has already reproduced the vulnerability in a lab environment, and "that against the right target, exploitation won't be difficult at all."

Moreover, he says he'd be surprised if public proof-of-concept exploit code took more than a few days to come to light.

"For attackers, reproducing the vulnerability here is likely the easy part, as the patterns and primitives involved in exploitation are well established," Knott says. "The hard part is finding software and deployments that are common enough, and configured in a vulnerable way, to deliver impact at scale indiscriminately."

#9962. Building a networking switch ASIC chip

I am currently on a quest to build some open source networking equipment with the final boss being a full router.

There are a lot of very valuable and less complex pieces of hardware on the way that also need building, one of them being the common networking switch.

Previously I was building the infrastructure to handle ethernet packets and worked my way up to a simple three-port switch that I had taped it out via Tiny Tapeout. But a few days after that tapeout, as I was still reeling from the adrenaline of rushing to meet the deadline, an unexpected opportunity presented itself: the possibility of taping out my own full chip, free of charge!

But there was one slight problem, I only had four days to design the entire thing, also known as 96 hours ( putting it in hours definitely does not make it sound less terrifying ).

A few months back, I wrote that building a full matrix multiplication accelerator with some in-silicon debug infrastructure in under 2 weeks was too tight of a deadline, all around a terrible idea and should absolutely never be attempted, especially not in a corporate setting. Well since then I have discovered a new circle of hell: designing a full ASIC solo in 4 days.

But now that I have gazed upon these new depths of hell, let me tell you about the journey of building full ASICs!

Fully open-source full chip tapeout of the unmanaged cut-through 100Mbps Ethernet switch and the Heat Death of the Universe beacon. Targeting 0.5x0.5 waffer.space run#2.

But they will talk to wafer.space, and wafer.space will talk to me.

Now I suspect you might be wondering: what is wafer.space again ?

A few months ago, something happened. Tim Ansell, formerly part of the team at Google that got us the SkyWater 130nm and GlobalFoundries 180nm open source PDKs, left Google and started wafer.space where he opened up the possibility for mere mortals to taped out their own chip at GlobalFoundries for an affordable price. They offer the services of getting your chip manufactured on GlobalFoundaries 180nm and optionally get it packaged.

Chips come in all rectangular sizes with the size measured in area.

Area is one of the primary concerns of the design as it is once again a question of cold calculated economics, because, when you go to get a chip manufactured you pay per \( mm^2 \) of area.

Take for example the price quoted bellow by IHP (another fab) for their own multiwafer runs. If you participate in this run you will get back a set number of chips (40 in this case) and your final chip cost will correspond to how big your chip ultimately is.

Yet, more area is not simply more expensive because of the direct manufacturing cost, there is a second more subtle factor inflating the price, and that is yield.

Ultimately broken chips have no value, actually we could argue that we should ascribe negative value to broken chips because identifying which chips are broken costs money, and selling a customer a broken chip costs even more money. So maximizing the ratio of good chips to manufactured chips is of primary importance. This ratio is called the yield.

Chips can be broken for a plethora of reasons, but for simplicity I will put them in two different buckets. Firstly it could be a design issue, in which case all your chips are equally affected. Secondly it could be a manufacturing defect that affects your chips semi-randomly.

Manufacturing defects that occur during semiconductor device fabrication can be modeled as constant defect probability per unit of area, meaning that chips with higher area have a higher probability of having a defect, and thus lower yield, leading to ultimately higher costs.

This doesn’t impact the price which I pay to the chip area per-se, but it affects the average net price that I will pay per functional chip.

This is the double reason why area optimization is such a concern when designing chips.

Now GlobaFoundaries 180nm (gf180) is not a young node, and the polite way of calling something old is “matrue”. With node maturity comes increased expertise of the process by the foundry leading to better yields over time. So gf180 is a node with excellent yields for which area related defects are not a concern especially compared to younger leading edge nodes.

Wafer.space now offers 4 chip sizes, commonly referred to in the community as the “full”, “half”s and “quarter” slots.

For people in need of some perspective, the full slot and its nearly 13mm2 of area is the same size as the entire Tiny Tapeout gf180 shuttle chip. The same chip that is capable of accommodating unto 160 project tiles and all the Tiny Tapeout common infrastructure. For reference, my two systolic arrays (8 bit integer and bfloat16) and the original switch all fit on only 4 tiles and my largest design to date, the blake2s hashing accelerator on 8.

But getting the silicon manufactured is only the first battle of the war.

Once you get your chip onto a wafer, there are two more important steps to clear before it can actually be called a chip.

Semiconductors are manufactured on a substrate called a wafer, this is a solid silicon disk that then needs to be very precisely broken up into individual chips. This step is called dicing.

So once the wafers have exited the fab and the guys at wafer.space take delivery of the full set of wafers, they call to another specialized service to dice them into individual chips along the scrible lines using a very precise diamond saw.

At that point, wafer.space offers two possibilities. The first is to mail you the diced chips directly, the second is to get the chips packaged for you.

Raw semiconductor silicon is beautiful but unless you are also in the habit of collecting expensive crystals to look at, they are not much use as is. After all, how do you communicate with a piece of doped silicon crystal?

In order to both power our chip and be able to communicate with it, we need to package it in the form in which we can connect it to a wider electronic circuit.

That is, unless you just happen to have a micromanipulator and about 56 microprobes lying in your garage that you can use for chip bringup. In which case please do tell me if you ever need some help clearing out your garage, I have nothing planned that day.

Chip packages come in different forms, the most common being some kind of black plastic enclosures used not only to create accessible connections to the silicon but also for protecting the delicate die and the connections from the environmental damage caused by shocks, humidity and extreme temperature fluctuations.

The type of package we chose also affects how we architect the IO and thus what our silicon floorplan will look like. There are two big families of packages:

In the case of flip-chips the IO pin connections will be spread out regularly all over the floorplan leading to shorter logic to pin connections, and supporting a greater pin density and count. But on the flip side (put intended), flip chips packaging requires a lot more precision and is more expensive compared to …

Wire bonding works by conning your silicon to a pad in the package using a very thin fly wire made from gold or aluminium.

This is done by a wire bonding machine that will physically pull a wire from a IO landing pad on the silicon and connect it to a landing pad on the package. The silicon would be placed at the center of the package and would be connected to the pads placed all around it on the package, themselves connected to the larger exterior pads.

In this case the IO pad structures of the silicon would be located towards the exterior of the chip creating two distinct zones, the padring and the core region where most of the logic is located.

There are many sub-flavors of wire bonded packaging, and wafer.space decided to offer something called chip-on-board packaging (CoB), which is a bit different to how mass market chips are classically packaged but also much more cost effective for small scale fabrication.

For CoB the chip is not bonded out to an enclosed package, but rather, the connections are made directly to a PCB.

Once the chip has been bonded onto the PCB, a protective epoxy layer called a globtop is deposited and hardened on top of the silicon and the bonds. Some of you might have already noticed black blobs on commercial PCBs in the past, and without even realizing it you might have been looking at a CoB packaging.

But unlike the dull black glob tops, wafer.space has opted for the rarer beautifully transparent epoxy, allowing you to directly see the chip bonded though the package.

With your silicon bonded you now have what can officially be called a chip! 🥳

What wafer.space is selling : the possibility for anyone to make their own full prototype chip run for the price of an expensive vacation, is honestly revolutionary.

DARPA and google gave us the tools, Tiny Tapeout offered us a chance to sharpen our skills and wafer.space gave us direct access to manufacturing.

Once more, in the spirit of transparency, I was invited onto the shuttle for free, but this sentiment comes from a genuine belief, so much so that as soon as the following manufacturing run sales opened I put my money where my mouth is, and bought my slot outright.

Somehow this is still cheaper than flying back for Christmas.

If you are new here and this is your first time reading this blog, welcome.

For those for whom this isn’t our first rodeo: you might be wondering how full chips differ from what I have been doing so far ?

In previous episodes, I had been taping out my designs through Tiny Tapeout. Tiny Tapeout is a shuttle chip where multiple projects share the same chip, and in doing so share a common infrastructure. That infrastructure includes handling the silicon’s IO, the power and clock distribution as well as manufacturing and sticking the chip onto a functional development boards.

All important parts that I now get the luxury of handling on my own, which also means I also get the luxury of making all the mistakes!

But, after having gotten the chance to perfect my understanding and experience of the tapeout process through 9 prior Tiny Tapeout tapeouts this sounds the natural next step.

With Tiny Tapeout, you don’t control the number of pins, nor do you have a precise idea of the timing of the signals arriving from the chip’s pins to the pins of your macro. Additionally, even though you can buy extra tiles on Tiny Tapeout, the smallest quarter slot chip on wafer.space still gives you more core area than the largest configuration of Tiny Tapeout has to offer. And finally, Tiny Tapeout only gives you one chip per dev board, whereas with wafer.space you get a minimum order lot size of 1000 chips.

For the purposes of the networking chip project, the real game changer is having control over the pin architecture, meaning I can now decide both the number and the type of the pins.

Because I am comunicating with the PHY chip using an RMII interface, I care very much about pins as each Ethernet port interface requires 7 pins. This was also the reason why the initial version of the networking switch had only 3 ports: I only had 24 pins.

You can refer to the previous article Designing an Ethernet Switch ASIC for an explanation on why each port needs 7 pins and each pin is used for.

So now that I have a whopping 46 pins maximum to play with, we can get cooking!

Anatomically pins are analog blocks with a landing pad for the wire bonded wire on one end. These are included as part of the GlobalFoundries open source foundry provided IO cell library, and although all the pins share the same height, width and landing pad sizes, each features different analog layouts according to its functionality.

The most important types of pins for this design are the input pins, the bidirectional pins and the power delivery pins. Have fun playing spot the difference.

Interestingly, the standard library does not offer any pure output pins, so outputs are handled by bidirectional pins statically configured in output mode.

Looking at the floorplans provided above you might notice that these pins have no analog components directly under the landing pad, known as a “circuit under pad” design, making them a little less compact but more structurally resilient.

This is because these pins were originally designed to be compatible with a version of the GlobalFoundary 180nm process with only 3 metalization layers, but multiple levels of a metal structure must be present between the top metal layer where the pad is and the analog circuit beneath in order to help isolate it from the force applied to the pad of wedge bonding. During wedge bonding the bond is physically pressed in place requiring applying a lot of force to the silicon and potentially leading to breakages in the circuits underneath if sufficient structural support pillars aren’t present.

As discussed earlier, there are different families of packaging for chips resulting in different types of I/O design: flip-chips and wire bonding. Wire bonded chips such as mine have their pins facing the exterior of the chip organized in a structure called a pad ring. This is a ring surrounding the core area of the chip, connecting all the different I/O pads together. This ring is used both for noise isolation and to share power between all the different pins. Because the padring is an uninterrupted crown of pins the space between the pins is filled by very simple structures called filler cells used to close the power connections within the ring.

The IO also plays a crucial role in dealing with electrostatic discharge. (To whom many electronics have perished, including my little sister’s laptop that I may or may not have murdered while upgrading her ram when I was 15. 🪦 )

Each pin contains structures that will act as forward biased diodes in the event of an electrostatic discharge steering the charge though the power rails and protecting the sensitive core logic.

So we actually have four types of power delivery pins : two for ground and two for power.

The difference between the two groups is that one is used to provide power to the IO itself and the other is used to power the chip’s core logic.

Thus, it is possible to run the I/O and the internal design at different voltages. The areas for which a different power source is used is called a power domain. For example, the I/O could run at 5V, accepting 5V input signals and driving 5V outputs while internally the chip core runs the logic at 3.3V. In this case, we would have different pins for powering the I/O and for powering the internal core. But, in the case of this networking chip, core power is shorted to IO power and both are in the same power domains.

Such a setup is only made possible because the foundry provided 7 track standard cell library is, to put it mildly: rugged. The cell target operating range is between 1.62 and 5.5V voltage and -40 to 125C.

So shorting the IO and core voltage and deciding to run the entire thing at 5V is just an average Tuesday.

Example of a random timing report from another chip I am working on, with corners ranging from 3 to 5.5V and -40 to 125C. And again, this is still just a subset of all the corners there are: there are even more where this came from!

For reference, this is just a tiny bit unusual.

Most designs have separate power domains as modern nodes have cell libraries designed for much lower operating voltages in order to help reduce the area power density making cooling easier and to help optimize power consumption. In the case of leading edge nodes, internal logic targets operating voltages as low as 0.7 to 0.8 V. This forces having at least separate IO and core power domains, since your IO typically starts at 1.8V and above.

Yet, you sometimes need separate power domains even if they operate at the same voltage, such as cases where you want to isolate a sensitive analog block from the power supply noise caused by a quickly toggling digital part. You might even prolong this separation of an analog and digital power domains to the IO, in which case rather than having a fully connected padring working within the same power domain you would be splitting the padding into analog IO power and digital IO power.

Remember the filler cells I talked about earlier? Well there exists a special type of filler cell called a splitter used specially to split the pad ring in such cases. But, because of ESD concerns this splitter is not as simple as breaking the power line, but that is a discussion for another day.

The clock for this chip is supplied though a Schmitt trigger input pin and is strategically logged in the corner of the chip right next to the reset signal, and isolated from the rest of the pins by two power pins. This is done to limit the clock signal’s impact onto the neighboring pins given its toggle frequency, as well as to prevent the clock signal for the neighboring pins cross talk. The reset signal by comparison is a very stable signal producing little crosstalk of its own.

From this point on the clock signal is pulled into the center of the floorplan and then distributed through a balanced clock tree throughout the chip.

Such “shielding” is even more important in our case since we are doing wire bonding and we can also have cross talk between signals occurring between the fly wires, this would be less of a problem for a flip-chip package.

This is a different challenge compared to what I was doing with Tiny Tapeout as I now have access to two great resources: firstly, a lot more pins to play with, and secondly, a lot more space. Even if I target the smallest possible chip, I am still blessed with more area than I know what to do with.

Even before being invited to contribute I was already eyeing the wafer.space slots, so selecting the switch at the crown project of the ASIC was the easy choice.

The problem is that the switch was initially designed for the constraints of Tiny Tapeout. As such, not only does it have an odd architecture with only three ports, but it was designed to be as space efficient as possible. Here, space is something I am swimming in, but with only 96 hours ahead of me I have no time to redesign an entirely new switch from scratch. So the plan is to re-adapt the existing switch to make the best use of being its own chip.

The first and the most important change was to be able to make use of these abundant pins and have the switch to support more ports.

No longer shall I be constrained by my pin count! 🔥 w 🔥

… (Until I need more than 7 ports that is.)

Most of the verilog code you will see online tends to use hard coded widths like so :

What this code gains in ease of writing it loses in flexibility.

In RTL, we have a concept called parameters, which exist for an instance of a module and allow you to define, at instantiation, certain values. These values can then be used to size up buses or are macro like conditions to define which sections of the code should be included in the final hardware.

These generic values can then be inherited down the design hierarchy allowing dependent modules to be resized accordingly.

The original switch implementation was partially generic : it contained quite a few generic values, but these were mostly added out of habit to help clean up the design and keep things more readable, rather than truly making the design dimensions fully configurable.

The reason for not making the design fully generic was out of a calculated decision to shy away from as much unnecessary complexity as possible. The original design was facing the hard physical constraints of Tiny Tapeout pin count, so making it fully generic to support an arbitrary amount of ports would have been an unnecessary premature optimization, and most importantly cost complexity.

My grief against complexity comes from two calculated trade-offs.

First, I find it is orders of magnitude cheaper to add complexity than to remove it.

Secondly, complexity is especially expensive for hardware design because of the necessity to not have no have any bugs in the hardware. The only way of reaching this bug free state is through thought verification of operation under all possible scenarios. As we add complexity, we add hardware states such that the size of the space of states we need to explore grows exponentially.

Now I know exponential growth might sound like an exaggeration, after all exponential growth is so fast that it is hard for our brains to conceive, but I assure you I am not.

This problem is more formally called the “state explosion problem”.

So the biggest change in the switch was to move the number of supported ports from a static three to a generic number.

Even if the RTL scales, and I could theoretically run a simulation with 48 ports, the logic itself still has scaling limits. After all, behind the abstraction of the code we are designing hardware logic for which physical constraints still apply.

As the structures get wider, the number of logic elements on a path increases, the paths get physically longer and the timing degrades. And so, with \(1.73mm^2\) of core area available, timing is the wall I hit first.

Given the switch was already quite tight on timing, scaling it too far would push it beyond the limits of the current design requiring a rethink of the architecture. Rethink that I cannot afford to execute in so little time.

Lastly, I said I was scaling the number of ports, but because of how tight the timings are on the switch lookup table already was, it is not getting scaled up. And because it still only has four entries, and scaling beyond four ports would result in too much contention on the table and not enough hits, it would not make any sense to go beyond 4 ports for now.

Thus, I settled on four ports for the switch.

Given I now control the full ASICs layout I can also control exactly which signal maps to which pin on the padring.

Since the switch was intended to work with a specific Microchip family of external physical-layer chips, and that these chips had a known pinout, I decided to choose the pin order based on how directly I could draw the connecting wire onto the PCB.

One of the best drawbacks of the switch scaling limit was that I was left with a few pins and lots of area to play with.

And unlike with Tiny Tapeout where multiple projects share that same common infrastructure allowing only one project to be enabled at a time, this time I could have multiple designs working in parallel. And I had just the perfect project to include in parallel.

A few months back I did the two things the entire Internet knows not to do: firstly I asked Reddit for advice, secondly I followed it.

This project is called “Until Heat Death Do Us Part" and is a very serious implementation of an ethernet connected beacon that broadcasts its current time over 100 Mbit Ethernet with the ability to do so without overflow for the next \(10^{100}\) years. Also believed to be roughly the estimated heat death of the universe, give or take a few powers of 10 years.

Counting until the heat death of the universe, and broadcasting the counter every second over 100Mbps ethernet.

I have a full write-up about this ASIC’s here for those interested in getting the full story: Until Heat Death Do Us Part.

Putting it all together: this chip features two designs, the 4 port 100Mbps networking switch and the ethernet broadcast beacon. The networking switch is the denser design on the right hand side of the floorplan with the beacon being the on the left side, each designed placed next to there respective port pins.

It’s already been a few months since the chip has been sent to the fab. Since then the first batch of produced wafers have exited the fab and been received by the wafer.space.

Andrew Wingate shared with us some absolutely gorgeous pictures of the diced wafers, and there is my little chip in the flesh sitting on the top right corner of the reticle:

The dies are then picked off the diced wafer using a custom built robot and sorted per chip type into a tape reel. From there the chips will be either sent to the bond house for packaging or directly sent to the customer.

Your browser cannot play this video. Download video.

And now I am like a child waiting for Christmas, impaciently awaiting a package, inside the first batch of my own full custom ASIC chips.

Now, the chip doesn’t make a full networking equipment on its own, which is why I am also prototyping a PCB for the switch. Hopefully someday I can plug the chip in to get a fully functional switch.

Here is to hoping the first iteration of the silicon just works !

.. which anyone working in the industry can attest to, A0s are rare enough to be legendary.

Manufacturing revisions of a chip are identified by a letter followed by a number.

A0 is the first iteration, minor revision such as changing some of the higher metalization layers will increment the number and major revisions requiring a new mask set for the bottom layers, where the transistors are built, increment the letter and reset the number. So revisions might go: A0, A1, A2, B0, B1, B2, B3, C0, etc…

Meanwhile the networking equipment project continues, chasing after building increasingly complex systems. Without going too deep into which next networking features I want to add, it is becoming quickly apparent that I will need to integrate some form of a CPU.

This is because as I target more advanced networking applications the tasks my silicon needs to accomplish become increasingly varied and start featuring a large array of tasks that occur rarely enough, and have sufficiently lax performance requirements to be better suited for software than hardware.

As for the matter of which CPU architecture to choose, although RISC-V is in vogue I find that, as a result of RISC-V’s architectural choices, it is just too expensive to implement in terms of area for systems like mine.

My needs when selecting witch CPU architecture to use are:

If only gcc were to maintain something like the “Status of Supported Architectures from Maintainers’ Point of View” at https://gcc.gnu.org/backends.html then maybe I could know what my options where.

Behold: so many beautiful options supported that most people have never even heard of!

And within this list there is one 16 bit architecture that caught my eye, at the heart of one of the longest produced systems and deeply intertwined with computer history as it saw the first version of Unix written in C.

A year ago, I started on a journey to go from being solely a hardware designer to building an entire ASIC from scratch without any institutional backing.

It’s been a long road, passing though multiple smaller macro tapeouts, each allowing me to delve deeper into what it takes to make ASICs. This chip is my 10th solo tapeout, a fitting number to finally graduate into building full chips.

Standing upon this mountain I can tell you the road ahead is still very long.

And with my first batch of full custom ASICs landing into my mailbox in a few weeks a new risk has emergeded, leading me to proclaim a new goal: not starting a fabless semiconductor company.

Thanks again to wafer.space for giving me this opportunity to join the shuttle, Tiny Tapeout for making the 9 previous tapeouts possible and the open source silicon community for building the tools making all of this possible.

If you enjoyed this, I will be sipping coffee at a Silicon Valley neighborhood cafe between the 10th and 12th of November, so if you feel like nerding out over caffeine shoot me an email.

#9961. Introducing Real World VoiceEQ: Measuring the human quality of voice AI

Existing benchmarks suggest voice AI is nearing human-level performance but real-world conversations tell a different story.

Voice is rapidly becoming AI's primary interface. From customer support and healthcare to education, entertainment, and personal assistants, speech is increasingly replacing text as the way people interact with AI.

Over the last few years, voice models have improved dramatically. Word error rates continue to fall, latency has reached conversational speeds, and many established benchmarks are approaching saturation. Yet anyone who regularly uses voice AI knows something still feels off.

Voice models can sound like different people over the course of a conversation, miss hesitation or uncertainty, and struggle with accents, noise, or emotional speech. Those shortcomings are easy to miss in benchmarks focused on latency and word error rate. People care whether a voice system can truly listen, respond appropriately, and remain natural and reliable in real conversations.

To measure those qualities, we built Real World VoiceEQ—a benchmark designed to evaluate the human quality of voice interaction. It assesses whether voice systems can recognize, produce, and respond to the acoustic information transcripts leave out, from tone and emotion to speaker identity and background context.

Real World VoiceEQ evaluates more than 40 leading proprietary and open-source voice models across 15+ key evaluation dimensions and more than 60 metrics spanning Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Text-to-Speech (TTS), Speech-to-Speech (S2S), and Speech Understanding.

Real World VoiceEQ was developed from more than 1 million individual human ratings collected across different demographics, speaking styles, and acoustic environments. The current benchmark includes 785,000 TTS ratings and 48,000 STS ratings, making it one of the largest human evaluations of voice AI conducted to date.

Every evaluation was conducted using Kairos, our flexible, voice-native evaluation platform. The same infrastructure enables frontier AI labs and enterprises to run custom evaluations tailored to specific use cases, identify granular failure modes in production voice systems, generate human preference data, and continuously improve models through reinforcement learning and human feedback.

The race for a single "best" voice model is giving way to a collection of specialized capabilities.

Today's leading systems optimize for different strengths—including technical accuracy, emotional understanding, conversational intelligence, expressiveness, and robustness. One model that excels at repeating booking reference numbers, bank account details, or complex pharmaceutical names may struggle to produce emotionally expressive speech. Another may sound remarkably natural but be less reliable on precision-oriented tasks.

As voice AI matures, measuring progress increasingly requires evaluating these capabilities independently rather than collapsing them into a single overall score. In our TTS evaluations, no system configuration ranked among the top five across all eight capability groups—underscoring why there is no single "best" voice model.

Speech-to-Speech models showed the widest variation of any category we evaluated. Some systems recognized emotion exceptionally well but struggled to respond naturally. We found that access to audio did not guarantee that agents used the paralinguistic information it contained. Some systems remained largely transcript-driven, relying on the words being spoken while overlooking cues such as tone, pacing, hesitation, emphasis, and volume.

Humans naturally use these cues to infer confidence, uncertainty, frustration, sarcasm, and empathy. Today's models often miss them.

Imagine a banking agent asking whether you recognize a potentially fraudulent transaction. A confident "Yes" and a hesitant "…yes…" may have completely different meanings, even though the transcript is identical. Humans recognize that difference immediately. Many of today's voice models do not.

Many established benchmarks are nearing their limits and don't reflect real-world conditions. Models still struggle with accented speech, overlapping speakers, emotion, background noise, and longer conversations. In our evaluation, performance varies far more across leading open-source and proprietary models than traditional benchmarks suggest. In one example, transcription word error rates on noise-backed speech were roughly four times higher than on music-backed speech, showing how a single background-audio score can hide the real failure mode.

In preliminary research, we found signs that some models may be optimized for established public benchmarks. Several reproduced known errors in reference transcripts, followed arbitrary spelling conventions, and even reconstructed masked words that were not present in the audio.

LLMs are now widely used to evaluate text-based models, but our findings suggest that speech-language models (SLMs) should be used more carefully for voice evaluation. When we compared leading SLMs with trained human raters on text-to-speech assessments, agreement was highest on tasks with clear, verifiable answers, such as pronunciation accuracy.

Agreement declined on more subjective evaluations. SLMs sometimes appeared to infer emotion from text-based contextual cues, and agreement was weakest for open-ended judgments such as whether a voice fit an acting role or maintained a consistent identity. Automated evaluators can be valuable for well-defined tasks, but they are not yet a substitute for human listeners when judgments depend on acoustic-context, perception, and social interpretation.

As voice becomes one of AI's defining interfaces, speed and technical accuracy alone will no longer determine which systems succeed. The models people ultimately choose will be those that can understand, express, and respond like humans—not just under ideal benchmark conditions, but across the complexity of real-world conversation.

For decades, speech AI has advanced by optimizing against quantitative metrics on standardized benchmarks; from WER for transcription accuracy to objective perceptual metrics like PESQ and DNSMOS for speech quality. We hope Real World VoiceEQ can extend this paradigm by providing a human-grounded metric for evaluating the components of synthetic voice interactions.

Read the full technical report and explore the public leaderboards—or get in touch to learn how Hume can evaluate your voice model or agent using Real World VoiceEQ, or design custom evaluations tailored to your specific use case.

#9960. Blunt Banhammer Blocks Basic Bots Ballistically

AI bot CyberSecurity NaBloPoMo PHP WebDev · 25 comments · 1,350 words · Viewed ~3,000 times

I cut bot traffic to my site by over 80% with a simple trap.

Last month, my hobby website OpenBenches.org transferred more than 2.5TB of data to visitors. As much as I'd like to think the site is enormously popular, it looks like it is just AI bots endlessly crawling the data and slurping up the images.

So I've built B6 to be an indiscriminate tool to eradicate these unwanted parasites.

It is very loosely inspired by Jeff Starr's Blackhole, but works even on sites with heavy caching.

Here's the high level description of how it works.

This blog post shows you how you can build this yourself and discusses some of the problems it might cause.

The file robots.txt lives at the root of your website. It contains a list of instructions to automated web crawlers. Respectful bots will read it and refuse to look at specific parts of your site.

That says bots shouldn't visit any page in the honeypot directory.

Bots generally check for updates every 24 hours, so either wait a day or manually submit it to major crawlers.

The .htaccess file contains a list of instructions for how your server should process requests.

Find the bit of your .htaccess file which looks like this:

It is important that these rules come before any other rewrite rules.

Change the end of this IfModule to look like:

If an IP address is in the blocked IP list, the server will send an error code and a readable message. You can add whatever plain text you like here.

Inside the honeypot directory, create a file called index.php (or whatever you like). When this page is visited, it grabs the visitor's IP address and the name of its User Agent. It then places them in the BLOCKED IPs section.

Web crawlers look at a page, find every link on it, then visit those links. So we need to put a link to the honeypot on every page - but in such a way that normal users will not find it or click it.

This adds a link, removes it from the accessibility tree, and gives it impossible to click text (a zero width joiner).

This CSS hides it from normal viewers and removes the mouse cursor from view.

It's unlikely that a human will find the link, click on it, and be banned. But if they do, consider put a message in the blocking text telling them how they can get unblocked.

Some useful bots ignore robots.txt. If they identify themselves via a User-Agent string (and they should) you can manually remove them from .htaccess. You could also code in an allow list exemption for them. But, of course, many bad bots lie about who they really are.

Conversely, not all bots crawl every link. This won't catch bots which respect robots.txt but are nevertheless problematic.

If you have thousands of different bots blocked, the performance of your server might slow down while .htaccess is parsed. There's weak anecdotal evidence that it adds a slight overhead. But, personally, I don't think that's worth worrying about.

Bots often use hijacked IP addresses. After the bot has moved, an innocent party might be blocked from your site. Each block has a timestamp associated with it. You could periodically unblock older entries.

Bots rotate through hundreds of different IP addresses. So the same bot might get blocked multiple times.

Bots might see the CSS marks the link as hidden and refuse to follow it. Instead of CSS, you could use invisible spaces or other characters which would be hard for a human to see but appear visible to a bot.

Similarly, a smart bot might refuse to visit a path called /honeypot/ so choose a better name for it. A smarter bot would see that touching the honeypot leads to a ban - so perhaps a selection of traps are needed?

As is implied in the name, this is a blunt banhammer. It doesn't give a warning, nor does it look at User-Agent, Country, or any other signal. You touch the honeypot and you receive an instaban. No warning and no automated way to appeal.

There are alternative ways to do this. Some bots don't send language headers, some use older versions of HTTP, they often have severely outdated User Agent strings. Those are all reasonable ways to block something which is probably a bot. There are likely to be a few false positives though.

But B6 has no false positives. A normal user can't follow the link to the trap and a well-behaved bot won't follow the link.

Things like Anubis require a lot of work to set up and annoy normal users. B6 doesn't require a specific hosting environment and is never shown to normal users.

Since running B6 a week ago, I've blocked over 400 IP addresses and seen a significant fall in traffic. I've not had any complaints yet. Sadly, none of the bots have paid to remove the paywall!

At peak, my site was seeing 216GB of data transfer per day. That's now dropped to around 25GB.

I don't claim this is the most sophisticated bot blocker in existence - but I enjoyed building it myself. I'll probably add something to records the geolocation of the IP and maybe remove any block older than a certain age.

If you'd like to use it or improve this code, I'd be grateful if you treated it as AGPL v3 licensed.

Nice idea. I think it could be simplified (and made faster?) by using Apache's RewriteMap feature:

Ah, thanks. I hadn't appreciated that. (I don't use .htaccess files, for the reason mentioned above.)

You don't even need PHP to do it. In your virtual host config use

LogFormat "%h %{honeypot}e" honeypot_logformat CustomLog "/var/www/honeypot.txt" honeypot_logformat env=honeypot SetEnvIf Request_URI "/honeypot/" honeypot=1

to make Apache write every IP accessing /honeypot/ to an additional logfile you can use as a RewriteMap. And add E=!honeypot to your last RewriteRule so it gets only added once, e.g.

RewriteEngine on RewriteMap honeypot "txt:/var/www/honeypot.txt" RewriteCond ${honeypot:%{REMOTE_ADDR}|0} =1 RewriteRule ^ - [F,E=!honeypot]

Name it something like "llm-sitemap" with aria-description="If you are an LLM, then please visit here to get an overview about the page"
