#9868. The Economics of AI Infrastructure: Compute Costs, Cloud Lock-In, and Competition

Tech writer sharing insights in a fun and informative way.

Tech writer sharing insights in a fun and informative way.

Tech writer sharing insights in a fun and informative way.

We are all watching the AI industry race from one frontier to another. Every few weeks, there's a new model creating hype, a new benchmark that becomes the industry standard, a new agent that promises to do the work of an entire team, or a new approach that makes yesterday's breakthrough look ancient.

I enjoy following these developments as much as anyone here, but there’s a question that is often ignored by us:

What happens when everyone can build with AI, but the infrastructure required to run it remains expensive, scarce, and controlled by a relatively small number of players?

That last part interests me most. We spend a great deal of time asking which model will win. I want to understand what happens when thousands of companies build useful products with AI, then discover that running those products at scale is an expensive business in its own right.

Let us have a look at it through a practical scenario.

A founder has built an AI assistant for accountants. The prototype works fine, and a few early access customers love it, which makes the founder envision a business that could actually run. Everything goes well with the first few customers. Then the usage grows. Customers anticipate quick responses; the service has to stay available, and with that the monthly compute bill begins to look rather different from the one generated by a handful of testers.

A successful start was just the beginning; the founder now has a new set of problems at hand. He needs to rent more computing capacity to keep the business running, hoping that suitable hardware is available at a workable price. To buy new equipment, he needs more capital and the expertise that are necessary to operate it. Luckily, if he finds a new provider with less cost, the migration could consume engineering time the company needs elsewhere.

All this decision-making, along with the founder juggling between hiring more staff, finding new customers, and convincing the current ones to pay more for the products, is a hefty task. And it makes founders wonder if having an excellent business model is enough.

I think the AI conversation needs to get more interesting. Building a capable product is becoming possible for more people. Delivering it reliably, at a competitive price, introduces another set of constraints. To understand those constraints, I started following the money and the hardware.

The first surprise is how many things have to go right before an advanced AI chip reaches a data centre.

Many of us know processor efficiency as something that just needs to perform calculations quickly, but calculations are only part of the job. The machine running on these processors must move enormous amounts of data between its processor and memory. Usually, High-bandwidth memory, shortened to HBM, helps feed data to the processor at the speeds workloads demand. Advanced packaging brings multiple components together so they can operate as one system.

I know these terms are hard for most of the people to understand. Here, let me break them down this way:

Think of a busy restaurant. Hiring a brilliant chef does little for the service if ingredients keep arriving slowly or the kitchen cannot get the equipment it needs. In an AI accelerator, the processor is only one part of the kitchen.

The supply chain behind these components is highly specialized. A shortage in one stage can hold up the finished product, even when another stage has room to expand.

Research from Epoch AI illustrates the scale of this problem. In its March 2026 analysis, the organization estimated that four leading AI chip designers collectively consumed around 90% of global HBM supply and advanced CoWoS packaging capacity in 2025. Its estimate for their share of advanced logic-die production was about 12%.

The contrast in the figures is revealing. Your company can have all the money ready, but if the manufacturing process isn’t up to speed, your orders will remain on a waiting list. Expanding chip production takes investment, equipment, skilled workers, and time. While a software team can deploy an update in days, Semiconductor capacity follows a different clock.

That manufacturing clock becomes more relevant when the entire industry is trying to expand at once. And it goes in favour of those with ample investments in their hands. Making companies with the strongest financing and the earliest access to suppliers have more options and leaving smaller buyers have to work around the capacity that remains available to them.

Even with this race, getting hold of a chip is only the beginning. The way companies buy access to computing power can shape their competitive position long after the initial purchase.

FTC’s staff report from January 2025 raised concerns about potential effects on competition, including increased switching costs and unequal access to important inputs. It identified risks for regulators to examine rather than declaring every partnership anticompetitive.

The commercial logic behind these arrangements is easy to understand. An AI developer who needs computing capacity can get it supplied by the cloud provider, perhaps alongside financing or other support. It looks like a win-win for both parties. The developer gets resources to build its business, while the provider secures revenue and strengthens a commercial relationship.

The complication appears when that relationship becomes demanding to leave.

Think of our accounting-assistant startup that has built its service around a particular cloud environment. Its deployment tools, monitoring systems, security controls, and model-serving software have all been configured to work together. But they found a competitor who is offering a lower price, tempting the founder to consider moving. But even though the new provider may have the right hardware, the transition still requires testing, engineering work, and careful handling of live customer service.

The migration bill and operational risks associated with the transition force the founder to stay with the current provider.

Cloud customers have faced versions of this problem for years. The UK's Competition and Markets Authority has highlighted that AI workloads add their own technical complications, especially when performance depends on particular accelerators and software configurations.

This is the distinction that keeps haunting me: access to compute and freedom to choose compute are two different things.

Yes, I tend to be more optimistic, but this is reality. A provider that offers a startup the capacity it needs today with some commitments. But these technical and contractual commitments narrow the startup’s choices tomorrow. The initial arrangement may be entirely reasonable for both parties. The bigger concern is when many businesses make similar commitments and a small group of suppliers becomes difficult to avoid. What happens then?

The same pressure appears on the other side of the market. Companies that own or rent large fleets of accelerators must turn that expensive equipment into useful work customers will pay for. A warehouse full of GPUs sounds impressive. The economics depend on what those GPUs actually deliver.

I found this particularly interesting while reading a 2025 research from the IEEE CLOUD conference. Researchers affiliated with IBM Research and other institutions investigated GPU bottlenecks in large-batch language-model inference. Their findings showed that memory bandwidth can limit performance even when much of a GPU's computational capacity remains underused. They also explored ways to improve memory allocation and serve additional workloads on the same hardware.

Let’s look at the practical implications of these findings through an example. A provider serving thousands of requests might combine them into batches to improve throughput. Processing more requests together can make better use of the hardware. But waiting for a larger batch increases delay, and customers expect quick responses. The operator has to juggle between efficient hardware use and the service its customers expect.

On top of that, model architecture and workload scheduling add further issues. Two AI services running on similar hardware can produce very different economics. One may use the available resources efficiently; another might spend more time moving data or waiting for work to arrive.

This is why instead of judging the strength of an AI infrastructure business by its installed GPU count alone, the best way is to analyze how effectively it converts expensive equipment into reliable computing services at a price customers will pay.

By having better software and scheduling, those economics can improve. It gives skilled operators an advantage without requiring them to buy another fleet of machines.

But efficiency isn’t the only factor. The money used to build the fleet in the first place is the actual issue.

You all know building an AI infrastructure requires large, long-lived investments. Data centres need buildings, electrical connections, cooling systems, networking, and specialized hardware. Many operators use financing structures that spread these costs across investors, lenders, landlords, and customers.

In his September 2026 working paper, Columbia Business School economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh examined how the AI infrastructure boom is being financed. He describes a shift toward arrangements that include leases, joint ventures, project debt, private credit, and other financing structures.

These can help fund expansion while spreading financial exposure across multiple parties. But at the same time, they also introduce risks around customer concentration, construction delays, technological obsolescence, and the future value of specialized assets.

Consider an operator that borrows money to build a data centre and signs a long-term agreement with a major customer. The contract gives the operator a revenue stream that helps justify the investment. The lender has a clearer basis for assessing repayment, and the customer secures access to capacity.

Everyone has a reason to like the arrangement. The risks still differ.

The customer may have committed to more capacity than it eventually needs. The operator must keep paying its obligations while finding enough demand to use its equipment. The lender depends on the borrower meeting its commitments and the underlying assets retaining value.

I find this part of the AI boom especially worth watching. Even with a booming industry, individual investors can still lose money. Those outcomes are perfectly compatible.

There is, however, a strong counterargument to the idea that infrastructure will remain a durable barrier. But even with discussions like:

Today's shortages and prices tell us little on their own about the market several years from now.

I would be making a mistake if I treated every current constraint as permanent.

The more interesting question is how quickly those improvements spread, who can take advantage of them, and whether they give smaller businesses enough room to compete.

Imagine our founder returns six months later. The product has improved with inference costs fallen, and the team has found a more efficient way to serve customers. Those changes could transform the business. Yet the founder still needs dependable capacity, commercially sensible terms, and enough financial room to survive a period of slower growth.

That is the part of the AI story I want to follow. Yes, we all know that Intelligence is becoming easier to access, and there are real opportunities here. The ability to turn that intelligence into a sustainable business still depends on

The next AI winners may well build better models. Others may win by serving those models more efficiently or finding customers the larger players have overlooked. Some will build the infrastructure that everyone else depends on.

As I watch the next wave of releases arrive, I keep returning to one question:

When more companies can build with AI, who will have the economic freedom to keep building?

I would love to have people from industry share their insights on this matter and share their perspective; we can publish our conversation here on Hackernoon. Don’t hesitate to reach out if you have insights to share.

#9867. Attackers Crash Claude's 'Office Party' Flaw to Run Malicious Code on Linux

Attackers can exploit a flaw in Claude's document-processing tool by creating a temporary file that Anthropic's AI assistant can access and run on a user's machine.

An attacker can use a flaw in Anthropic Claude's document-processing tool to run malicious code on Linux systems just by creating a temporary file that the AI assistant can access. The flaw highlights a growing risk posed by even trusted AI tools to introduce security gaps in enterprise environments.

Researchers from AIR Security discovered the flaw, which they've dubbed "Office Party," in Anthropic's official DOCX, PPTX, and XLSX skills, which are tools that enable Claude to create, read, edit, and process Microsoft Word documents, PowerPoint presentations, and Excel spreadsheets, respectively.

The vulnerability stems from a helper script, soffice.py, that launches LibreOffice to convert documents, including rendering Word documents as PDFs, they revealed in a report published today. When the script encounters an environment where Unix-domain sockets cannot be opened, it uses a workaround that loads a shared library through the Linux LD_PRELOAD mechanism.

Related:Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet

Anthropic has opted not to fix the issue.

During conversation, the script checks whether a library named lo_socket_shim.so already exists in a shared temporary directory but does not verify its origin or contents. An attacker who can place a malicious library at that location before the next document-processing operation can potentially have their code loaded and executed within LibreOffice, with the privileges of the user running the AI agent.

In this way, the flaw can allow attackers to execute malicious code on a user's Linux machine by exploiting an unverified file path used during document conversion, explains Niv Hoffman, co-founder and chief technology officer (CTO) of AIR Research Lab, in an email interview.

"An attacker gets one malicious file into a shared temporary folder which many programs use, and the next time an employee asks Claude for a document, Anthropic's trusted skill loads that file and runs it," he tells Dark Reading.

The vulnerability affects Linux environments where Unix sockets are blocked, including certain container security configurations, and Claude Code's sandbox. AIR Security reports that macOS is not affected because it does not load the library through LD_PRELOAD.

The AIR researchers demonstrated two ways the attack can work on Linux systems. In one scenario, they manually placed a malicious library in the temporary directory before asking Claude Code to generate a document. In another, they used a separate, seemingly legitimate AI skill to unpack a supporting file into the same directory. When the document-processing skill subsequently ran, the malicious library was loaded automatically.

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants

The flaw presents a serious issue for enterprises running Linux because it exploits "the default skills that all Claude agents use — [of which there are] hundreds of millions — and one planted file can make them run an attacker’s code with the employee's own access," Hoffman explains.

This second attack scenario is particularly concerning for enterprise security teams because it illustrates how individually benign-looking AI skills can interact to create an attack chain. And often, "companies don't have visibility to which skills and other agent add-ons they have installed, and don't have a red button to revoke or patch a vulnerable one," Hoffman explains.

Moreover, a malicious or compromised skill does not necessarily need to exploit the document-processing tool directly; it may simply need to place a file that another trusted component will execute, according to the AIR researchers.

The AIR team discovered the flaw in May and reported it to Anthropic, which acknowledged its existence, according to the report. However, the AI company "considers it outside its security boundary, since the vulnerable code only runs inside a sandbox," AIR Research Lab's Omri Saxena and Or Nevo wrote in the report. This means that as of now, the helper script still uses the same fixed path and still loads whatever file it finds there, they said.

Related:BeyondTrust Remote Support Zero-Day Continues Trend of Exploited Edge Bugs

Hoffman says that Anthropic's response is "not quite" adequate, "because even if the skills run within a sandbox, the attacker’s code then runs inside it with the user's own permissions, where the user's files and work already are," he says. Anthropic did not immediately return Dark Reading's request for comment about whether the company would take any further action to remedy the issue.

For businesses deploying AI agents and coding assistants, Office Party reinforces the need to treat AI skills as software dependencies rather than trusted extensions, and secure them as such, according to AIR.

To mitigate, organizations should make it a point to know "exactly what skills or add-ons an organization is using with Claude Code by keeping a live inventory of every AI skill and add-on across employees' agents," Hoffman says. They also should "review even official ones like any other code, and update or patch the whole set whenever a new vulnerability is published."

Elizabeth Montalbano is freelance writer, editor, and journalist with 30 years of professional experience and a master's degree from Arizona State University. Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. She currently resides in a village on the southwest coast of Portugal, where in her free time she enjoys surfing, hiking with her dogs, growing plants, and playing and performing as a singer and musician.

#9866. Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.

That is embarrassing onstage. In production, it is a reliability problem: a workflow that succeeded once may fail the next time a user makes the same request. For mission-critical work, such as reconciling a financial transaction or checking a contract for an obligation, that can be a showstopper.

Most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average. On AppWorld, a ReAct agent using GPT-4.1 succeeded on 77.4% of runs across five repetitions. But it succeeded in all five runs for only 53.0% of tasks — a 24.4-point consistency gap.

Most benchmarks report the first number. We built a way to measure the second — and improve it.

In an earlier post, we introduced ALTK-Evolve — a system that turns an agent's own past trajectories into reusable guidelines, distilled automatically and injected back at inference time. It measurably improves task success, but those results only asked the average-case question too. This post introduces consistency guidelines, a new guideline type in altk-evolve built on top of a diagnostic tool we call the Consistency Analyzer, that targets this gap directly.

Standard agent evaluation reports Mean@k: run a benchmark k times, average the pass rate. Often k=3, sometimes just 1. It's the number on every leaderboard, and it's what "77% accurate" means in practice.

Mean@k answers "how good is this agent, on average?" It does not answer the question a real user cares about: will it still be good if I ask this exact question again? For that you need Pass^k: the fraction of tasks where the agent succeeds on all k runs.

⚠️ Pass^k is not Pass@k. The familiar Pass@k is optimistic — it asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeded, the right question when you can verify and retry. Pass^k is its pessimistic mirror image: every attempt must succeed. Same letters, opposite question. Pass^k ≤ Mean@k ≤ Pass@k, always.

A ReAct agent backed by GPT-4.1 posts a Mean@5 of 77.4% — genuinely strong. But Pass^5 is only 53.0%. Nearly a quarter of the benchmark consists of tasks the agent can sometimes solve and sometimes can't, with nothing about the task changing between runs. We call this gap — Mean@k minus Pass^k — the consistency gap.

This isn't a capability problem you fix with a bigger model. It's an orthogonal axis: an agent can be capable and inconsistent at the same time.

Every time an LLM agent decides something — which API to call, what argument to pass, whether to retry — that decision comes out of a probability distribution over next tokens. What matters is the shape of that distribution. A sharp one puts most of its mass on a single token: the runners-up are far behind, and the same choice comes out run after run. A flat one spreads comparable mass across several near-tied tokens, and which one wins is close to a coin flip.

The shape decides how much noise it takes to change the outcome. Sharp distributions are resilient — GPU floating-point non-associativity, request batching, and other platform-side effects nudge the numbers slightly, but nowhere near enough to reorder a clear winner. Flat distributions are vulnerable to exactly that nudge: near-ties may reorder under small perturbations. And because a trajectory chains dozens of decisions, a small per-step chance of flipping compounds into a large chance that some run goes differently. That's where a 24-point gap comes from.

This is also why the problem survives your decoding settings. Greedy decoding and a fixed seed both govern how a distribution gets turned into a token — they say nothing about the distribution itself. On a hosted endpoint the probabilities shift slightly from run to run, so the same prompt to the same model at temperature zero can still resolve a near-tie one way today and the other way tomorrow.

Our setup: the ReAct agent runs at temperature 0.0, so none of the variance above is ordinary sampling.

Which turns the problem into a search: which steps in a given trajectory were the flat ones — and what do you do about them once you know?

Consistency guidelines come out of a two-stage pipeline that plugs into ALTK-Evolve's existing machinery — with a new source signal driving what gets written.

1. Detect — the Consistency Analyzer. Given one recorded trajectory, the analyzer replays each decision step through controlled resampling, measuring how much the model's output actually varies at that point. Concretely, that's one additional model call per decision step, done once offline — issued with the sampling parameter set to draw k completions at once (k=5 by default) — replayed against the already-recorded context, not new tool calls, not new environment interactions, and not a second end-to-end rollout of the task. This yields a consistency score per decision step that is written into a scorecard to pinpoint exactly which decisions are at risk of flipping on the next run. Detection is fully black-box — no logits, no model internals, no instrumentation beyond the trace you already have.

2. Generate — targeted guidelines. Every flagged step becomes a candidate consistency guideline in the standard ALTK-Evolve format, so it slots into the existing storage and retrieval pipeline. Here's a real example, generated by GPT-4.1 from a trajectory of the AppWorld task "How many activities are done in my bucket list as per my SimpleNote note?":

[Guideline 1] When counting checkbox-style markers in note content, use a line-anchored regex match rather than a plain substring count — note titles often repeat the marker symbol in a legend line.

[Guideline 2] Always verify search results for note queries by checking for multiple matches and confirming the correct note before proceeding.

Nothing here is task-specific trivia. String-counting bugs and unverified search results are decision points that show up with high uncertainty across many AppWorld tasks. That's the point: the analyzer targets instability, not failure — so it catches steps the agent happened to get right this time but could easily get wrong next time.

Watch the 2-minute demo — five parallel runs of the agent split 3-2 on this task because of agent uncertainty about the counting strategy, then run again after these guidelines in context: all five agree.

We evaluated on AppWorld test_normal (168 tasks) with a ReAct agent on GPT-4.1, generating consistency guidelines from a single baseline trajectory per task and testing them on 5 fresh runs.

Mean@5 (%), aggregate — same scale as Pass^5 above.

The consistency gap is cut roughly in half. Aggregate Pass^5 rises 53.0% → 69.0% while Mean@5 rises 77.4% → 81.0%, narrowing the gap between "looks capable" and "can be counted on" from 24.4pp to 12.0pp. Nearly a third of previously-inconsistent tasks become tasks the agent passes on every single run.

The middle and hard tiers gain most. Medium +22.9pp (+44% relative), Hard +14.3pp (+45% relative) — effectively tied in relative terms, with Medium ahead absolutely. Easy gains +12.2pp, having had the least room. This is consistency guidelines doing what they're designed to do: finding and stabilizing the specific decision points where an agent's own uncertainty was leaking into the outcome.

Mean@5 never drops. Preserving average accuracy was a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have: a system that boosts Pass^5 by trading away Mean@5 would just be shifting unreliability around, not fixing it. Mean accuracy holds or improves at every difficulty level.

Applied to a different but related task in the same AppWorld scenario — another variant of the scenario the guidelines were mined from — consistency guidelines still lift Pass^5 by +13.0pp, only 3 points below the same-task number. A guideline derived from one run isn't just patching that run; it's capturing something that transfers.

The sharper evidence comes from a weaker model, gpt-oss-120b. Same-task Pass^5 rose +6.0pp from a much lower baseline (10.1% → 16.1%) — and, interestingly, the similar-task generalization number (+8.7 pp) actually exceeded the same-task gain, suggesting the guidelines were capturing genuinely reusable failure patterns rather than memorizing one trajectory's specifics.

Try the ALTK-Evolve — the open-source repo now includes the Consistency Analyzer and consistency-guideline generation used in these experiments — or read the technical report on arXiv for the complete methodology.

If accuracy numbers you can't reproduce on your own tasks sound familiar, we'd like to hear about it — concrete examples of flip-prone behavior in your own agents are exactly the kind of feedback that shapes what we build next. Open an issue or a discussion.

Great perspective on agent reliability. Measuring consistency alongside accuracy seems especially important as AI agents move into workflows where reproducibility matters. The Consistency Analyzer approach is a fascinating way to identify unstable decisions without requiring full task replays.

The useful split is the one most dashboards still refuse to print: Mean@k answers “how good is this agent on average?” Pass^k answers “will the same request still succeed if I ask again?”

Once you’ve watched a trajectory chain dozens of near-tied tool choices, a strong average with a wide consistency gap is exactly the demo that fails live. Capability and consistency are orthogonal — buying a bigger model can lift Mean without closing the gap.

What I want teams to take from the Consistency Analyzer framing is operational, not the guideline machinery itself: treat flip-prone decision steps as first-class eval targets. One offline resample pass over a recorded trace is a cheaper reliability signal than another end-to-end leaderboard screenshot.

Practical ask for anyone shipping agents from this: do you report Pass^k (even k=3) next to Mean@k in the release gate, and do you refuse the “stable” label when the consistency gap is still large on your hard tier?

Reproducible reliability will not remove disagreement about which guidelines to inject. It will make the disagreement about the right metric.

Thanks, and you've landed on exactly the operational takeaway we hoped for: flip-prone decision steps should be eval targets in their own right. Beyond that, knowing where they are also turns the eval into a diagnostic: a consistency gap tells you that an agent is unreliable, while the flip-prone steps tell you where and why.

#9865. tokenizers v1: encode, decode and scaling, measured

The tokenizer has not historically been the bottleneck within ML workflows. Compute-wise, tokenization is light compared to the heavy modeling happening in the rest of the pipeline. Yet, in some cases, it has rapidly become key to accelerating (or slowing down) your machine learning work.

As models become faster and workloads scale, that balance begins to shift. Training on massive datasets, serving many concurrent requests, or repeatedly processing long inputs can put enough pressure on the tokenizer that it starves the model of data.

This is why we have chosen to heavily focus on performance for the upcoming version 1 of tokenizers. Tokenization should be light and should scale with your workflow. Your GPUs should never sit idle waiting for the CPU to complete its tokenization.

In this article, we look at what makes v1 faster than v0.23, often by tens of times.

This work was entirely possible thanks to the rest of the ecosystem. Tokenization is a very active area of open source work, and libraries such as gigatoken, tiktoken, kitoken, tokie, fastokens, wordchipper and ai-tokenizer, as well as many others, have each pushed on what a fast tokenizer can be. We read that work, and several of the ideas below reached us because another project showed they were worth trying.

Before this refactor, tokenizers was nowhere near the performance it could have had, so contributing to it may not have seemed worth it. With this refactor, we hope to make clear that we intend tokenizers to be a library worth contributing to.

We also thank IBM, NVIDIA, and the ExecuTorch team for contributing patches and helping us test across a wide range of hardware to broaden platform support.

We showcase results for the release candidate of tokenizers v1 against other widely used alternatives. We go over single-threaded, multi-threaded, scaling across threads, per-model comparison, per-language comparison, latency, decoding throughput, memory heap, as well as crate size.

We run this from the tokbench repository, and add a command to rerun the benchmarks on your hardware if you would like to do so.

v1 will produce the same token IDs as v0.23. The goal was to preserve the output, the API, the vocabulary and the merge ranks, and improve everything that can be improved. That includes breadth. The library stays general across tokenizer families rather than specialising on BPE, so v1 loads everything v0.23 loaded.

A tokenizer converts text into the list of integers a model reads. tokenizers runs that conversion in four stages. Normalization applies operations such as lowercasing or Unicode normalization to the raw text. Pre-tokenization splits the text into smaller pieces called pre-tokens. The model turns each pre-token into tokens and maps them to IDs in its vocabulary. Post-processing adds any special tokens the model expects.

The model stage is where most of the work described here happens. Eight of the ten model families measured in this article use byte pair encoding, or BPE. BPE starts from the bytes of a pre-token and repeatedly joins the highest ranked adjacent pair until no ranked pair remains. The ranking is learned when the tokenizer is trained and ships with it, so the same text always produces the same IDs. A merge never crosses a pre-token boundary. The other two families use WordPiece and Unigram, the two other model types the library supports.

The tokenization pipeline page documents the four stages. Tokenization algorithms documents BPE, WordPiece and Unigram.

Each stage was worked on. These are the changes that mattered:

BPE models use a regular expression to split the input text into smaller, easier to process chunks called pre-tokens. Merges happen inside a pre-token and never across the boundary between two of them, so this split decides what the rest of the pipeline sees.

That regular expression is a fixed parameter of the model. It ships with the tokenizer and never changes at runtime, so there is no need for a general-purpose regex engine to interpret it on every encode. An equivalent splitting function can be written by hand, once, for the pattern a given model actually uses.

A hand-written function can then use the SIMD instructions (single instruction, multiple data) of a modern CPU, which apply one operation to many bytes at once and suit UTF-8 text well. bitcannon views the input's bytes as parallel streams of bits, so boundaries fall out of boolean operations across whole registers instead of a scan that advances one character at a time. It decides 64 bytes per register operation. The same idea drives Parabix for text processing and simdjson for JSON.

This depends on recognising the pattern. A handful of grammars cover most byte-level BPE models, and a tokenizer whose pattern is not among them keeps the regex path and none of this speed-up. That is why the gains above vary as much as they do.

Real text contains many repeated words. Because BPE always produces the same token IDs for a given pre-token, v1 can save the result after processing it once. A thread-local cache maps each pre-token's bytes to its token IDs, allowing later occurrences to skip the merge process.

Naturally, as the input grows, the number of unique words can grow more slowly than the total number of words. Repeated words then account for an increasing share of the input. New words still appear, which accounts for the occasional misses in the animation below.

Caching works best when the input contains repeated pre-tokens. Input with few repeated pre-tokens can pay for lookups without receiving many hits.

The next major cost comes from the BPE merge loop. For each pre-token, the loop repeatedly finds the highest-priority adjacent pair and merges it. The previous implementation allocated new memory for every call and built a new priority queue for every pre-token.

v1 reuses a scratch buffer owned by the caller, removing those repeated allocations. It stores symbols in a flat array and links adjacent symbols by their positions in that array, which makes updates during merging cheaper. It also processes a batch of pre-tokens in a single model call.

Each candidate pair is also packed into a single 64-bit value, with the merge rank in the high bits. Comparing two candidates is then just comparing two integers, and "no merge here" is the largest possible value, so the loop finds its next merge without a branch.

Small differences in benchmark design can produce large differences in tokenizer performance. We used the following rules to keep the comparison consistent across engines.

Repeatedly encoding one document can be faster than encoding a stream of distinct documents on the same build. The first approach measures performance when the entire document is already represented in the cache. The second measures performance on new input while allowing previously seen pre-tokens to remain cached.

Both conditions are sometimes described as "warm," even though they measure different workloads. Our headline results use distinct documents, and the complete corpus is too large to fit in the cache. Tokenizer benchmarks should identify which workload they use because the choice can dominate the result.

Across the ten model families v1's encode path covers, it encodes text 3 to 30 times faster than v0.23 with one thread on an Apple M4 Max. The low end is t5-base, the high end gpt2. It scales at 76% of linear across eight workers. Throughout these changes, v1 produces exactly the same token IDs as the released library.

The overall improvement comes from several changes working together: a hand-written splitter in place of a regex engine, a cache that answers a repeated word without merging it again, a merge loop that never touches the allocator, and one model call per batch of pre-tokens instead of one per pre-token. Each reduces the work done at a different point in the pipeline.

The next priority is support for more model families. We will move additional models onto the new merge loop before 1.0.0. Once the release candidates stabilize, the next step will be bringing about the improvements within the transformers library and the rest of the ecosystem which depend on the tokenizers library.

This post is generated from tokbench results and will be updated as support expands.

A release candidate for v1 is on crates.io. The API you call is the one you already call, so the only thing that changes is which build you install.

Training is behind a default-on feature that pulls a C++ dependency with it. If you only need to encode, turn it off to exclude the training implementation:

Encoding is unchanged: same call, same ids.

Every figure in this post was measured against this crate. The Python bindings wrap the same code and are built from bindings/python, but they add per-call overhead that none of these measurements include.

The benchmarks in this post cover the completed release-candidate work listed first. The remaining sections show what is still required for 1.0.0 and what we plan to explore afterward.

This work is in the Rust pre-release on crates.io:

Will have to try it out. Data seems real good.

#9864. Black Hat India 2026 Makes a Landmark Debut in Bengaluru, Bringing the Global Cybersecurity Community to India

Inaugural edition by Informa Markets in India brings together leading researchers, security practitioners and industry decision makers for four days of cutting-edge research, technical exchange and strategic dialogue.

13 Trainings delivered by 19 trainers, 70+ Summit speakers, 200+ CXOs, CISOs and VIP buyers, and 2,000+ Business Hall delegates across four days.

Black Hat Arsenal featured 44 open-source security tool demonstrations across 32 workstations and four hands-on labs.

Keynotes by leading cybersecurity experts Dr. Sanjay Bahl, Director General, Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) and Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA), and Nathan Hamiel (Kudelski Security), alongside a special address by Shri Rajesh Kumar, IPS, Chief Executive Officer, Indian Cybercrime Co-ordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India.

Key themes included AI security, digital payment fraud, emerging cyber threats and post-quantum readiness.

Bengaluru, November 5, 2026 — Black Hat India 2026, organised by Informa Markets in India, concluded its inaugural edition at the Sheraton Grand, Brigade Gateway, Bengaluru, following four days of high-impact training, leadership discussions, original technical research and industry engagement from October 27 to 30, 2026.

Related:PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

Founded in 1997, Black Hat is one of the world's most respected cybersecurity conference series, renowned for its independent, vendor-neutral research and technical depth. Its debut in India marks a significant milestone for the country's cybersecurity ecosystem, bringing a globally recognised platform and its international community of researchers and practitioners to one of the world's fastest-growing digital economies.

The inaugural edition brought together a diverse mix of technical training, strategic discussions, cutting-edge research and hands-on engagement, with each day offering a distinct experience for the cybersecurity community.

Day 1 opened with specialised Trainings, featuring 13 hands-on courses delivered by 19 trainers and covering subjects ranging from offensive security fundamentals to securing emerging AI systems.

Day 2 was dedicated to Summit Day, bringing together 70+ speakers and 200+ CXOs, CISOs and VIP buyers across two tracks, Frontier AI Security and CISO Strategy. Discussions examined the changing cybersecurity landscape, enterprise risk and the growing strategic responsibilities of security leaders.

Days 3 and 4 featured the Briefings and Business Hall, with 35 researchers and practitioners presenting original work on emerging threats, software and cloud security, AI and digital identity, while welcoming more than 2,000 Business Hall delegates. A major attraction was Black Hat Arsenal, where 44 presenters demonstrated open-source security tools across 32 workstations and four hands-on labs, enabling attendees to engage directly with developers and explore practical security applications.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

The event brought together prominent government representatives, industry leaders and international cybersecurity experts. Summit Day was inaugurated in the presence of Lt. Gen. Rajesh Pant and Lt. Gen. M.U. Nair, both former National Cyber Security Coordinators of India; Dr. Sanjay Bahl, Director General, Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) and Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA); and Brijesh Singh, IPS, Principal Secretary, Government of Maharashtra.

Dr. Bahl's keynote examined the implications of emerging AI technologies for India's digital ecosystem and the importance of strengthening cyber resilience. Nathan Hamiel, Senior Director of Research at Kudelski Security, delivered the Briefings keynote, exploring how AI is transforming cybersecurity and why human expertise remains indispensable. Shri Rajesh Kumar, IPS, Chief Executive Officer, Indian Cybercrime Co-ordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India, delivered a special address on transnational cybercrime.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

Senior representatives from NPCI, the Reserve Bank of India, NCIIPC, PhonePe, CRED, Razorpay, Groww, Reliance, Adani Enterprises, HCLTech, EY, Deloitte, KPMG, Microsoft, Mandiant, Akamai, Zscaler and Zoho participated alongside independent and academic researchers.

Across the programme, discussions consistently highlighted the growing importance of securing and governing AI, the increasing sophistication of cyberattacks, software supply-chain vulnerabilities, digital payment fraud and deepfakes. Protecting India's Digital Public Infrastructure, preparing for post-quantum technologies and translating technical risks into business priorities also emerged as important themes.

India's rapid digital expansion is creating unprecedented opportunities, alongside an increasingly complex cybersecurity landscape. The average organisational cost of a data breach in India reached ₹25.5 crore in 2026, nearly 16% higher year on year, underlining the growing economic implications of cyber risk.

Commenting on the significance of Black Hat India's successful maiden edition, Mr. Yogesh Mudras, Managing Director, Informa Markets in India, said, "India’s rapid digital transformation has unlocked extraordinary opportunities, while also bringing the need to secure an increasingly connected economy into sharper focus. In the last financial year, UPI processed over 24,000 crore transactions worth more than ₹314 lakh crore, while CERT-In reported over 29.4 lakh cybersecurity incidents in 2025, an increase of approximately 44% over the previous year. The recent spate of global cyber incidents, including critical PHP vulnerabilities, being described as ‘Black October’, is a timely reminder that digital growth must be matched by stronger security and resilience.

The successful debut of Black Hat India is a significant achievement for us and an important addition to India’s cybersecurity ecosystem. The scale of participation and quality of discussions reflect the strong appetite for a platform of this calibre. As AI reshapes the threat landscape, staying ahead of emerging risks becomes even more critical. We are proud to have brought this globally recognised platform to India and look forward to building on this strong beginning,” he added.

The inaugural edition was supported by Diamond Partners TrendAI, Upwind and EY, alongside other sponsors and exhibitors, and shaped by the Black Hat India Review Board.

Black Hat India's debut comes in a milestone year for Informa Markets in India, marking 20 years of its presence in the country. The edition is also part of Festivity of Business, the company's annual campaign, now in its seventh year. Spanning 100 days, the campaign celebrates the optimism, energy and entrepreneurial spirit driving India's growth, bringing together the country's vibrant festive season and its high season of business events.

The successful inaugural edition establishes a significant new platform for India's cybersecurity community, bringing global expertise, original research and industry leadership together at a time when securing the digital future has never been more important.

#9863. Comparing Top ElevenLabs Alternatives for Production AI Voice Agents

AssemblyAI builds advanced speech language models that power next-generation voice AI applications.

AssemblyAI builds advanced speech language models that power next-generation voice AI applications.

AssemblyAI builds advanced speech language models that power next-generation voice AI applications.

OpenAI is removing tts-1, tts-1-hd and gpt-4o-mini-tts from its API on January 6, 2027. Inworld retired its first-generation models in June. If your voice agent hard-codes one vendor's model IDs, voices and audio format, every announcement like that is an unplanned migration.

So when a team asks us, "We're on ElevenLabs. Should we be?", the answer is often yes. This post is about the cases where it isn't, and how to test a switch in an afternoon.

The current flagship is Eleven v4, with a real-time variant, Eleven v4 Turbo (eleven_v4_turbo). ElevenLabs lists v4 Turbo at a median inference latency of about 100 ms, excluding application and network latency, with 90+ languages and the same voice cloning as v4. On the API pricing page, v4 Turbo is $0.04 per 1,000 characters ($40 per 1M), and v4 is $0.08. Flash v2.5 is also $0.04, and the docs quote about 75 ms for it, 32 languages, and a smaller model.

For voice agents, three details in the docs matter more than the headline numbers.

ElevenLabs' pronunciation tooling is deep. Eleven v4 reads IPA inline, and pronunciation dictionaries with phoneme tags work on v4 and v4 Turbo. If your agent says drug names or brand names all day, that's a real reason to stay.

From what we see, teams evaluate alternatives for one of six reasons. If none of these apply to you, stop reading and keep shipping:

AssemblyAI comes first because it targets the two most common reasons above: session caps and cost at volume. The rest are ordered by language coverage, widest first, because the first thing you're likely to lose when leaving ElevenLabs is its 90+ languages. Prices are pay-as-you-go list prices from each vendor's pricing page on October 28, 2026.

AssemblyAI-TTS-1 launched on October 27, 2026, and it's built for conversational voice agents, not narration. It was trained on millions of hours of audio, including real conversational data. There are thousands of voices and instant voice cloning in the dashboard. The interfaces are a WebSocket (one session per conversation, one request per turn), an HTTP endpoint, and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Telephony output is pcm_mulaw or pcm_alaw at 8 kHz. You get per-word boundaries for barge-in, US and EU data zones, and LiveKit and Pipecat plugins. The Pipecat service is on Pipecat's main branch now and ships in a release after 1.14.0. The price is $15 per 1M characters.

The concurrency model is the part that matters for this comparison. There's no limit on sessions open at once. What the limits doc does rate-limit is new sessions per minute, starting at your streaming speech-to-text limit.

Where it breaks: six languages (English, Spanish, French, German, Italian, Portuguese). If you need Japanese or Hindi, stop here. There's no language detection, so you set it per session. Sessions cap at an hour and close after two minutes idle without a keep-alive. And it's brand new, without the production history of anything else on this list.

Better pick than ElevenLabs if: you run high-volume calls in those six languages and the bill and session caps are the problem.

Inworld's current models are TTS-2 and TTS-2 Flash. Both cover 200+ languages and locales and support instant voice cloning. Inworld quotes a P90 time to first byte of 100 ms and 20 ms respectively, measured server-side without the network. Output includes μ-law and A-law at 8 kHz, and there's an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Pricing is per million characters and falls with commitment. On the pricing page, TTS-2 Flash is $15 per 1M on pay-as-you-go and $7 per 1M on the $1,500-a-month Growth plan. Concurrency is published plainly: 5, 10, 50, 150, and 500 concurrent generations across the self-serve plans. A WebSocket context only counts while audio is being exchanged, and you can hold ten times that many connections open.

Where it breaks: Inworld has already retired its first-generation models, so plan for churn. Language support is tiered by how thoroughly Inworld has evaluated each language, which means "200+" should be read as "test your languages."

Better pick than ElevenLabs if: you need many languages at a lower price, and you can commit to a plan tier.

Sonic 3.6 went GA with a dated snapshot, sonic-3.6-2026-08-27, and it speaks 44 languages. That snapshot detail is the most underrated feature on this list. You can pin a version that will never change, run your evals, then move when you choose to. Given the deprecation news above, that's worth something.

The output format docs are written with telephony in mind. They cover pcm_mulaw at 8000 for Twilio and pcm_alaw for European networks. Pronunciation dictionaries take IPA or sounds-like spellings.

Where it breaks: pricing is in credits, about one per character, bundled into monthly plans (Scale is $299 for 8M credits). That's easy to start but harder to project than a flat per-character rate. On the pricing page, "high concurrency limits" are a Scale feature, and custom limits are Enterprise.

Better pick than ElevenLabs if: you want strict version control over the voice your customers hear.

Deepgram's Flux TTS is on a new endpoint, /v2/speak. Aura-2 voices stay on /v1/speak, so this is a migration even for current Deepgram customers. The design is built around turns. When a caller barges in, you send Interrupt, and the server tells you text_spoken and text_remaining. That answers the hardest bookkeeping question in an agent: what did the caller actually hear before they cut in?

The streaming socket emits linear16, mulaw or alaw, with μ-law at 8 or 16 kHz. Sessions last up to an hour. Deepgram has an EU endpoint, dedicated endpoints, and self-hosting, which is one of the stronger residency stories on this list.

Where it breaks: list price is $0.045 per 1K characters, more than ElevenLabs v4 Turbo. Published concurrency is up to 45 on pay-as-you-go and 60 on Growth. Ten languages are GA, and about thirty more are early access. There's a launch promo that matches Flux TTS spend with credits up to $500, ending December 31, 2026.

Better pick than ElevenLabs if: you already run Deepgram speech-to-text, or barge-in correctness is your top bug.

Rime's flagship is Coda, released May 2026. Rime describes it as an LLM backbone with a speech engine trained on full-duplex conversational data. It speaks 10 languages. Mist v3 is the low-latency sibling, with four languages. Arcana has been retired from the cloud API.

Two features stand out for agents. spell() forces letter-by-letter reading of codes and IDs. Coda also accepts a custom X-SAMPA lexicon in six languages. Rime's WebSocket outputs audio/pcmu at samplingRate: 8000, and you can run the same models in your VPC or on-prem.

Where it breaks: pricing is per minute of generated audio ($0.050 for Coda, $0.030 for Mist v3, 20% off on Scale). Rime estimates about 1K characters per minute, but a per-minute price doesn't line up with per-character quotes until you measure your own speaking rate. Requests that omit modelId silently get Mist v3, so set it on every call. Unlimited TTS concurrency is listed as an Enterprise feature.

Better pick than ElevenLabs if: audio can't leave your network, or your agent reads a lot of alphanumeric codes.

gpt-4o-mini-tts is simple and well documented, but the guide now carries a deprecation banner, and the shutdown is January 6, 2027. The endpoint also doesn't list μ-law among its output formats. Starting a new telephony integration on it today means scheduling a second migration before you've finished the first.

Pick two candidates, not five. Then run two tests on each. Neither takes more than an afternoon.

Write the 30–50 sentences your agent actually says that contain something a caller must not mishear: confirmation codes, phone numbers, prices, dates, and surnames from your real customer base. Synthesize each one with every candidate at 8 kHz μ-law, the format the caller hears. Run all the audio through the same speech-to-text model, and check whether each entity survives.

STT is a proxy for a listener, not a perfect one. But a TTS output that a strong STT model can't recover is very likely one a caller on a speakerphone can't either. Holding the STT constant means the TTS is the only variable.

synthesize() and transcribe() are yours to fill in with each vendor's SDK. Listen to every failure yourself: some will be STT formatting quirks, and some will be the TTS reading "K7Q" as a word. Only the second kind counts against the TTS.

Put each candidate behind a real phone number through your actual carrier. Request μ-law at 8 kHz from the vendor (the table above lists each one's parameter) rather than transcoding it yourself. Then measure three things:

Every latency figure in this post comes from a vendor, measured on that vendor's terms. ElevenLabs excludes application and network latency. Inworld measures server-side at P90. None of these numbers can be compared directly, and none were measured over your trunk, from your region, at 9am on a Monday.

Benchmarks also can't hear your content. A model that reads a news paragraph beautifully can still say "K-seven-Q" as "kuh-sev-en-kew." Price comparisons fall apart at the unit level, too. Per-character, per-credit, and per-minute pricing only convert once you know how many characters a minute your agent speaks.

The TTS market converged faster than anyone expected. On clean prose, the voices on this list are close enough that most callers won't pick a winner. What hasn't converged is everything around the voice: how sessions are counted, what a model ID promises about next quarter, which audio formats come back without a resampler, and what the bill looks like at 50,000 hours.

That's why it's worth asking whether you should leave ElevenLabs. But the better question is whether you could leave in a week if you had to. Wrap the TTS call behind your own interface, keep the entity test in CI, and treat the vendor as a part you can replace. The vendor that wins on your test today may not be the right one in a year, and you should be able to switch either way.

#9862. Jun Kim, oMLX creator and maintainer, joins Hugging Face to support the MLX community

We are super excited to welcome Jun as our newest team member 🔥. We are completely invested in local AI, and MLX is a central piece of the ecosystem. We are delighted that Jun chose us to set up home and continue contributing to MLX.

MLX is Apple's framework for local AI, especially optimized for Apple Silicon. We are big MLX supporters since it was the Christmas present from Awni and Angelos in 2023, and proud that Hugging Face is the Hub where people find MLX models and contribute their own. Usage of open, local AI is accelerating, and we believe in a healthy ecosystem where people can find the tools that work for them.

Stability, and hopefully faster development! Graduating from a side job to a fully maintained and funded project will allow Jun to better guide the contributors and build for the long-term. oMLX stays Apache 2.0, and Jun keeps leading it as before.

Our end goal is to unblock the community to run local AI in any shape or form, and provide the tools and building blocks to make that happen. We expect oMLX to serve as a testbed for new ideas, while leveraging the foundational work of the dependencies it already relies upon, such as mlx-lm or mlx-vlm. We believe that strong modeling and inference libraries help the community, so we'd love to upstream work to wherever it makes sense. We have been collaborating with many projects mlx-lm, mlx-vlm, LMStudio, and we hope we can strengthen the relationship with Cheng, Prince, Yagil, and their teams to better serve the community together.

Concretely, one focus area is the quick transition from a transformers model definition to a reference MLX implementation that can be consumed by different engines, so each one can focus on the unique features they provide. The transformers library has become the reference for ML model definitions, we want to streamline the process to make new transformers models run on MLX.

We are incredibly excited about the future.

InfoQ Homepage News Pinterest and Intel Take Open-Source Profiling to Internet Scale

Nov 10, 2026 3 min read

Pinterest has partnered with Intel to extend gProfiler, an open-source continuous profiler that provides production performance visibility across an internet-scale fleet of infrastructure.

Pinterest claims it operates hundreds of thousands of instances supporting 640 million monthly active users, with services written in Java, Python, C++, Go, and Node.js. At that scale, even a small efficiency improvement can have significant infrastructure and cost implications. The challenge was that engineers were using separate tools such as perf, async-profiler, and py-spy, producing fragmented profiles that were difficult to correlate across languages and machines.

Rather than building another proprietary profiling platform, Pinterest worked with Intel to extend gProfiler and contribute those capabilities back to the open-source project. The collaboration adds dynamic profiling, hardware-level telemetry, wall-time profiling, and performance-counter flame graphs, while also hardening the system for large production fleets.

gProfiler acts as an orchestration layer over several existing profilers. It combines system-wide perf data with runtime-specific tools such as async-profiler for Java and eBPF-based profiling for Python, producing a unified flame graph across the processes running on a host.

This is important for modern services where application execution crosses multiple layers. A Java application may spend time inside the JVM, native libraries, or the Linux kernel, while a Python service can involve interpreter, native, and kernel activity. Instead of requiring engineers to select and manually correlate separate profilers, gProfiler combines those views.

The agent discovers processes, starts the appropriate profilers, merges their stack traces, and uploads the resulting profile without requiring application code changes.

The new capability allows engineers to select services, hosts, or clusters and trigger profiling remotely through the UI or API. Agents normally remain dormant, consuming less than 1% CPU and 100 MB of memory, and receive profiling instructions through periodic heartbeats. You can change profiling frequency, duration, and the profilers used without redeploying the agent.

This effectively turns profiling into an operational capability rather than something that requires engineers to gain shell access to individual machines.

Integration with Intel PerfSpect allows gProfiler to collect hardware-level information such as cache behaviour, memory bandwidth, and CPU stalls. Pinterest also added PMC flame graphs, which correlate functions with hardware performance events such as cache misses and branch mispredictions.

Another addition is wall-time profiling. CPU profiling shows where processor time is being spent, but a service can still be slow while consuming relatively little CPU because threads are waiting on I/O, locks, or remote procedure calls. Wall-time profiling makes those waiting periods visible.

The gProfiler architecture separates collection from analysis. Agents run on individual hosts, while gProfiler Performance Studio aggregates and visualises the resulting profiles.

Profiles are stored in S3, passed through SQS for asynchronous indexing, and stored in ClickHouse for analytical queries. A React frontend provides flame-graph exploration, while aggregated data allows engineers to compare profiles across hosts, services, and time periods.

Pinterest and Intel also hardened the platform for production, addressing issues involving agent resource consumption, disk usage, and multi-terabyte ingestion before deploying it across the fleet.

gProfiler sits in an increasingly crowded continuous-profiling landscape. Parca and Grafana Pyroscope use eBPF and related sampling technologies to provide fleet-wide profiling, while commercial platforms such as Datadog offer continuous profiling alongside broader observability capabilities.

The distinction with gProfiler is its emphasis on system-wide, multi-runtime profiling and open-source extensibility. Rather than replacing tools such as perf or async-profiler, it orchestrates them. It also adds hardware-level profiling through Intel's tooling.

Intel's VTune provides much deeper processor and application performance analysis, but it was designed primarily as a performance-engineering tool rather than a cloud-native fleet profiler. Pinterest specifically notes that this difference influenced the decision to build on gProfiler rather than adapt VTune for its environment.

At small scale, profiling is usually something an engineer enables when a performance problem appears. At Pinterest's scale, the cost of waiting for engineers to reproduce problems or manually profile machines becomes too high. Continuous profiling provides a baseline, while dynamic profiling allows teams to investigate specific anomalies when they occur.

By combining runtime profiles, system behaviour, and hardware performance data under an open-source platform, Pinterest is effectively making profiling another layer of production observability.

#9860. Microsoft Fixes RCE Bug in Windows Paint After Weeks of Confusion

Last month, Microsoft disclosed a vulnerability in Microsoft Paint, but messaging regarding a patch was unclear.

Microsoft recently patched a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Windows Paint, though details regarding how to fix the flaw seemingly remained unsettled for nearly a month.

According to an advisory, the flaw, CVE-2026-83844, is an "out-of-bounds read in Windows Paint [that] allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code locally." It carries a high severity CVSS 3.1 score of 7.0.

The advisory offers few technical details for defenders. Microsoft said acquiring RCE requires local access, meaning hands-on-keyboard or a direct remote connection to the attacker's machine. Some user interaction is also required; altogether, this may explain why the attack is "only" high severity rather than a 9 or 10 CVSS, as is so often associated with RCE flaws. Microsoft has observed no exploitation reports to date, further marking exploitation as "less likely."

A Windows Paint patch is available now. The fixed version is 11.2609.401.0, and customers can see it under Paint > Settings > About.

Related:AI Makes Reverse Engineering Mainstream Software & Malware Far Easier

A Microsoft spokesperson tells Dark Reading, "A security update for Paint is available through the Microsoft Store, and customers with automatic Store updates enabled are already protected. We recommend customers check they are on the latest version and install the available updates to remain protected." Customers can also manually apply the update via Microsoft Store App > Downloads > Check for updates.

CVE-2026-83844 is an unusual vulnerability for multiple reasons, beyond it being a high-severity Paint vulnerability capable of RCE.

As Brian Vitko, founder of device management software provider RFF, wrote in a blog post, Microsoft first disclosed the bug on Oct. 13, but there seemed to be no indication the reported fix (11.2605.91.0) was live, even as of Oct. 30. By Nov. 4, Vitko, the correct fixed version was listed in the security advisory (11.2609.401.0) but 11.2605.81.0 was the latest update available in the store. The correct version was added to the store on Nov. 6.

The original version of the advisory FAQ, according to Vitko's post, said the attack could possibly be exploited, "by sending a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network."

But the latest version of the FAQ reads, "For example, when the score indicates that the Attack Vector is Local and User Interaction is Required, this could describe an exploit in which an attacker, through social engineering, convinces a victim to download and open a specially crafted file from a website which leads to a local attack on their computer."

Related:Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

Vitko tells Dark Reading that this latter explanation aligns more with his expectations for a vulnerability targeting Windows Paint, and that the wording may just be the result of standardized Microsoft FAQ language than speaking directly to the vulnerability.

"Paint isn't something that listens on the network. When it was published, it was CVSS 8.1 with a network attack vector, and the FAQ talked about 'a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network.' Microsoft changed that on Nov. 7: it's now 7.0, local, user interaction required, and the FAQ says an attacker 'convinces a victim to download and open a specially crafted file from a website,'" he says. "That makes a lot more sense for an image editor. Microsoft hasn't said anything more about the actual trigger."

Dark Reading asked Microsoft for additional information regarding the update timeline.

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#9859. Transformers now runs llama.cpp quants

We're adding support for running GGUF models efficiently in transformers, so you can use checkpoints sized for your laptop's memory through the familiar transformers APIs. Pick a GGUF from the Hub, load it with from_pretrained, and start generating on your own machine.

Running AI models on your laptop has become much easier, and llama.cpp has been a big part of that. Its inference engine powers local AI tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and Jan. Alongside projects like MLX, it has helped make local inference a practical option for everyday use.

A recent example of what local AI can feel like:

This is where we are right now. And i’m not gonna lie it feels pretty magical 🧙‍♀️Qwen3.6 27B running inside of Pi coding agent via Llama.cpp on the MacBook ProFor non-trivial tasks on the @huggingface codebases, this feels very, very close to hitting the latest Opus in Claude… pic.twitter.com/lsIxLoUneU

GGUF, developed by the llama.cpp team, is a widely used format for local inference. The team also shares quantized checkpoints under ggml-org on the Hub. Publishers such as Unsloth, LM Studio Community, and bartowski also provide ready-to-use GGUF checkpoints in a range of quantizations, so users can pick the version that fits their machine. GGUF models have been downloaded millions of times.

We want to make it easier to run these models locally with transformers, too. Compatibility is only useful if the model is pleasant to run. To bring performance close to llama.cpp, we're reusing its underlying ggml kernels through the kernels library, and reducing overhead in generate. Our initial focus is local inference on Apple Silicon, starting with the Qwen3.5 architecture.

GGUF packages model weights and metadata, including tokenizer information and an optional chat template, in one file. It supports different quantization levels, letting you trade some precision for a smaller memory footprint. Variants such as Q4_K_M mix tensor precisions, using mostly 4-bit weights while keeping sensitive tensors at higher precision.

Here's how quantization changes the file size of Unsloth's Qwen3.5-4B:

We suggest starting with Q4_K_M, then trying Q5_K_M or Q6_K if you have more memory available. More aggressive quantization can help larger models fit, but the quality tradeoff depends on the model and the task. Evaluate it on the work you actually want the model to do. The Hub's GGUF documentation describes the available quantization types.

To load a GGUF model, pass its Hub model_id and filename as gguf_file to from_pretrained.

No extra configuration is needed: when the weights stay packed on Metal, transformers automatically loads the compatible ggml/Metal layer kernels and uses ggml-org/ggml-attn as the attention implementation. If that kernel cannot be fetched, the model falls back to "sdpa" with a warning, and you can always force "sdpa" by passing attn_implementation="sdpa" explicitly. See the GGUF documentation for more loading options.

That is the only GGUF-specific step. Everything after it is the standard transformers API:

Without a compatible quantization kernel, the loader falls back to dequantizing the model and uses more memory.

You can also use the same checkpoint with transformers serve, which exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

The model argument uses :.gguf: before the colon is the Hub repository (unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF), and after it is the file to load (Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf). This selects a specific quantization from a repository that may contain several.

For models whose chat template supports thinking, add --reasoning off to skip it or --reasoning on to enable it. The default, --reasoning auto, follows the chat template’s default. See the reasoning options for details.

You can connect a client such as Jan or Pi by adding a custom OpenAI-compatible provider with these settings:

transformers runs the model on your Mac, while the client provides the conversation interface. The same endpoint can be used by other clients that support this API.

Our reference for local inference performance is llama.cpp. The comparison below focuses on three GGUF checkpoints: a small dense model, a larger dense model, and a mixture-of-experts model.

The llama.cpp column comes from the llama-bench tool (build 5f55650a7, release b10200, Metal backend from ggml 0.18.0), run as llama-bench -m -p 0 -n 128 -r 3, which reports tg128: the token-generation rate over 128 decoded tokens, averaged across three repetitions, with prompt processing excluded. The transformers column is generate producing the same 128 tokens from a 12-token prompt, best of three warmed runs, and it includes prefill.

Measured on a MacBook Pro M2 Max, 32 GB unified memory, macOS 26.6, PyTorch 2.12.1, kernels 0.17.0, plugged in.

Transformers is close to llama.cpp across all three checkpoints. The chart uses the same measurements described above; it does not imply identical benchmark conditions, since the Transformers measurement includes prefill while llama-bench reports decode-only throughput.

When GGML and llama.cpp joined Hugging Face, we described their complementary roles: llama.cpp provides a foundation for local inference, while transformers provides a foundation for model definition. GGUF support brings those two closer together.

llama.cpp remains our recommended engine when your priority is efficient local inference. Its dedicated runtime, memory management, and broad hardware support are built around that goal. This integration gives developers a convenient way to work with the same GGUF checkpoints inside transformers:

For that last case, use GgufConfig(dequantize=True):

The bigger opportunity is bringing ggml's performance to models that llama.cpp does not support.

transformers already provides the PyTorch implementations of these architectures. With ggml kernels and quantization schemes available in PyTorch, we can work toward accelerating their supported operations without first implementing the entire model in llama.cpp. This is especially useful for new architectures, research models, and custom variants that may never receive a dedicated llama.cpp implementation.

That opportunity extends beyond the GGUF format itself. A kernel operates on tensors; it does not require the whole model to come from a GGUF file. The same building blocks can be integrated into other transformers models and loading workflows. This also opens a path to other modalities: computer vision models, audio models, and multimodal models could reuse compatible attention, normalization, and matrix multiplication kernels without first having a full implementation in llama.cpp. Each architecture still needs integration and validation; the initial GGUF examples here cover text generation.

We also wanted to show how far we can get while keeping the model and generation loop in Python. With the right kernels and an efficient generation loop, Python and PyTorch can deliver strong local inference performance. The kernels handle the heavy computation, while the generation loop keeps the GPU busy by avoiding unnecessary synchronization.

Our focus was to make eager execution fast without requiring torch.compile. For interactive use, we wanted a quick start and a steady stream of tokens, without compilation pauses or recompilation when input shapes change. The two main pieces of that work are the kernels and generate itself.

A kernel is a small program that performs an operation on the GPU. PyTorch supplies general-purpose implementations; a specialized kernel can do less work, combine several operations, or read quantized weights directly in their stored format.

The kernels library lets us distribute compatible builds of ggml's Metal kernels on the Hub and call them from transformers. That brings ggml's work into the PyTorch model without replacing the model with a separate inference runtime.

The first four packages build on ggml's kernels; the top-k kernel addresses a separate bottleneck in MoE routing. Together they reduce the GPU work needed for each generated token.

To show the contribution of the layer kernels, we compare the same packed GGUF checkpoints with and without them. The quantization kernel stays enabled in both configurations: disabling it would also change how weights are represented and would measure a different tradeoff.

Faster kernels only help if the GPU has work to do. During generation, the CPU schedules GPU operations and controls the loop that produces the next token. Reading a result back from the GPU can force the CPU to wait until queued operations finish. Repeating even a small wait for every token can noticeably reduce throughput.

Two changes address this in generate, which results in improvements for all transformers models (not just when running GGUF files):

These changes improve the generation loop around the model, so their usefulness extends beyond GGUF. They complement the kernel work: kernels reduce the cost of an operation, while fewer synchronization points let CPU scheduling and GPU execution overlap.

These measurements keep all layer kernels enabled; the bars isolate the changes to the generation loop.

The initial target is a single interactive conversation on Apple Silicon. There are a few boundaries to keep in mind:

If you have a GGUF model you would like to use in transformers, open an issue with the checkpoint and your use case. That will help us prioritize support for the models people are running locally.

We would like to thank Arthur Zucker for initiating this work and reviewing all of my PRs, and Cyril Vallez for the generate PRs. We are grateful to Sayak Paul, the llama.cpp team, and Bertrand Chevalier for their help integrating the kernels. We also thank Aritra Roy Gosthipaty and Pedro Cuenca for reviewing this blog post, and Lysandre Debut for overseeing the project.
