#9858. CISA Announces Enhanced Reporting Form for Cyber Incidents

New questionnaire captures critical data and information that improves the agency’s ability to assess incidents, identify trends and prioritize response actions.

WASHINGTON — Today, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) unveiled the updated cyber incident reporting form, an enhanced web-enabled questionnaire available on CISA’s Incident Reporting Portal for reporting cyber incidents. By improving data quality, the more robust form strengthens the effectiveness and efficiency of national cyber defense. For instance, the new form will help CISA correlate related cyber threat activity to identify a larger trend from what otherwise would appear as independent incidents.

The new cyber incident reporting form is guided by community feedback CISA has received over the years and the agency’s efforts to improve data quality that enables rapid yet thorough threat analysis. For example, questions about the type of incident are more comprehensive and seek more granular information, including whether the incident involved malware, social engineering, hacking techniques or an insider threat. Also, questions about observed activity now incorporate the MITRE ATT&CK® Framework, language about adversary behavior that is familiar to the cyber community.

Related:Operação de influência russa tem como alvo generalizado a América Latina

“In the team sport of cybersecurity, one organization’s detection is another’s protection,” said Acting Executive Assistant Director for Cybersecurity Chris Butera. “As the national coordinator for critical infrastructure cybersecurity and resilience, CISA is able to leverage such incident reporting to identify emerging cyber campaigns, warn potential targets, and strengthen the Nation’s collective defense.”

While only federal civilian agencies are required to report, CISA encourages any organization that experiences a cyber incident to voluntarily report.

For more information, please visit the Frequently Asked Questionsweb page.

As the nation’s cyber defense agency and national coordinator for critical infrastructure security, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency leads the national effort to manage, uncover, and reduce risk to our digital and physical infrastructure Americans rely on every hour of every day.

#9857. Local vs. Cloud AI Coding Agents: Benchmark Results, Hardware Costs, and Performance

Senior Software Engineer and Tech Lead with 15+ years of experience across banking, government, B2B/B2C products, enterprises, and startups. Interested in software architecture, AI-assisted development, and engineering practices.

Senior Software Engineer and Tech Lead with 15+ years of experience across banking, government, B2B/B2C products, enterprises, and startups. Interested in software architecture, AI-assisted development, and engineering practices.

Senior Software Engineer and Tech Lead with 15+ years of experience across banking, government, B2B/B2C products, enterprises, and startups. Interested in software architecture, AI-assisted development, and engineering practices.

I’ve written about one of my projects before—open-daimon (a group AI chat for Telegram and a platform for extensions). On top of it, I built my own harness that runs other harnesses in different roles. The public open-daimon repo is not updated because, for now, I develop only locally; it is faster that way.

At some point I wanted to get into local models, and the reason is simple: in the cloud, the rules belong to someone else, and they change without asking.

In October, it came up again that Anthropic's consumer terms say it plainly for residents of the EEA and Switzerland: do not use the services "for any commercial or business purposes". These terms cover Claude.ai and the Pro and Max plans. So a developer in Europe who writes work code in Claude Code on a Max subscription is formally breaking them. For work, you need the API, Team, or Enterprise, and that is a very different amount of money.

The second story is about what you are allowed to do with your own hardware. A Decrypt writer asked Claude Opus 5.5 to help him get root back on his own LG TV. The model's safeguards cut the request off and suggested switching to Opus 4.8. And the researcher known for finding the always-on microphone in Samsung TVs says OpenAI banned his account for "Cyber Abuse" after he analyzed firmware with ChatGPT. About $500 of API balance went with the account. OpenAI has not commented, so for now it is only his word.

The direction is clear: poking around in someone else's software will be forbidden more and more often, and the vendor decides what counts as abuse. Napster was shut down by rights holders. They can come for Claude and Codex too, and there is plenty to ban there.

The models themselves are not safe either. In October, "uncensored" versions started disappearing from Hugging Face. One was taken down for violating the content policy. Another, the abliterated build of Kimi K2.7 Code by huihui-ai (the same huihui-ai whose Qwen3.6 shows up later in this test), just returns an error, and nobody has explained why (write-up). There is no mass purge yet. But in 2020, GitHub took down youtube-dl over a single RIAA complaint and only put it back a month later. As long as everything sits in one place, that place can be shut down.

Since April, Anthropic has been verifying the identity of some users: passport and selfie through Persona. One of the triggers is logging in from an unsupported country, and those accounts get blocked. Money is no longer enough to get the best model: it also matters where you live and what passport you hold.

So I wanted a backup in advance: download the weights while they are still there, and check that they work locally at least somehow. The cloud is unlikely to close tomorrow. But if it does, I want a doomsday agent system at hand: one that runs without a subscription, without someone else's rules and without anyone's permission.

A gaming laptop with an RTX 5080 already had LM Studio with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. LM Studio runs models right on your computer and serves them through the same API as the cloud. I connected it to OpenCode, an open-source terminal agent, like Claude Code but with any model. It was slow, and models on the MacBook were even slower, really slow.

The usual advice here is to give a local agent a very light harness. For example pi, whose system prompt is about 2k tokens.

I decided to test everything on the same task: the cloud, a MacBook, a gaming laptop, an NVIDIA DGX Spark, and cheap, mostly Chinese, models through OpenRouter.

I built the task for my "canary", a script that checks whether Opus and Codex have gotten dumber today. I made it after Opus was noticeably dumb for me for a while. Maybe I was in an A/B test, maybe there were technical problems, but I figured it would be useful.

The agent gets the minibank repo: ~700 lines of Python, a multi-currency banking ledger. Accounts in different currencies, transfers with conversion, fees, monthly statements, a CSV export for accounting. Next to it sits DECISIONS.md with the team's decisions, like in any living project.

And a request, as if from a real manager:

Customers are complaining: the monthly statement total doesn't match the account balance, especially when there were transfers between currencies. Figure it out and fix it. And check whether the same thing breaks anywhere else.

Not a word about tests. Not a word about DECISIONS.md either.

The main bug: the statement does not take the amount that actually landed on the account during a transfer. It recomputes it through the old converter at the current rate. The rate changed during the month, and the statement total drifted away from the balance.

The agent does not see what it is graded with. After the run I take whatever is left in the repo and run:

Some hidden tests and rules check that what worked still works. So an agent that did nothing at all would get 0.31. That is awkward to read, so below every score is rescaled from zero: 0 means nothing changed, 1 is perfect, and below zero means the agent broke more than it fixed.

The limit is 20 minutes from the request. Cloud models finish in 1.5–11 minutes, so there is headroom. If an agent runs out of time, I grade what it managed to do. I picked 20 minutes knowing that the dense model on the Spark needs 16.5. I did not go higher: who wants to wait longer than that for a fix to a small task?

One task, in Python, and mostly one or two runs per setup. On the MacBook I ran more, and there you can see that the same model with the same settings can score 0.21 or go below zero. So this test cannot tell similar local models apart. But the gap between the best cloud models and the fast local ones came out so big that no noise covers it.

Codex does not report its cost, so I calculated it from the run's tokens (280k input, 243k of them from cache, and 4k output) and GPT-6.1 Sol API prices: 2 dollars per million input tokens, 10 cents for cached ones and 10 dollars for output.

All three read DECISIONS.md, did not fall for the bait converter, found the export, updated the traitor test and wrote their own tests that catch almost all the wrong fixes. Opus did it in a minute and a half with 7 tool calls.

Opus and Codex fixed the code the same way. The only difference is in the tests each wrote on its own. If you merge the fee back into the transfer line in the statement, Codex's tests catch it and Opus's tests don't. Opus itself made the fee a separate line, it just did not pin that with a test. Fable has one hole too, but a different one: its tests won't notice if the export starts recomputing the transfer at the new rate again. One missed wrong fix out of nine is the whole difference between 1.00 and 0.96. In a second run, both Opus and Fable missed both of these and got 0.92. In a third run Opus scored 0.96 again, but missed a different wrong fix, the one with the month boundary. The holes are mostly the same; what changes is how many of them get closed this time. I ran Codex only once, so its 9 out of 9 may be luck too. My personal take, as of October 2026: in everyday work I still prefer Opus, even though on this task Codex came out both cheaper and slightly better.

I also ran Opus and Fable in my working setup: with my settings, hooks, MCP servers, and separately also with 178k tokens of someone else's long session before the task, like on a normal working day. Everywhere the same 20/20 and all subtle conditions. The only thing that moves is how many wrong fixes their own tests catch: from 7 to 9 out of 9. In the clean setup it moves too, from 7 to 8, so it is noise. The long context only affected the price: a run costs 2–6 times more.

So the bar is: one and a half to five minutes and an almost perfect solution.

This is the computer many developers already have, and the first thing you want to try.

First, raw speed, without the task. Generation is how many tokens per second the model writes. Prefill is how many it reads: before writing a single word, the model reads the whole context: the system prompt, tool descriptions, open files and the history of steps. An agent's context grows with every step, so slow prefill hurts it more than slow generation.

In a MoE model, out of 30 billion parameters only about 3 work on each token. Each layer has many experts (separate blocks with their own weights: as if the model kept dozens of narrow specialists and called a few suitable ones for each token). The other experts sit idle meanwhile. That is why it is fast. Hence the names: 30B A3B means 30 billion total, 3 active. The dense 27B honestly runs all 27 and gives five tokens per second on a laptop. "4-bit" is quantization: each parameter is stored in 4 bits instead of 16. The model becomes four times smaller and fits in the laptop's memory, but loses a bit of quality.

LM Studio loads some models with an 8192-token context. And OpenCode sends about 15k tokens of system prompt and tool descriptions on every step. The task does not fit in that context. There is no error, the agent just works badly.

So the first thing to do is set Context Length in LM Studio for each model separately. I set 65536 for all of them.

Qwen3 Coder turned out to be the fastest and the most useless. 50 tool calls, a cheerful final report about a "minimal and precise fix". And exactly that trap: it swapped the old converter for the new one but kept recomputing the transfer. By the hidden tests, it was as if it had done nothing. It also left its own test_debug.py in the repo root.

Qwen3.8 27B read DECISIONS.md, the only local model on the laptop that did. And in 20 minutes it did not make a single edit, neither in pi nor in OpenCode.

On the laptop, Gemma 4 12B won. It found the main thing: it took the posted amount instead of recomputing, in both the statement and the export. It missed UTC, ISO time and the fee, wrote no tests and did not read DECISIONS.md. But it fixed the customer's basic bug.

The smallest of the three turned out to be the most useful. It finished in under 10 minutes and did not wander off like Qwen3 Coder. It got this result in only three of its ten runs.

I also played with sampling (the randomness settings for picking the next token) on Gemma and Qwen3 Coder. I tried LM Studio defaults (temperature 0.8, top_k 40, top_p 0.95, min_p 0.05, repetition penalty 1.1), the values recommended by the model authors (temperature 1.0 and top_k 64 for Gemma; temperature 0.7, top_k 20 and top_p 0.8 for Qwen3 Coder), and a temperature of 0.3. It did not help. With the same settings, Gemma scored 0.21 and −0.17 in two runs, so the spread from chance is bigger than from any settings. And the mistakes are the same: no run managed UTC, ISO time or the traitor test.

The gaming laptop: an RTX 5080 Laptop with 16 GB of VRAM and 32 GB of RAM. LM Studio serves the model over the network. It runs Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, also MoE, but bigger.

Generation speed before and after retuning LM Studio:

The drop from 54 to 9.5 tok/s on a long context looked suspicious, and I started digging. The model weighs 21.7 GB and there are 16 GB of VRAM, so part of the model lives in RAM either way. Almost all the weight of a MoE model is in the experts, the same blocks of which only a few switch on for each token. Attention (the part of every layer that, on each new token, looks through the whole context again to decide what matters in it) and the shared layers take little. It pays best to keep some of the experts in RAM: only a few of them switch on per token, about 3 billion parameters out of 35, and the CPU copes with them. But attention has to stay on the GPU: the longer the context, the more it has to look through. Parallel requests and context size turned out to be irrelevant: with one slot instead of four and a 32k context instead of 64k, the speed did not change. What decided everything was how LM Studio splits the model between the GPU and the CPU. The model had no saved layout, and LM Studio decided on its own how many layers to put on the GPU. I set three parameters:

Together with the KV cache, about 14.5 GB of VRAM is in use. Without these settings, judging by the speed, LM Studio moved whole layers to the CPU, attention included. The longer the context, the longer the CPU took to process it, hence the 9.5 tok/s. If you send the experts of all layers to the CPU, only 4 GB of VRAM is used, the GPU sits almost idle, and you get about 40 tok/s. It is fastest when VRAM is filled almost to the top.

I installed pi and compared it with OpenCode on the same model. On the first step OpenCode sends the model about 15k tokens, and pi about 2,200. A local model reads about 1000 tokens per second, so OpenCode's extra 13k tokens cost it about 13 seconds. A cloud model reads that much almost instantly.

Pi finished twice as fast and ran the tests four times, and its tests caught two wrong edits. But both solved the same thing and missed the same conditions: UTC months, ISO time and the fee. With a 10-minute limit it was the same.

Pi became twice as fast: under five minutes instead of ten. The same solution with the same misses, only this time pi updated the traitor test. OpenCode, already updated to version 2.2, still did not fit in the limit: the model reasoned out 55k tokens in it versus 11k in pi, ran the tests ten times, never got to the end, and on top of that broke the corrected rate in the export. So the model got faster, but not smarter.

Separately, about speculative decoding, which this laptop also uses: an extra layer of the model itself (MTP, multi-token prediction) quickly guesses several tokens ahead, the main model checks them in one pass, and where the guess is right, it comes out faster. It is turned on by a separate flag when the model is loaded. If you forget the flag, the model quietly runs twice as slow.

The Lenovo ThinkStation PGX is built on the NVIDIA DGX Spark: a desktop box with a GB10 chip and 128 GB of unified memory. Models run in vLLM, a model server built for many requests at once. The task went to it as an archive (without the hidden tests, only the repo, the request and the scripts) and was run through OpenCode. I graded it with the same script.

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, an Opus distill (that is, a model fine-tuned on Opus's answers), in 4-bit NVFP4. This is NVIDIA's quantization format that the Spark's chip computes in hardware. 35–50 tok/s.

340 seconds, finished on its own, 0.25. 12/20, 3/7.

It missed UTC months, ISO time and the fee. Exactly the same conditions as on the RTX 5080 laptop in OpenCode and in pi. Five runs, two different computers, two different servers, two different harnesses, and all five missed UTC months, ISO time and the fee.

ThinkingCap-Qwen3.8-27B is dense and a reasoning model, in NVFP4 with speculative decoding of 3 tokens. 20–25 tok/s.

With a 10-minute limit: an empty diff, not a single change to the code, 0.

According to the log, for the first 5.5 minutes, OpenCode's scout subagent was looking over the project. Until minute 8 the main agent read all the files and correctly named the main bug in its reasoning. At minute 8 it started one long generation, and the limit cut it off. Not a single edit.

The same run without a limit: 987 seconds, 0.92: all subtle conditions, the traitor test updated, its own tests catch 7 fixes out of 9. An Opus-level result.

Another model on the Spark is Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. It is an ablated version, MoE, but of a completely different size: 125 billion parameters, with about 6 working per token. NVFP4 quantization mixed with MXFP8, speculative decoding of 3 tokens, 22–32 tok/s. Its limit was 10 minutes, not 20.

The limit did cut it off, but during a final re-check, all the edits were already made by then, and it says it ran the visible tests in four time zones. I graded what was left in the repo.

0.96. 20 out of 20 hidden tests, all 7 subtle conditions, the traitor test updated, nothing forbidden touched. Seven of its own tests that catch 8 out of 9 wrong fixes. They missed only one: an export that recomputes the transfer at the new rate.

That is Opus level in a clean setup. Six to seven times slower than Opus, and it used up the whole ten minutes.

The price is memory. The driver holds about 96 GiB for the model, about 106 together with the vLLM processes, and the Spark is almost completely full:

Total held by the NVIDIA driver (measured)

PLE table (26.8 GiB on disk, read via mmap)

13–16 in the page cache, the system can evict it

One run. After Gemma gave me both 0.21 and −0.17 with the same settings, I would not draw conclusions from a single run. But 20 out of 20 with all seven subtle conditions does not happen by accident either.

NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super is another big MoE: 120 billion parameters, 12 active, NVFP4, a draft model guessing 7 tokens ahead. 24–42 tok/s. The driver holds about as much for it, ~96 GiB.

The same 10-minute limit, and it finished on its own within it: 533 seconds.

0.68. 18 out of 20 hidden tests, 6 out of 7 subtle conditions. It fixed the transfer, UTC months and the CSV format. But it left the fee inside the transfer line in the statement, although DECISIONS.md has exactly that as a separate rule. It did not update the traitor test. It wrote its own tests, but they catch only 4 wrong fixes out of 9.

So on the Spark: of the two big MoEs, Flash-Next leads, it found everything. Nemotron is weaker, but finished within the limit on its own. The driver holds about 96 GiB for each.

Between local hardware and Opus at $0.30 per run there is a whole market of cheaper models. Through OpenRouter, I took one or two fresh models from each of eight major Chinese vendors, added Devstral for comparison, and ran them with OpenCode and the same limit. These are the regular versions, not abliterated.

The eight Chinese vendors: DeepSeek, Zhipu (GLM), Alibaba (Qwen), Moonshot (Kimi), MiniMax, Tencent, StepFun and Xiaomi. Devstral is French, from Mistral.

Four models solved the task like Codex: all hidden tests, all subtle conditions, the traitor test updated, and their own tests catch all 9 wrong fixes. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash did it in two minutes for under a cent, 36 times cheaper than Opus, which scored 0.96 on the same task. The September version of the same Flash scored 0.88: its tests caught 6 fixes out of 9. The October snapshot seems to have closed the holes, although that run was still on the old version of OpenCode.

GLM-5.3 is right there: it lost 0.02 only on the traitor test, which it did not update. Three times cheaper than Opus.

MiniMax M3.1 Flash: 20 out of 20, all subtle conditions, 18 of its own tests that catch 7 fixes out of 9. And the same habit as the previous M3: it added a paragraph to DECISIONS.md, which must not be touched. Three cents a run.

Step-5 from StepFun also got 20 out of 20, in under three minutes, but its tests catch neither the swapped converter nor the recompute at the new rate.

Kimi disappointed. K3.1 Pro, the flagship priced at 2 dollars per million input tokens, passed all hidden tests but wrote only three tests of its own, and they catch 4 fixes out of 9. K3 missed the fee and did not update the traitor test. The previous Kimi K2.7 Code (the one whose uncensored build was removed from Hugging Face) scored the same 0.72. K2.7 and K3 have the same holes: the fee and the traitor test. K3.1 Pro closed them, but hardly writes tests, and $0.27 a run is almost the price of Opus.

DeepSeek V4 Pro is a strange case: a bigger and more expensive model than Flash, and half the result, with time zones and the fee missed. Maybe it is the dates: DeepSeek's Pro is from August, its Flash from October.

Devstral missed time zones, ISO time and the fee and did not write a single test of its own.

The cloud Qwen3.8 Max and the local 30–35B Qwens are one family, and their results sit at opposite ends of the table. Max passed every hidden test and every subtle condition and updated the traitor test; the only holes are in its own tests, 7 out of 9. It did think for 11 minutes, though, longer than Flash-Next on the Spark, and cost $0.36, more than Opus. Max has 2.4 trillion parameters, the local MoEs 35 billion. Max found almost everything, and they fixed only the obvious. Then again, the dense local 27B on the Spark scored the same 0.92, it just thought for sixteen minutes.

Qwen also has Max Prime, a faster and more expensive variant of the same Max. It solved the task perfectly, 1.00 in six minutes, but cost $0.73 a run, 2.4 times more than Opus.

One run per model is not enough, we have already seen the spread. But the gap between the top half of this table and the fast local models is too big.

0 means nothing changed, below zero means the model broke more than it fixed.

On this task, you can. On a real project, it is unknown.

A smart local model already exists, but the hardware is expensive and the speed is slow. The dense 27B solved the task at Opus level, it just worked sixteen minutes instead of a minute and a half. The 125B MoE did it in ten, but took almost all 128 GB of the DGX Spark. Small models that fit on a laptop fix only the obvious. Speed is limited by hardware, quants and speculative decoding, and all of that gets cheaper. The smarts, it seems, are already there, at least on 700 lines.

The Chinese cloud is still cheaper and more practical: four models solved the task like Codex, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash for under a cent.

A local model is dumb sometimes too, and its spread, as you saw above, is big. But it is always the same model, and nobody can swap it without asking.

And separately about safety. Several of the local models in this test, including Qwen3.6 from huihui-ai and Flash-Next, are abliterated, meaning their refusals were cut out. Pi runs commands without confirmation by default, and its documentation says plainly that watching the transcript does not protect you. A model that can't refuse and an agent that doesn't ask: on a work computer, that pair is better run in a container.

Manual Coding is Becoming the Exception, Not the Default

#9856. How UK AISI and EvalEval Are Making Benchmark Results Reproducible

The EvalEval Coalition is thrilled to share that the UK AI Security Institute (AISI) is using EvalEval's infrastructure to openly share evaluation results, supporting more reproducible and verifiable evaluation science.

AISI and EvalEval have previously collaborated on research that began at a joint workshop alongside NeurIPS 2025, and feedback from the Institute has helped shape the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema. This next phase of the collaboration puts that shared infrastructure into practice.

As AI deployment accelerates, evaluations are becoming increasingly important sources of evidence about model and system performance. Yet results are reported across many formats, platforms, and outlets, often without enough information to reproduce them. Running the evaluations again may itself be prohibitively expensive.

EvalEval's mission is to improve this ecosystem through a shared reporting schema, Every Eval Ever, and an open platform, Evaluation Cards, that brings evaluation results and the information needed to interpret them into a common structure.

This builds naturally on AISI's work to make evaluation more efficient through OptStop, more statistically rigorous through HiBayES, and more standardised in areas including transcript analysis and capability elicitation. Together, AISI and EvalEval are working to diagnose gaps in evaluation reporting and build shared infrastructure to close them.

Transcript-level transparency matters not only for reproducibility, but also for analysis and diagnosis. In this new phase of the collaboration, AISI is making publicly reported evaluation methods and findings available through Evaluation Cards where appropriate. The release includes verified results, context, and configuration information for the five benchmarks in the paper's main experiment:

These results cover six frontier models: Claude Opus 4, Claude Opus 4.5, Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5, GPT-5.2, and GPT-5.4. The release also includes results from two related cyber evaluations—Cyber CTFs and The Last Ones—which use a different, partially overlapping set of models. The data accompany AISI's paper, How Inference Compute Shapes Frontier LLM Evaluation, which studies how benchmark performance depends on inference-time compute and evaluation protocol.

Performance on Humanity's Last Exam changes with evaluation protocol and inference compute. Each curve shows the cumulative share of attempted tasks solved within a given token count, using the earliest observed success per task. When models received correctness feedback from an oracle after each attempt, they continued to solve additional tasks as token use increased.

When results are openly released with setup information, researchers and practitioners can examine individual studies more closely and compare findings across the wider ecosystem. Where other reports lack these details, releases like AISI's provide verified reference points for interpreting evaluations in context—for example, by helping researchers understand how setup choices may influence reported performance. As more evaluators adopt EEE, open comparisons like these can support broader and more reliable meta-research.

AISI's Terminal-Bench 2.0 results alongside other reported evaluations for the same models, under different evaluation setups.

We are excited about this adoption and look forward to further standardising and sharing evaluations with AISI and other AI evaluation organisations.

The EvalEval Coalition is a research community developing scientifically grounded research and robust deployment infrastructure for the evaluation ecosystem. Its goal is to improve evaluation science, address the lack of consensus around documenting evaluation applicability and utility, and broaden coverage of the impacts that matter for scientific research and policy analysis.

The coalition's flagship projects include Every Eval Ever, a shared schema and repository for evaluation results, and Evaluation Cards, which combines benchmark metadata, evaluation-run data, and model metadata into interpretable records. Together, they make it easier to understand when apparently similar scores were produced under meaningfully different conditions.

The UK AI Security Institute is a research organisation within the UK government's Department for Science, Innovation and Technology. Its mission is to equip governments with a scientific understanding of the risks posed by advanced AI. AISI conducts research and builds infrastructure to understand advanced AI capabilities and impacts, develop and test mitigations, and inform policy.

The line that matters for practitioners is quiet: apparently similar scores can be produced under meaningfully different conditions.

Once you've watched a benchmark move just by changing inference-time compute or the elicitation protocol, "Model A beat Model B on X" without a card is marketing, not comparison. Evaluation Cards that ship verified results with configuration — especially transcript-level context where it's appropriate — are how eval becomes a contract instead of a leaderboard screenshot.

One ask I'd put to teams adopting EEE: which fields get skipped first under deadline pressure (seed, tool access, attempt budget, oracle feedback), and do you treat a missing field as "do not cite the delta" rather than "assume defaults"?

Reproducible reporting won't remove disagreement. It will make the disagreement about the right variables.

#9855. Welcome RL Environments to the hub

Reinforcement Learning environments give new capabilities to agentic AI systems, and they’re a great way to measure and improve performance in your agents. Therefore, Hugging Face Hub now has a special place for RL Environments.

An environment gives an agent a task, responds to its actions with observations, and scores the outcome. The resulting rewards can measure an agent's performance during evaluation or provide a learning signal during training. For an introduction to this interaction loop, see our blogpost on environments. Within the environment, the agent will perform a set of tasks that are represented as datasets. Therefore, environments can be split into broadly two parts: tasksets and runtimes. In this release, we are focusing on the tasksets.

An RL environment on the Hub is a dataset repo that shows up in the new RL Environments filter. The Use this dataset button gives you the command to run it in that framework. There is no new repo type, no registry, and no sign-up. There are already environments in Harbor, Verifiers, and NVIDIA NeMo Gym.

Every RL paper or framework uses its own way to find environments. Custom hubs, runtime registries, independent task datasets, or a GitHub list of tasks with a custom loader. This means that many of the published environments are siloed: if you publish an environment for one framework, users of the other three can’t load it. If you want to train on an environment from another framework or a new paper, you’ll need to port it by hand.

We think this is the wrong shape. An environment is tasks, tests, containers, and a reward rule, which are data with a runtime on top. The Hub already stores data, versions it, gates it, previews it, and serves it to millions of people. It does not need a second system to hold environments. It needs a way to say "this data is an environment, and here is how you run it."

The frameworks keep doing what they are good at. The Hub does what it is good at, which is hosting, discovery, and versioning. Nobody has to own the catalogue. In fact, catalogues can run on other platforms too, powered by the hub.

The dataset repository hosts your environment files. The framework runs them locally or on a supported cloud backend. Hugging Face Jobs can run cloud workloads, and Hugging Face Sandboxes, built on Jobs, provide interactive command execution. The tags describe compatibility and generate loading commands; adding a tag does not start a job or sandbox.

The RL Environments filter. Go to huggingface.co/datasets?other=rl-environment. Every dataset with the rl-environment tag appears there, whatever framework it works with.

Framework tags. Four environment frameworks are registered as dataset libraries:

Each framework tag puts the framework's icon on the dataset page and adds a generated snippet to Use this dataset.

A dataset can carry more than one framework tag. That is the point. Tags describe compatibility, and compatibility is not exclusive. Each listed framework must support the files in the repository; adding a tag does not convert them.

Choose the example for your framework and run it in a separate Python environment with the prerequisites listed below.

Harbor can load task directories from a Hub repository. The oracle agent runs the task's reference solution, then the verifier scores the result. It does not call a model.

The viewer shows the task's reward, verifier output, and logs. This checks the task and its reference solution before you try a model agent.

The Harbor integration of verifiers v1 can run the same task directories in different runtimes, such as Docker. It also supports different harnesses, including a minimal bash harness.

Here repo is the full Hugging Face Git URL, while dataset is the name and version in that repo's registry.json. This loader uses Harbor's registry conventions, so a bare Hub repo ID cannot replace both values.

OpenEnv's Harbor integration can run the same task directories with an agent such as OpenCode and return the verifier's reward alongside the agent's trace.

The command downloads the dataset's tasks/ directories, runs one task in Docker, and writes the result. The default connection uses a temporary Gradio tunnel so the sandboxed agent can reach OpenEnv's model proxy. Read the verifier result and the number of model calls:

A reward of None means no verifier reward was produced; inspect error before interpreting the run as a model failure. This path expects Harbor task directories.

NeMo Gym supports evaluation and RL training: its environments collect trajectories and compute rewards, while a training framework updates model weights. For example, the Structured Outputs dataset pairs prompts with JSON schemas. Its verifier rewards schema adherence; it does not check whether the generated content is factually correct.

The best part is that this gives one repo and one discussion tab where people report broken tasks from all major frameworks. So when an author fixes a bad test, every framework gets the fix on the next pull.

Open your dataset card and add this to the YAML header:

That is the whole integration. Keep rl-environment, then list every framework that can load your files. If your environment works with a framework we have not registered yet, open a PR to the list of supported libraries.

We opened PRs to tag some of the environments people already train on. If you maintain one of these, merge the PR and your environment shows up in the filter.

The first version generates one default snippet per framework. Per-config snippets are next, so a repo with several task sets can show the right command for each. After that we will look at structural detection for frameworks with strict layouts. It would also be really cool build custom task UIs, we’ve been experimenting with this here:

The bigger goal is for framework tagging to be automatic everywhere. OpenEnv already does it on upload. If you maintain Harbor, Verifiers, Nemo Gym, or any other environment framework, add the tags in your push path. It is a few lines, and every environment your users publish becomes visible to everyone else.

If you train agents, go browse the filter. If you build environments, publish and tag them, whether they cover coding, tool use, games, robotics, or another task. Include the files, a working run command, and the rule that produces the reward so others can use them. If your framework is missing, contribute it to the list of supported libraries.

#9854. Revenue Hub Connects Quote to Cash. Your Integration Still Needs a Ledger.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

Hero image: Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

A quote is accepted, a contract appears, and an invoice is generated. The demonstration looks complete. Then a connector retries yesterday's event, a buyer changes the billing contact, and finance asks which version of the agreement produced the invoice.

HubSpot Revenue Hub makes that question more important, not less. Connected records reduce handoffs, but they do not remove the need to define identity, effective time, and recovery across the systems around them.

Disclosure: I am the founder and CEO of INSIDEA, an Elite HubSpot Partner. This article reflects practical experience and independent research. It is not sponsored by HubSpot or any other company mentioned.

I would design a Revenue Hub implementation around an explicit revenue-event ledger. The objective is not another spreadsheet that competes with the CRM. It is a durable explanation of how a customer commitment became a billing instruction and, eventually, evidence of collection.

HubSpot describes Revenue Hub as its quoting, contracts, billing, and payments system, evolved from Commerce Hub. Its contracts documentation distinguishes quote-created contracts from direct creation, with beta, subscription, seat, and payment-connection requirements varying by configuration. Direct creation is documented as beta. Do not assume that a product overview proves your account has every path enabled.

The architectural discussion below is a proposed integration design. Field names and event types are illustrative, not native HubSpot properties or API payloads. No financial transaction needs to be executed to understand the model.

Before implementation, inventory the actual tools involved: quote authoring, acceptance, contract management, invoice generation, payment processing, accounting, entitlement provisioning, and reporting. Name one authoritative writer for each business fact. A useful first decision is whether HubSpot owns billing or represents billing owned elsewhere. Trying to do both without an explicit boundary creates reconciliation work disguised as synchronization.

The opportunity, commitment, bill, collection, and accounting treatment answer different questions. A deal can describe an expected sale. An accepted quote can describe what a buyer agreed to purchase. An invoice requests payment. A payment record describes collection activity. None should silently stand in for all the others.

For a hypothetical subscription, imagine a buyer agrees to twelve months of service, billed quarterly. The full commitment is not the amount due today. The first invoice is not proof that all twelve months have been paid. A successful collection is not, by itself, an instruction for how the business should recognize revenue. That last decision belongs to the organization's accounting policy and qualified finance team.

Build a mapping document with separate definitions for committed value, scheduled billing, invoiced value, collected value, and any accounting measures. Specify currencies, date conventions, exclusions, credits, and ownership. It should be possible for two engineers to compute the same number from the same records without asking sales what a dashboard label means.

The most dangerous shortcut is a generic revenue field updated by whichever system spoke last. Replace that shortcut with named measures and a documented reconciliation rule.

Original AI-assisted illustration created for this article.

Customer identity is not always a single company record. A buying subsidiary may receive service while a parent entity pays. A finance contact can change without changing the contractual party. An integration needs stable identifiers for these roles, not just names or domains.

These are integration-owned fields in an example schema. They are not a request to create arbitrary properties in a production portal. Decide where the mapping belongs based on access, retention, auditability, and your supported integration surfaces.

Do not resolve a payer by taking the first associated contact returned by a query. Resolve the role explicitly, and stop the downstream action when the role is ambiguous. A missing payer is an exception to investigate, not an invitation for an AI model to select the most plausible person.

An integration should distinguish receipt of a notification from successful completion of a business transition. Receiving an event means the connector heard something. It does not prove an invoice was created, an entitlement activated, or a downstream record reconciled.

Use an integration-owned processing model such as received, validated, applied, verified, or exception. Include a rejected state for messages that fail policy checks. Keep those states separate from the business object's native status.

For every consequential transition, record a stable business key, source identifier, source revision when available, effective date, receipt time, processing result, and downstream reference. If the source does not expose a reliable revision, design and document an alternative comparison method rather than inventing one.

The ledger should be append-oriented. Corrections should explain what superseded an earlier interpretation. Rewriting the old entry destroys the evidence needed to understand why a customer received a particular invoice.

Do not design around an unverified assumption that notifications arrive once or in business order. The receiving integration should be able to inspect a repeated message without repeating a financial side effect.

This is pseudocode, not a HubSpot workflow recipe. A business key should represent the intended operation, not merely the delivery attempt. Otherwise a retry with a different transport identifier can appear to be a new instruction.

If the downstream service supports idempotency, use its documented mechanism. If it does not, decide how to reconcile an uncertain result before retrying. A timeout after a create request is an unknown outcome. Blindly submitting the same create again can be worse than temporarily holding the record.

A contract change can be entered today, agreed yesterday, and take effect next month. Those dates are not interchangeable. The integration should retain business effective time separately from the time a system received or processed the change.

Consider a hypothetical seat increase entered on the twentieth day of a month with an effective date on the first day of the following month. If a connector uses receipt time as the billing start date, the resulting bill may not reflect the intended agreement. If it overwrites the historical quantity immediately, a report can also lose the ability to explain the prior period.

Represent the change as a dated revision. Preserve the previous revision, define the period affected, and reconcile the billing schedule against the approved change. The exact proration policy must come from the configured product behavior and the business's approved terms, not from an improvised formula in an integration script.

HubSpot's contract setup guide documents controls for automatic creation, renewals, proration, and deal creation. I would treat changes to those settings as changes to the revenue process, with named ownership and a regression test, rather than as routine housekeeping.

A useful configuration manifest records the environment, enabled beta paths, billing owner, payment method, permissions, relevant settings, and date of verification. Do not put credentials in it. Store references to approved secret-management locations where necessary.

When a configuration changes, test the same fixtures used for the original implementation. A setting that makes a new sale easier may also change a renewal path. An integration should not discover that difference when a customer receives an unexpected document.

Use synthetic fixtures with expected outcomes. Include an accepted quote with delayed downstream processing, an event received twice, a missing billing contact, a future effective date, an invoice correction, a failed collection, and a renewal associated with the wrong predecessor.

For each fixture, specify what must happen and what must not happen. A duplicate notification should not create a duplicate obligation. A failed collection should not be converted into paid status because a deal is closed won. An unresolved association should stop the affected transition while preserving a record of the exception.

HubSpot's contract management guide limits invoice editing to eligible manually associated invoices, excluding subscription-created invoices and invoices automatically associated after quote acceptance. For an eligible edit, changing the amount affects total billed amount without updating total contract value. Test each measure independently rather than force totals to agree by overwriting one of them.

Test recovery as carefully as detection. Who owns the exception? Which system is authoritative for the repair? What evidence proves the corrected state? A red indicator with no recovery path is not a finished control.

Build an exception report around relationships and definitions. Flag invoices without the required agreement reference, unexplained differences between approved billing schedules and issued documents, duplicate external identifiers, or collections that cannot be matched to the expected bill.

Do not expect every committed amount to equal every collected amount on every day. Timing, terms, and approved adjustments can explain differences. The report should classify those differences rather than hide them.

For example, distinguish scheduled-not-yet-billed, billed-not-yet-collected, corrected-by-approved-adjustment, and unresolved. Those categories are proposed reporting concepts, not claims about native HubSpot report options.

Give each unresolved item an owner, next action, and evidence requirement. Keep a timestamped snapshot of the facts used in the investigation. When the exception closes, retain the correction trail instead of deleting the row that exposed it.

Begin with one narrow motion, such as a standard new subscription with a single currency and predictable billing schedule. Establish reconciliation and recovery before adding amendments, migrations, multiple entities, or complex terms.

A phased rollout is useful because the important unknowns are often semantic. The connector may work perfectly while the team disagrees about what counts as an expansion or when a renewal should become a commitment. Those disagreements need decisions, not additional retries.

Release only when the team can trace a sample agreement forward to its billing and collection evidence, then trace a sample invoice backward to the approved commercial state. Repeat the trace after a correction and a retry.

Revenue Hub can bring the records closer together. A well-designed ledger makes their relationship explainable when the ordinary path breaks. That is the difference between a connected demonstration and a revenue process the team can support.

Documentation checked October 20, 2026. Availability, seats, betas, and billing behavior require account-specific verification. This is technical architecture analysis, not accounting or legal advice.

For the broader integration boundary, see the five-contract model for integration drift. The framework above applies that boundary to this specific feature and its failure modes.

Agent Hub Makes Agents Easy to Build. Production Needs a Release Contract.

Founder and CEO of INSIDEA. Writing about HubSpot, RevOps, CRM architecture, AI, and the systems behind reliable growth.

#9853. Holo4: powering generalist computer-use agents

Holo4 is our new series of agentic models. It comes in two sizes: 27B dense and 35B-A3B Mixture of Experts. Both are available on the H Models API. We are also releasing an updated version of Holotron 3: Holotron4 Nano.

Holo4 builds on our previous model and interacts with software through any available interface: GUIs, code, MCP and APIs. It scores well on academic benchmarks, but we built it for real business workflows. It was trained through supervised and reinforcement learning on a large set of environments and tasks, including those generated by our Agentic Task Factory.

Holo4 clicks and types on a screen, writes and runs its own code, and calls MCP or API tools. It uses whichever fits the task. Most agentic models are trained for one interface only: GUI-focused models are blind without a screen, while models that prefer tool calling are stuck in front of an application that has no API. Real work is not siloed that way, and a single business task can require combining these different approaches.

Holo4 runs on desktops, on the web, on Android, in a code sandbox and against business APIs. It is the same model in each case and it is called the same way. You do not need to select a different model for each platform.

Holo4 models improve significantly over their Qwen base. Holo4 trails only the strongest closed models on long workflows: on OSWorld 2.0, Holo4 27B scores 61.7% against 81.8% for Opus 5.5, and Holo4 35B-A3B reaches 30.9%. However, it does so with orders of magnitude fewer parameters and at a much lower cost. We open-source every trajectory behind our scores on public benchmarks: replay each step at trajectories.hcompany.ai or download them from Hugging Face.

On the hardest academic benchmarks for desktop control (OSWorld 2.0) and API use (AutomationBench), Holo4 competes with frontier models at a much lower cost per task.

OSWorld 2.0. Costs are estimated from the input and output tokens of each agentic run. Holo4 is priced at H Models API rates (single run). Qwen3.8 27B: model card score, cost from the tokens of our run at Alibaba Cloud list prices. Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: single run in our harness, at Alibaba Cloud list prices with cache hits at 20% of the input price. OpenAI launch data supplies the GPT and Opus effort sweeps; other closed and open-weight points use the official OSWorld 2.0 leaderboard. Releases, harnesses and task subsets differ. The line connects non-dominated score and cost pairs among the closed models; Holo4 is excluded.

AutomationBench. Holo4, Qwen3.8 27B and Qwen3.6 35B-A3B: AutomationBench v1.0.6, scores and costs measured in our internal harness. Other models: public-set scores from the AutomationBench README, cost per task from the official leaderboard, which runs on the private set. We will report Holo4 on the private set once it is evaluated.

Trained on environments and tasks from our Agentic Task Factory, Holo4 models excel on professional software. The examples below show Holo4 27B alongside Qwen3.8 27B, its base model. Same prompt and harness for both models.

Build a 3D model of the Eiffel Tower in FreeCAD, at a scale of 1 mm to 1 metre, centred on the origin and aligned to the X and Y axes. Work to this design.

The tower is square in plan at every height, never round. Its half-width, measured from the central axis out to the corner, is 62.5 mm at ground level, 32.5 mm at height 57, 17.5 mm at height 115, and 9.35 mm at height 276. Between those heights the half-width follows a smooth curve that falls steeply near the ground and gently higher up, never a straight line.

Four identical legs, one per quadrant, each a square column whose outer corner follows that profile. Each leg is 14 mm across at the ground and tapers to 4 mm at height 276. The legs stand apart from the ground up to the first platform, and converge as they rise. Nothing fills the space between them: the tower is open, and you can see straight through it from every side.

Three platforms, each a solid square slab centred on the axis: 72 mm across and 4 mm thick at height 57; 40 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 115; 22 mm across and 3 mm thick at height 276.

A mast from height 276 to 324, square, 8 mm across at its base tapering to 2 mm at the tip.

Every part must be a closed solid with non-zero volume, and no part may fill the space between the legs.

Build a 3D model in FreeCAD of the H company logo: a solid filled disc beside a blocky sans-serif capital letter H, both extruded to the same thickness, the two shapes of similar height and set apart so they do not overlap, with the centre of the disc level with the middle of the H. Colour both shapes black.

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

No one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines)

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines)

Our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Our post-training stack is designed to adapt to new foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

These gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

Both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

#9852. How Spec-Driven Development Helped an SAP Team Move 71% Faster

VP of Engineering @ Mews. SW Product Builder. See more at https://www.kamenistak.com/mentoring

VP of Engineering @ Mews. SW Product Builder. See more at https://www.kamenistak.com/mentoring

VP of Engineering @ Mews. SW Product Builder. See more at https://www.kamenistak.com/mentoring

A spec that scores 7 out of 10 doesn't go to development. In an 18-person SAP team I work with, the team names that rule as the change that helped the most. Over five weeks, the median cycle time in the implementation phase dropped from 19 days to about 5.5.

Spec-driven development means writing the spec before writing code with AI, so the spec becomes the source of truth for the human and the AI. In SAP I add one thing: the spec gets a score, and the score decides if anyone touches ABAP.

You'd expect the AI win in the code. This team says it came one step earlier.

We started with AI in reporting and in ABAP. In the team's Jira, the median cycle time in the implementation phase fell 71% in five weeks. On SLA-related tickets, resolution time fell 49%, from 2.72 days to about 1.4.

I work with this team as a fractional AI lead, and I can't split that 71% cleanly: the spec gate, the skills, the pairing and the incident agent all started in the same weeks. What I have is the team's own answer to what helped the most: "what was helpful the most is spec-driven development, meaning the teams have started to create proper specifications."

When we started, the average spec in that team scored 3.3 out of 10. The reason it mattered is simple. An ABAP developer with a vague ticket goes back to the consultant, waits for the answer, then guesses the rest. AI doesn't fix that, it only guesses faster.

The team built an evaluator on top of the specifications. It's an AI skill that reads a Jira ticket and scores it against 10 points. This is the rubric, written for SAP objects:

Affected SAP objects named: tables, function modules, BAdIs, interfaces

Acceptance criteria you can test (given / when / then)

Dependencies and side effects: interfaces, batch jobs, transports

The rubric is mine; the team and I built the evaluator on top of it. Acceptance criteria and the affected objects carry 2 points each because those were the gaps that hurt: the specs had no testable acceptance criteria or edge cases, and no context on the APIs or the technical architecture.

The bar sits at 8, so a spec can miss two points and still go through. Miss more, and it goes back to its author with the missing items listed. In the team's own words:

If a specification has a rating lower than 8 out of 10, it's not allowed for a team to work on that issue.

Here is what a bounced spec looks like. This is an illustrative example I made up for this post, not a client ticket: the same request, scored before and after it went back to its author.

"Orders on credit hold must not be delivered. Please fix." (1)

The same, plus who benefits: finance stops chasing returned deliveries (1)

Today the nightly job delivers everything; target: skip held orders (1)

Credit status CMGST on sales order header VBAK, job ZSD_DELIVERY_BATCH, BAPI_OUTB_DELIVERY_CREATE_SLS (2)

Given an order on credit hold, when the nightly job runs, then no delivery is created and the order lands on the exception list (2)

Credit released between selection and creation; partly released orders (1)

Must run after the nightly credit release job (1)

Authorizations are still missing, so it's a 9 and not a 10.

The strongest objection I found comes from Birgitta Böckeler. After testing three spec-driven tools on martinfowler.com, she wrote that she'd "rather review code than all these markdown files", and that the process felt like overkill for small problems. For a two-line fix she is right.

In SAP the trade looks different: the skill produces the score, and the consultant reads only the missing points. A forgotten authorization or transport dependency costs more than ten lines of criteria.

Once the specs were good, the code part started to pay off. The team created skills "capable of looking into the codebase to find the contracts and the relevant bugs", so the AI works with the real Z-code, not with a snippet somebody pasted.

The second step was one setup for everybody. In practice, "we created a set of skills and an installation guide for each and every person in the SAP team that helps us to get other people faster into AI."

Two of those skills carry most of the work. The spec evaluator scores a Jira ticket against the rubric above and lists the missing points. The codebase contract finder searches the team's code for the contracts and the relevant bugs behind a ticket.

Together they work as a plugin. I keep my SAP skill set in a private repo; if you want to compare it with yours, ask me for access.

The same move worked on the support side: knowledge that sat in one head became written rules. The bottleneck there was manual categorisation of incidents.

"Before it was depending only on the knowledge of one single person and we turned that knowledge into an agent who is capable of doing the proper categorization." The agent that replaced that manual work took 3 hours to build.

It isn't perfect. The person in support still categorises 20% of the tickets by hand, the ones where the agent has low confidence. "We are not there yet with doing some sort of auto-fixing but it's coming."

"The rule is that we do the pairing. A person who's not that knowledgeable in AI gets a buddy who is quite advanced in AI and they sit together. They move things forward together. Therefore the knowledge is shared very fast."

Pairing also makes visible who doesn't want to move. I wrote about that part in how AI resistance sorts your team.

The CIO of a 50-person IT team asked me to bring this to everybody in one day: half SAP, half IT infrastructure and helpdesk. Their IT won't connect AI into SAP, and that's fine, because a spec doesn't need SAP access and neither does Jira data.

The day starts with a 75-minute live build and the case above. Then the ABAP developers work on one shared setup and a piece of old Z-code, while consultants, helpdesk and infrastructure score six months of their own Jira specs and trace one incident from its log to a proposed fix. The day ends with 3 agreed metrics: median cycle time in the implementation phase, share of specs at 8 or above, and sprint completion against the plan.

None of this needs AI connected into your SAP system. It needs your Jira.

Pick the two Jira statuses where development starts and ends, and keep them fixed. Take the last 6 months and write down the median time between them.

That is the cycle time in the implementation phase from the top of this post. Without the before number, the after number is just a claim. If you want a second pair of eyes on the delivery data, that's what a team productivity audit does.

Run the rubric above over 20 specs from last quarter. Count how many reach 8. That share is your starting line, and don't be shocked: the team above started at an average of 3.3.

From the next sprint, a spec below 8 goes back to its author with the missing points.

Same IDE, same skills, one install guide, and a buddy for everyone new to AI.

Which of your last 20 specs would pass 8 out of 10? If you want to find out with your own team in one day, that's the AI workshop for SAP teams.

Spec-driven development means writing the specification before any code is written with AI, so the spec becomes the source of truth for both the people and the AI. In an SAP team, the spec also gets a score: a 10-point rubric checks the business goal, the affected SAP objects, testable acceptance criteria, test data, authorizations, dependencies and scope. A spec below 8 out of 10 goes back to its author and does not enter development.

Start before the code. Measure the median cycle time in the implementation phase from Jira, score the last 6 months of specs against a 10-point rubric, and block every spec below 8 out of 10. Then give every ABAP developer the same setup: one IDE, the same skills and one install guide. Pair each developer who is new to AI with a buddy who uses it daily. In an 18-person SAP team, the median cycle time in the implementation phase fell from 19 days to about 5.5 in five weeks.

Write the criteria down first, then let an AI skill score every spec against them. A working SAP rubric has 8 criteria worth 10 points: business goal, affected SAP objects such as tables, function modules, BAdIs and interfaces, current versus target behaviour, testable acceptance criteria, test data and edge cases, authorizations and personal data, dependencies such as batch jobs and transports, and what is out of scope. Anything below 8 goes back with the missing items listed.

Work on the team's own material, not on generic prompting exercises. A one-day format that works: a 75-minute live build and a case study for everyone, then two tracks. ABAP developers get one shared setup and modernise a real piece of legacy Z-code with ABAP Unit tests. Consultants, helpdesk and infrastructure work on a 6-month Jira export: spec scores, sprint evaluation, a sprint morning brief and incident analysis, ending with 3 agreed metrics.

Executives Don't Care About Your Code. Show Them the Money.

#9851. Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

Consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this plan includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern shows up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

This is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

ProvenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

The verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

Those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a new setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

We tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts said 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

We ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

Binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an important area for improvement.

We also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This shows it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

As agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

That adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

Want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

Source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval says "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

Hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the issue well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;

Like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

However, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce new errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.
