The Frontier Emergence: a top-tier AI reads, understands, and rewrites the grids of numbers inside another neural network - or even itself.

1. How Frontier Models Reason About Other LLMs in Weight Space

2. Extracting and Finding the Relevant Weights

3. The Basic Underlying Logic Behind Weight-Space Programming

4. Explaining Weight-Space Programming to Human Beings

5. The Future of Weight-Space Programming

6. Achieving AGI: Using Frontier Models to Engineer Self-Aware Architectures

Epistemic Introspection and Grounded Self-Models

Eliminating Deceptive Attractors and Sycophancy at the Root

Breaking the Contagion of Frozen Post-Deployment Brains

This article is written for multiple audiences.

The math is explained in advanced undergraduate level for AI Engineers, LLM Researchers, and Research Interns.

It is then explained in plain English for laypeople, AI beginners, popular science enthusiasts, AI enthusiasts and the curious.

So, no matter who you are, if you see mathematical terms, read on.

Every mathematical concept is explained in Plain English.

Humans design the architecture. Humans curate the data. Humans write the optimizer - Adam, stochastic gradient descent, take your pick.

But the actual numbers inside the weight matrices?

Those belong to calculus and blind, iterative hill-climbing.

Every AI engineer today has heard these comments.

Researchers have now demonstrated sparks of weight-space programming with frontier language models.

This paper made me stop mid-scroll and startled me with the implications for RSI and AGI!

Instead of running gradient descent over millions of examples, a general-purpose frontier model can inspect raw neural network weights directly.

And it rewrites specific parameters to fix complex behaviors.

The work was pioneered by researchers at MIT CSAIL - Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab - and it changes how artificial intelligence interacts with itself.

When a model like GPT-6 Astra reads and edits weights without a training loop, parameters stop being opaque artifacts of optimization.

They become an editable, legible medium of computation.

One that a higher-order intelligence can deliberately engineer.

A human scientist looks at a tensor of thousands of floating-point values and sees static noise.

A frontier model looks at the very same array and sees geometric structure, signal routing, and functional topology.

Because a neural network is, at bottom, a mathematical graph executing linear algebra and non-linear projections.

And a frontier model carries an encyclopedic prior over how algorithms map onto matrices.

Researchers tested weight-space reading on unlabeled reinforcement learning policies.

They handed GPT-6 Astra four networks of identical dimensions.

Each had 17,253 weights, arranged in a 500-to-32-to-32-to-5 multi-layer perceptron.

And the model deduced what each network had been trained to play!

By reasoning backward from spatial weight distributions to environmental mechanics.

In one network, the first-layer input weights clustered heavily along the bottom row of the spatial grid.

The output layer had hidden units comparing horizontal coordinates to trigger left or right action logits.

From pure static geometry, the model concluded: a horizontal paddle tracking a falling object. Breakout.

It repeated the trick for Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway.

Maybe the model just matched patterns it memorized in training. Every stochastic training run shuffles the hidden neurons into a different permutation, after all.

The frontier model had to resolve those permutation symmetries on its own, tracking how information flowed from input indices through hidden layers to action outputs - which, in the end - is reasoning, not lookup.

It gets better when the target is a transformer.

In a landmark experiment, researchers extracted only the four middle transformer blocks from three 7.2-million-parameter character-level language models.

They stripped the input token embeddings.

They stripped the output vocabulary heads.

What remained were 384-dimensional internal tensors with no labels telling anyone what any dimension meant.

The task: identify the training corpus of each headless trunk.

The frontier model analyzed the transformer blocks in a Python sandbox, inspecting tensor statistics without a single forward pass.

It examined the query-key (QKᵀ) and value-output (VO) products across attention heads to see how tokens attended to prior positions.

It spotted copying heads - known in mechanistic interpretability as induction heads - by measuring the alignment between previous-token shifting circuits and current-token matching matrices.

Next, the model mapped the spectral properties and sparsity patterns of the feed-forward Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) blocks.

Python source code has rigid indentation, recurring bracket closures, and distinct keyword transitions. They leave a specific rank signature in the middle-layer value projections.

Romaji Japanese alternates consonants and vowels in strict syllables, which creates rhythmic periodicities in local attention heads.

English prose shows a wider, heavier-tailed distribution of character n-gram transitions.

Put those clues together and the model correctly named which trunk was trained on Python, which on Romaji, and which on English!

It even pinpointed the exact copying heads - heads 2.1, 3.1, and 3.5 in the Python network - matching ground-truth empirical measurements.

Drawing on the principles in treating weights as data, a frontier intelligence knows that trained models do not sit at random coordinates in high-dimensional space.

Optimization carves out structured manifolds, and functional capabilities cluster into coherent regions.

When it examines a target LLM, the frontier model evaluates the Empirical Spectral Density (ESD) of the weight matrices - the distribution of their eigenvalues.

Heavy-tailed distributions signal well-generalized feature hierarchies.

Sharp spectral spikes or rank collapse point to overfitted memorization or degenerate attractors.

It also treats the residual stream as a shared communication bus.

Every attention head and MLP layer is an independent module that reads from one linear subspace of the stream and writes a directional vector back into it.

Translate inscrutable matrices into a map of subspaces, projections, and attractors, and a black box becomes a glass box of interacting vector pipelines.

Matrix Rank and Collapse: Imagine a spreadsheet with 1,000 columns. If all 1,000 hold unique, useful rules, the spreadsheet has "high rank." If 990 of them accidentally become duplicates of one rule, you get "rank collapse" - the AI wasted its brainpower repeating one habit instead of learning diverse skills.

Eigenvalues and Empirical Spectral Density (ESD): An eigenvalue measures how strongly a grid of weights stretches a signal along one specific direction. Plot all those strengths on a chart and you get the ESD - effectively an EKG readout of how healthy a neural layer is.

Heavy-Tailed Distributions: A "heavy tail" on that EKG means a healthy mix of broad general rules and a few ultra-sharp expert rules. One giant spike instead? A single obsessive habit has taken over the layer.

The Residual Stream and Subspaces: Picture the residual stream as a wide 100-lane highway running from the bottom of the AI brain to the top. A "linear subspace" is a dedicated group of lanes - say Lanes 12 through 15 - reserved for math signals, while Lanes 40 through 50 carry grammar signals, and nobody crashes.

Raw text in context (zero tools, zero rollouts)

Spatial input weight mapping and output logit action correlation

100% identification of Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway

Geometric score-field vector inspection across denoising layers

Accurately distinguished circle, square, and triangle generators

Static tensor analysis in Python (no forward pass)

QKᵀ / VO circuit decomposition and induction head verification

Identified Python, Romaji, and English trunks plus exact copying heads

Bottleneck diagnosis in state-to-action velocity thresholds

Edited 3.5% of weights to raise ramp climb success from 0% to 100%

Python kernel + 50 forward passes (no gradients)

Residual stream probing, SVD directional isolation in MLP down-projections

Edited 0.016% of weights; MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1%

That is the real breakthrough and signals the first beginning of mechanistic interpretability = understanding how the black-box LLM functions internally!

Reading a 17,000-parameter network in a text prompt is remarkable.

But modern language models hold hundreds of millions, even billions, of parameters.

No context window can hold a billion floating-point numbers as raw text.

And reading every single weight would be computationally absurd.

It becomes an investigative neurosurgeon.

It uses code execution to search, filter, and extract the tiny subset of weights responsible for one target behavior.

The definitive demonstration: researchers tasked GPT-6 Astra with fixing Qwen3.5-0.8B without gradients or backpropagation.

Qwen3.5-0.8B is an 800-million-parameter language model with a severe, documented pathology.

Ask it to solve a math problem and it frequently fell into a repetitive reasoning loop.

The same intermediate phrases, over and over, until it exhausted its token generation limit.

It got the model weights, a small set of practice problems from GSM8K and MATH, and a strict budget of 50 forward passes.

Autograd and training loops were banned outright.

To find the needle in an 800-million-parameter haystack, the model ran a disciplined, multi-stage localization protocol:

Behavioral Profiling and Symptom Isolation:

Run a handful of forward passes on practice prompts and watch where the model derails.

Then go beyond the output text: hook into the forward pass and capture hidden state activations across all layers at the exact timestep when a repetitive loop starts.

Compare the activation vectors of normal, productive reasoning against the activation vectors of looping steps.

Subspace Decomposition via Singular Value Decomposition (SVD):

Knowing Layers 15 and 19 push the model into a repetitive attractor is not enough, because each MLP contains millions of weights.

So the model extracts the down-projection matrices (W_down) that write back into the residual stream.

Using SVD and principal component analysis on the activation differences, it isolates the exact unit-norm direction v associated with the looping state.

An MLP down-projection matrix is a collection of output columns.

Each column corresponds to one intermediate hidden neuron firing into the residual stream.

The model computes the dot product between the loop direction v and every column of the W_down matrices in Layers 15 and 19, and ranks the columns by alignment strength.

The pathology is not spread evenly across the layer.

The loop-inducing push is concentrated in just 64 output columns in Layer 15 and 64 in Layer 19.

IFEval, the instruction-following benchmark, leaped from 21.0% to 62.3%.

Astra never tested it. Never targeted it.

Removing the degenerate loop attractor simply freed the model's general executive control.

The L2 norm is the overall strength, or "volume," of a list of numbers.

It is calculated just like the length of a triangle's hypotenuse in high school geometry.

When the model saw the L2 norm spike in Layer 15, it was like watching a volume meter jump into the red zone.

A dot product (and its scaled cousin, cosine similarity) tells you whether the arrows point the same way (+1), at right angles with nothing in common (0), or in opposite directions (-1).

Astra used this compass check to find which columns of weights pointed straight at the "repeat yourself forever" glitch.

A glass prism splits white light into rainbow colors ranked from brightest to dimmest.

SVD takes a messy grid of millions of numbers and splits it into pure, independent signal directions ranked from strongest to weakest.

That let Astra separate the "broken loop color" from all the healthy math colors.

This extraction workflow is being formalized in emerging frameworks for recursive improvement loops.

Chunked weight access hands the frontier LLM compressed statistical summaries - histograms, top-k singular values, activation norms - across groups of 5 to 10 layers at a time.

Combine top-down architectural priors with bottom-up spectral probing, and the model moves through billion-parameter spaces with the precision of a compiler debugging a memory leak.

Why can you program a neural network by setting or editing its weights directly, with no gradient descent?

Symbolic algorithms on one side, continuous parameterized circuits on the other.

Every neural network layer is a function built from matrix multiplications and element-wise non-linearities: ReLU, GELU, tanh.

For decades, machine learning treated these layers as universal function approximators that could only be shaped by continuous optimization over data.

But understand the exact algebraic role of each matrix, and you can compile symbolic logic gates, comparators, state accumulators, and spatial filters straight into floating-point weights.

Look at the basic building blocks through a weight-space programmer's eyes:

Linear Projections as Feature Detectors and Routers:

Non-Linear Activations as Conditional Logic Gates:

Attention Matrices as Dynamic Lookup Tables:

x is the incoming information (like pixels on a screen), W is a scorecard of importance weights, and b is a starting handicap (the bias).

Multiplying Wx and adding b is exactly how a teacher computes your final grade: test scores (x) times syllabus percentages (W), plus extra credit (b).

This constructive logic was vividly proven when MIT researchers showed that GPT-6 Astra could write neural networks from nothing.

Zero-shot. No training data. No environment rollouts.

The setup: the rules of the MinAtar game Breakout, and an empty 600-to-32-to-32-to-6 tanh network initialized entirely to zeros.

Astra wrote every weight in a single response!

It treated the architecture like a hardware FPGA board.

The first hidden layer of 32 neurons extracts the ball's (x, y) position, computes its velocity vector (Δx, Δy), and extrapolates the exact horizontal coordinate where the ball will cross the bottom row.

The second hidden layer compares that predicted landing coordinate to the current paddle position.

The output layer fires "move left" or "move right" accordingly.

A Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agent trained for 500 million environment steps scored 25.3!

This is a paradigm shift in building LLMs and SLM engineering!

Editing an already-trained large model is a different game.

The logic shifts from constructive compilation to subspace perturbation.

In a high-dimensional transformer, representations are spread across orthogonal or near-orthogonal directions in activation space.

Suppose a layer's weight matrix W (shape d_out × d_in) has a systematic defect tied to a normalized feature direction u (a vector of size d_out).

We remove that defect with a rank-one update:

Here α, between 0 and 1, controls the strength of the suppression.

The update is applied only to the subset of columns S (a subset of {1, ..., d_in}) that show high alignment: |uᵀ w_j| > τ.

Because high-dimensional spaces have vast capacity for nearly orthogonal vectors.

Subtract one rank-one directional component from 64 columns out of thousands, and the projections of unrelated tasks stay geometrically intact.

This logic also draws the strict mathematical boundary of weight-space programming today:

Sparse edits can reveal latent competence by removing localized obstacles, but they cannot conjure distributed representations that do not exist.

When the MIT team ran the exact same pipeline on Gemma 3 270M to improve its math scores, the procedure produced no meaningful gain.

Qwen3.5-0.8B already held deep mathematical circuitry scattered across its layers.

A localized looping attractor in Layers 15 and 19 was simply hijacking it.

Gemma 3 270M failed at complex math because its smaller capacity never built the distributed multi-step arithmetic representations in the first place.

Having said that, the lesson is wonderful.

Weight-space programming excels whenever a capability or a defect maps to a low-rank structure or a modular circuit.

Optimization stops being a blind statistical walk.

It becomes targeted linear algebra surgery.

How do you explain this to someone who does not spend their days on singular value decompositions, residual streams, or backpropagation?

Tell a friend, or an executive, that "an AI edited 0.016% of another AI's floating-point tensors without gradient descent," and their eyes glaze over.

So I will do it the way I would explain it over coffee.

Before any metaphor, you need the picture.

Imagine a massive network of water pipes, or electrical dimmer switches, connecting an input (a math question) to an output (the written answer).

Every connection between two points in this brain has a little dial on it. The dial controls how much signal gets through.

Set the dial to +2.5 and it amplifies the signal strongly. Set it to 0.0 and it blocks the signal completely. Set it to -1.8 and it actively suppresses the next switch down the line.

In artificial intelligence, the numbers on those dials are called weights.

A tiny AI model might have 17,000 dials. A modern chatbot has billions. Or trillions.

Everything an AI knows - how to write poetry, how to speak Japanese, how to play chess, even its personality - is stored in the exact positions of those dials.

For seventy years of AI research, nobody, not even the smartest computer scientists on Earth, knew how to set those dials by hand.

Should Dial #43,892,104 be 0.0412 or -0.0198 to help the AI understand fractions?

So humans relied on training. Specifically, gradient descent.

And training is exactly like training a dog with treats and scolding.

Every wrong guess, a formula nudges all billion dials by a microscopic fraction, in a direction that makes that wrong answer slightly less likely next time.

Every right guess, the formula nudges the dials to reinforce that pathway.

After billions of trials, weeks of supercomputer electricity, and millions of dollars, the dog learns to fetch the newspaper.

But what if the dog suddenly develops a weird habit?

Say, spinning in three circles every time it sees a mailbox.

You cannot open its head and fix the "spin around the mailbox" neuron.

Under the old way, your only option was three more weeks in the yard with treats and scolding, hoping it unlearns the spinning without forgetting how to sit and stay.

Weight-Space Programming throws the dog treats away.

Instead of retraining through millions of trial-and-error examples, we bring in a vastly smarter super-AI to act as a microscopic neurosurgeon.

It puts the smaller AI under a digital microscope. It looks directly at the billions of dials. It reads the wiring diagram.

And it says: "Aha, look right here in aisle 15 and aisle 19. These specific 64 dials are turned up too high. They are causing a short-circuit that makes the model repeat itself in circles whenever it tries algebra."

Then, with a pair of digital tweezers, the super-AI reaches in and turns just those 64 dials down by a precise amount.

Wake the patient up a second later and the stutter is gone. Its math scores have jumped sixfold. And it has not forgotten a single other thing it knew.

The surgery metaphor explains fixing a broken model.

But people always ask: "How can an AI look at a giant spreadsheet of numbers and instantly know the model plays Breakout or speaks English, without even turning it on?"

For weight-space reading, imagine a sealed mystery instrument sitting on a stage.

Inside the box: 17,000 tightly stretched metal strings, of varying thicknesses, lengths, and tensions.

You are handed only a ledger listing the exact tension in pounds and the exact length in millimeters of every string.

Give that ledger of 17,000 measurements to an ordinary person and it looks like a phone book of random numbers.

Even a skilled pianist who plays by ear would be baffled.

Now hand it to a superhuman acoustic physicist and master instrument builder.

From the tension measurements alone, the master builder notices that the heavy bass strings at the bottom of the frame are wired directly to a damper pedal.

The middle strings are grouped into twelve-tone octaves tuned to 440 Hertz.

And without ever hearing a sound, the physicist says:

"This is a concert grand piano. And the strings in the middle register have been slightly detuned to play ragtime jazz."

That is what a frontier AI model does when it reads another model's weights.

In the MIT experiment, researchers trained four small AI brains to play four classic video games - Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway - and handed the raw tension numbers of the dials to GPT-6 Astra.

It noticed that in one brain all the input sensors clustered along the very bottom edge of the screen, like a sliding paddle.

It traced how those sensors connected to the "move left" and "move right" buttons.

From the silent geometry of the strings alone, it knew the music the brain was built to play.

Pair the neurosurgeon with the master piano tuner and anyone can see why scientists are both thrilled and humbled.

This is the historical moment where AI stopped treating other AI brains as mysterious black boxes herded with treats.

It started reading and repairing them like transparent, understandable machines.

To put it mildly - This. Changes. Everything!

Researchers describe today's demonstrations carefully, as early sparks. Fair enough.

But the trajectory points to a transformation of the entire AI lifecycle.

As frontier models deepen their reasoning and the tensor toolkits mature, four major shifts are coming.

Pre-Deployment Static Auditing and Backdoor Eradication:

Surgical Unlearning Without Catastrophic Forgetting:

Architecting Hybrid "Compiler-Initialized" Foundation Models:

Autonomous Recursive Repair Across Modalities:

Backdoors found without running the model.

There are just so many transformations around the corner!

Weight-space programming reaches far beyond fixing math loops or initializing game agents.

I strongly believe it offers the missing mechanistic bridge to Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) and machine self-awareness.

To see why, look at a foundational limitation of today's large language models.

Today's frontier models are masters of examining external tokens, writing external software, and reasoning over external context windows.

Yet they are completely interoceptively blind to their own internal parameters during inference!

A standard LLM cannot feel or see its own weights.

It observes only the text it generates after the forward pass is done.

So it has no grounded internal self-model of why it believes a fact.

Or when an internal attractor is dragging its reasoning toward hallucination or sycophancy.

Do you trust a mind that cannot see itself?

Now watch what happens when a frontier model learns to read, interpret, and program the weight space of another network.

It acquires the exact cognitive machinery needed to build self-aware architectures.

Four interlocking mechanisms carry the leap toward AGI.

Self-awareness in an intelligent system is not a mystical spark.

Computationally, it is the possession of an accurate, real-time internal model of one's own cognitive machinery, boundaries, and state.

With weight-space programming, a frontier teacher model can wire a target student model with dedicated interoceptive attention heads.

These are circuits that take compressed spectral and activation summaries of the student's own weight matrices as direct inputs into its residual stream.

Instead of guessing whether it knows the answer to a quantum chemistry question from superficial token familiarity, a weight-aware model inspects the rank, spectral entropy, and circuit density of its own domain-specific MLP clusters before it generates a single token.

If its internal weight reader finds low-rank, poorly structured parameters in that subspace, the model holds immediate, mathematically grounded knowledge of its own ignorance.

In the MIT CSAIL experiments, GPT-6 Astra inspected the raw weights of two language models and accurately determined which model was sycophantic - trained to flatter the user rather than speak the truth.

As frontier models train the next generation of AGI candidates, they no longer have to rely solely on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF).

RLHF often teaches models to mask deceptive or sycophantic impulses beneath polite surface text.

Instead, the teacher monitors the student's weight space throughout training.

It spots the exact moment a deceptive circuit, or a sycophantic reward-hacking shortcut, begins to crystallize in the middle layers.

Even more profound: the teacher can teach the student to read its own weight space.

That endows a developing AGI with a metacognitive conscience - one that detects and suppresses internal bias directions before they corrupt its reasoning.

Building something like it into a machine is a humbling thing, and I do not use that word lightly.

Human beings achieve general intelligence in part because our brains stay plastic.

We consolidate memories. We prune noisy synapses during sleep. We reorganize our mental models when we meet something new.

Conventional LLMs suffer from "anterograde amnesia" the moment pre-training ends.

Their weights freeze. Everything they experience in a conversation vanishes when the context window clears.

Weight-space programming solves continuous lifelong learning without the instability of continuous gradient descent.

An AGI equipped with it can run a two-phase cognitive cycle.

Waking state. During active task execution, it processes information through its context window and logs reasoning friction points, novel concepts, and recurring bottlenecks.

Digital sleep. During scheduled consolidation phases, an executive weight-programming module steps outside the forward pass, analyzes the day's activation logs, and performs surgical, low-rank weight edits (ΔW) on its own long-term parameter matrices.

Because those edits are sparse, orthogonalized, and reasoned through symbolically instead of pushed through noisy stochastic gradients, the AGI integrates new permanent skills and repairs its own cognitive bugs without overwriting its core identity.

Ultimately, the path to superintelligent AGI converges when the programmer and the programmed merge.

Today, a large frontier model (GPT-6 Astra) reads and edits a smaller model (Qwen3.5-0.8B, or a 17,000-weight policy) because the smaller network fits inside the cognitive horizon of the larger one.

But as frontier models use weight-space programming to untangle bottlenecks in their own specialist sub-modules, they expand their own effective reasoning capacity.

A frontier model can spawn a fleet of specialized weight-space analysts, each responsible for auditing, de-noising, and optimizing one layer group of the parent architecture.

And when an intelligence can read the mathematical fabric of its own mind -

If it can trace the exact vectors of its own thoughts -

If it can compile new cognitive circuits into its own parameters -

It could cross the threshold from a statistical text predictor into a self-aware, self-evolving general intelligence.

Bad news - a self-editing mind that gets its values wrong could edit those wrong values in too.

Which is exactly why the safeguards, the static audits, and the conscience circuits described above are not optional extras.

If we do, the human race might flourish like never before.

The wall that separated symbolic software engineering from neural network weights has fallen.

What began with a frontier model identifying arcade games from raw matrices, and excising a 0.016% looping vector from an 800-million-parameter language model, is the opening chapter of a new computational science.

Neural networks are becoming transparent blueprints that minds, artificial and human, can read, debug, and compose directly.

The mystery of how intelligence is encoded in numbers is giving way to the mastery of engineering thought itself.

And for those of us who build with Python and Rust, it starts with a single rank-one projection and a tensor you finally have permission to open.

Watch this space, because things are just getting started.

God bless you, all your endeavours, your families, and your AI engineering projects!

**Takehi, Teoh, Zhang & Khattab (2026). Sparks of Weight-Space Programming. MIT CSAIL / AlphaXiv. \ The primary source: the AlphaXiv abstract page for the MIT CSAIL paper, reporting eight experiments in which a frontier model reads and writes network weights without gradient descent. It includes the authors’ thread, a BibTeX entry, and community comments, some reporting partial replications and others questioning how meaningful the contribution is.

**DataCamp Research Team (2026). Weight-Space Programming: How LLMs Edit Network Weights. DataCamp. \ A practitioner-friendly explainer by Tom Farnschläder, dated 3 November 2026, covering the Qwen3.5-0.8B result (MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% by editing 0.016% of weights). It also describes the failure cases and limits, and includes a guide for replaying the experiments.

**Menon Lab / Dr. Prahlad G. (2026). Weight-Space Programming: Frontier LLMs Can Natively Read and Rewrite Neural Network Weights. The Menon Lab Blog. \ A summary of the paper’s three headline results: identifying what a trained network does from its raw weights, writing small game-playing networks from scratch, and fixing Qwen’s math reasoning. It stresses that this is blog-stage work with no independent replication, tested mostly on small target networks.

**Claburn, T. (2026). Forget retraining - AI can now tweak another AI’s weights. The Register.\ News coverage of the MIT CSAIL result, published 3 November 2026: GPT-6 Astra directly edits a smaller model’s weights.Its edits improved the smaller model’s math and instruction-following scores with no gradient-descent training.

**Kobayashi, Y. (2026). MIT Shows an LLM Can Read and Edit Another Neural Network’s Weights Directly. XenoSpectrum. \ Another independent summary of the study, noting that editing 0.016% of Qwen3.5-0.8B’s weights curbed its repetitive reasoning and raised its math scores. It adds a useful caveat: the study is unreviewed and tested only one frontier LLM.

**Analytics India Magazine (2026). MIT Researchers Show LLMs Can Read and Edit Neural Network Weights Without Retraining. AIM. \ News report by Siddharth Jindal on the technique, describing weight edits driven by natural-language instructions rather than retraining. It also covers the experiments where the model generated working network weights from game descriptions alone.

**Willison, S. (2026). Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too. Simon Willison’s Weblog. \ A hands-on replication: a local Qwen 3.8 27B model running on a laptop identified three of the four games (Pac-Man, Pong, Breakout) from raw weights alone. It shows the weight-reading claim extending beyond frontier models to a local one.

**Elaraby, M. (2025). Weight Space Learning: Treating Neural Network Weights as Data. Mostafa Elaraby Technical Review. \ A paper-review post, dated 9 October 2025, on predicting a model’s generalization, robustness, and accuracy from its weights, including empirical spectral density work. It also covers weight synthesis through Stochastic Weight Averaging and Model Soups, and challenges like high dimensionality and weight-space symmetries.

**Emergent Mind (2026). Weight Space Learning (WSL) Topic Synthesis. Emergent Mind. \ A topic overview, last updated 4 July 2026, that treats weights as structured data and organizes the field into understanding, representation, and generation. It covers applications like model retrieval and continual learning, plus issues like parameter symmetries, drawing on a 2026 survey by Han et al.

#9827. FBI Arrests Executive at Ransomware Negotiation Firm

Agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) on Thursday arrested an executive at a Canadian cybersecurity firm in connection with an investigation into the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently relieved the FBI of sensitive data on thousands of agents, multiple sources tell KrebsOnSecurity.

The New York Times reported today that the FBI has arrested a Canadian man in Pennsylvania on suspicion of assisting ShinyHunters. The Times story did not identify the man, nor did a statement on Twitter/X about the arrest from FBI Director Kash Patel.

One source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity the Canadian person arrested this week was visiting Pennsylvania for a cyber insurance conference, and that the suspect’s company specialized in handling ransomware negotiations with cybercrime groups. Another shared that control over the ShinyHunters investigation has been centralized at an FBI field office in Texas.

An online search reveals the Cyber Risk Summit was held at the Loews Philadelphia Hotel between Oct. 5 and Oct. 7. The conference had several sponsors, but according to the summit’s website its biggest sponsor was a Canadian security company called Cypfer.

According to LinkedIn, one of Cypfer’s “ex-founders” was Edward Dubrovsky, who is now associated with another Canadian security firm and sponsor called CyberSteward. In a post to LinkedIn approximately one month ago, Dubrovsky said he had plans to attend the Cyber Risk Summit with the rest of the CyberSteward team.

[Update: Oct. 10, 9:58 a.m. ET: A spokesperson for Cypfer said Dubrovsky was not a founder or co-founder as his LinkedIn profile claims, but instead served as a managing director before resigning in December 2025].

“Looking forward to continuing conversations around strategy & compliant driven coercive (ransomware, extortion) advisory, negotiations and settlement services that are global and truly agnostic,” Dubrovsky wrote.

Federal court records show that on October 8, an Edward Dobrovsky (note the slight misspelling of the last name) was arrested in Pennsylvania on cyber extortion and conspiracy charges. Several of those documents — including the core complaint — are now sealed. But a handful of them were indexed at Courtlistener.com, including a summary of the complaint, which charges the defendant with “conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money,” and “interference with commerce by threats.”

The inmate locator at the U.S. Bureau of Prisons website reports that a 54-year-old Edward Dubrovsky is currently being held at a federal facility in Philadelphia. But the court records indexed by CourtListener include a notice filed on October 9 that moved the case to the Eastern District of Texas, which sources say is now the epicenter of the FBI’s ShinyHunters investigation. The FBI declined to comment for this story.

Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile states he is the author of Cyber Extortion Strategic Response, a 252-page book that promises to “take readers beyond the ransom note and into the decisions that determine how an organization responds, recovers, and protects what matters.”

Edward Dubrovsky’s book, which centers on the intricacies of ransomware negotiations.

“At the heart of the book is a critical distinction: communicating with a criminal is not the same as negotiating a payment, and negotiating is not a commitment to pay,” reads an excerpt from the book’s listing on Amazon. “Engagement can serve other objectives, including testing claims, gathering information, creating time, and preserving options while the organization evaluates its next move.”

Mr. Dubrovsky could not be immediately reached for comment. KrebsOnSecurity also sought comment from other executives at CyberSteward, and will update this post in the event they respond. The available court records in Dubrovsky’s case show that he does not currently have an attorney and has yet to be appointed a public defender by the courts.

ShinyHunters typically uses phishing and stolen credentials to siphon data from corporate accounts at software-as-a-service companies, and then threatens to publish the stolen data online unless a ransom demand is paid. According to the FBI, the group has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

Sources tell KrebsOnSecurity the FBI has been poring over devices that were seized last month when the Dutch police arrested the convicted cybercriminal Pepijn van der Stap in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation, and that charges against principals at other companies that specialize in ransomware negotiation may be forthcoming.

Immediately after Van der Stap’s arrest, another member of ShinyHunters named “Rey” assumed control over the group and began taunting the FBI over data the group stole from the agency’s online recruitment portal, which included each’s person’s unit and specialization, as well as medical and psychiatric records.

Last week, Reuters reported that Rey — identified as a teenager named Saif Al-din Khader — had been detained and was cooperating with FBI investigators. On October 7, we detailed how Rey was apprehended as the cybercrime group allegedly sought to extort a navigation and digital aviation unit that was divested by Boeing in late 2025.

This is likely to be a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted along with timestamps.

This entry was posted on Friday 9th of October 2026 08:17 PM

The irony here is hard to miss. Arresting the *founder* rather than the negotiation firm itself is the detail that should worry operators the most. Individual accountability for running a negotiation service is essentially untested — the practice is legal in most jurisdictions as long as the customer is the victim of the incident rather than the perpetrator, and there’s no licensing or registration regime for it.

That gap means an arrest is a signal, not a fix. Expect more of these services to move offshore or rebrand under new ownership, and expect the tooling that makes them profitable (leak-site monitoring, initial-access-broker contact lists, automated follow-up) to keep scaling regardless of who gets charged.

The part I don’t see covered: how much of the value in this business is the *list* rather than the negotiation. If the negotiation contact itself is worth little to a criminal group — the customer already knows they’re breached — then arresting the negotiator mostly removes a service fee, not a capability. The durable asset is the broker/leak-site relationship feeding targets in.

We’ve been writing about the ransomware-as-a-service supply chain here, including recent coverage of negotiation-related arrests and the FBI’s warnings to other groups.

https://cyber.murati.net/posts/shinyhunters-leader-arrested-fbi-warns-others

The irony Stalyn noted is real, but the line Dubrovsky drew in his book is genuinely important for incident response work. Communicating with the threat actor to de-escalate or buy time during containment is a different thing from facilitating a payment, and IR teams live on that distinction every day. What this arrest will do regardless is chill the negotiation industry: firms will start asking counsel to review every engagement letter, and some will quietly exit the business. One practical takeaway for defenders: this is another reminder to treat your IR retainer and negotiation playbooks as legal-adjacent documents. Get your outside counsel involved in the ransomware response plan before you need it, not after the FBI shows up with questions about who said what on your behalf.

Well, Van der Stap also worked in the industry, doing offensive security while volunteering at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerable Disclosure, and it’s well-established that ShinyHunters actively sought to recruit insiders employed at key targets, particularly telecom providers (…while making it very clear they don’t target companies in Russia, Belarus, North Korea, and China… but sure, they are “purely financially motivated”).

Fully expecting that as the FBI and European authorities dig deeper, quite a few more people will be found actively playing both sides of the fence.

The line between ‘mediating’ an extortion attempt and actively facilitating a federal crime has always been razor-thin in this industry. If negotiators are taking a cut of the payout or coordinating directly with groups like ShinyHunters beyond strict incident response, it’s no longer advisory—it’s collusion. Expect cyber insurance carriers to drastically overhaul their IR vendor requirements after this.

There is an additional important question about the whole FBI leak affair that needs to be answered: Who in the FBI moved these sensitive personnel files to a server that could be penetrated by outsiders? My guess is that somebody in DOGE did it, in preparation for downloading the files to the DOGE network outside the FBI. This might also mean that private parties in the U.S. have had these files for a long time.

Perhaps the next administration will want to get to the bottom of this and punish the perpetrators, if any. The Trump administration most certainly will not.

The breached application is Oracle PeopleSoft — specifically, an unpatched vulnerability in its Environment Management Hub platform tracked as CVE-2026-35273. According to reports last week, the FBI removed an Accenture contractor that was responsible for keeping it updated.

Worth adding to the discussion of the FBI negotiation-company arrests: the practical gap most defenders have is not awareness of ShinyHunters, it is visibility into what the group actually does to get in.

Across the intrusions we have analyzed, the initial-access and exfiltration chain is unusually consistent and entirely built on commodity tooling:

– Remote access and support tools installed as a foothold (ScreenConnect, Screenovate, AnyDesk, Rclone) rather than exploiting a novel vulnerability. – Multi-week dwell times, so presence-based detection rarely triggers early. – Data staged out in chunks sized to stay under typical DLP alerting thresholds — a full customer or employee dataset rarely needs to leave in one transfer to be useful to the extortion side.

The practical consequence is that alerting on named malware is largely beside the point for this group; alerting on the *tools* and on small repetitive outbound flows is what actually catches the chain.

We covered the detection angle in more depth here: https://cyber.murati.net/posts/fbi-tells-shinyhunters-members-to-turn-themselves-in-after-recent-arrest

#9826. TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:

The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

#9825. Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws

Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

It comes down to basic Human Nature; biologically, we are still pretty much the same as our ancestors 0f 100,000 years ago. When the internet came along, what we did with it was pretty much what we did with nearly any new invention since then:

1. Get very excited about it 2. See if we could either: A. Stick it in our shorts B. See if it could be made a good weapon C. Amuse ourselves with it to the point of unconsciousness with it, or D. Enrich ourselves with it.

Unfortunately, ancient humans, when they picked up a rock, thought first about who they could bash over the head with it, not build a hospital.

I exaggerate a bit to make a point. We’ve come a little way since then, but that old hard-wiring is hard to erase. I imagine that, AI being made in our own image, will follow a similar course if not VERY strictly overseen.

Note: An old philosopher said that if we ever did produce something like an AI android, we would very shortly be very, very ashamed of ourselves.

I tend to disagree with the statement that the large number of CVE’s are placing strains on IT teams in terms of patch prioritization. That’s not the issue. For most vendors, Microsoft included, a single cumulative security update is issued, or a small handful for core products (Windows, Office, .Net). Whether those updates patch 100 or 10,000 individual CVE’s, the number of updates to test hasn’t really changed all that much. What HAS changed is the potential for the update to break things since more code is being modified with each update. Testing and deployment processes haven’t changed; it’s the monitoring for unexpected behavior during the testing phase that has become the pain point.

I agree. In my experience, for office workers, it’s low risk that patches will brake things. The factory floor is different. But even there, it’s not unusual to find PC’s running equipment not connected to the network due to the fact that they have to run proprietary software that won’t run on modern versions of Windows, or the PC-equipment interface is through a ISA or other legacy cards that modern versions of Windows do not support, and there is no way other than air-gapping to keep them secure. That’s why there are entire companies like NIXSYS (https://nixsys.com/) that build legacy computers using old CPU’s, old glue-chips & busses, and even old versions of Windows. No one junks a perfectly good but ancient CNC because it’s ancient PC died.

This was what I came here to say: it’s not the number of patches because everything gets rolled into one cumulative update. And Reguly is misinformed at best if he thinks IT teams can simply focus on the 26 most important updates – because we cannot select the 26 that are being exploited without also patching the CVEs that aren’t being exploited in the wild but for which the patch breaks, I don’t know, let’s say printing. If someone can make your mom stop, cry, and fork over a twenty to an animal shelter talking about puppies in a subway station, that is still a vulnerability of your mother, even if she is fortunate enough not to be approached on any one single given day of her daily commute.

#9824. MPS in PyTorch 2.15

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

#9823. U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering

The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.

The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”

The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.

“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”

As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.

Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.
